VAULT-102: Esther has come before the king without being summoned, which could cost her her life, to plead for the Jewish people. She faints instead. Artemisia was the most celebrated woman painter in seventeenth-century Italy, and she changed her mind as she worked here: a boy holding back a dog once stood between the two figures, and traces of him still show through the paint.
VAULT-129: Indian poetry and painting sort heroines into eight types by their situation in love. This is the abhisarika, the one who goes out to meet her lover and lets nothing stop her: not the dark, the storm, or the snakes underfoot. This version was painted at Kota, in Rajasthan, in the mid-1700s.
VAULT-106: Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionists and showed in seven of their eight exhibitions, more than most of the men the group is remembered for. She painted the private rooms that women of her class actually lived in, with brushwork looser than almost anyone's at the time.
VAULT-002: Homer made several trips to the Bahamas and worked this up from his sketches years later: a man alone on a dismasted boat, sharks circling, a waterspout behind him, and a ship on the horizon that may or may not have seen him. Viewers worried about the sailor so much that Homer wrote, with some sarcasm, that they could be told he gets rescued.
VAULT-143: Anna and Michael Ancher were married, both painters, and both at the centre of the artists' colony at Skagen, the fishing town at the northern tip of Denmark. They painted this one together. It shows the two of them at home at the end of the day, looking over a picture.
VAULT-003: Turner was about seventy when he painted his handful of whaling pictures. He seems to have hoped they would sell to Elhanan Bicknell, a collector who had made his money in whale oil. By this point Turner's ships, sea and sky were dissolving into one another, which baffled many critics.
VAULT-108: Cassatt was an American who spent her working life in Paris and showed with the Impressionists. The steep view from above and the clash of patterns come from Japanese woodblock prints, which she had studied at a big exhibition in Paris in 1890.
LIT-221: Shevchenko wrote this in December 1845, when he was seriously ill and thought he might die. He asks to be buried on a hill above the Dnieper. After his death in St Petersburg in 1861 his body was taken back to Ukraine and buried at just such a place. The poem is sung in Ukraine almost as a second anthem.
VAULT-161: Pamela Colman Smith drew all seventy-eight cards of what became the world's best-known tarot deck in a matter of months in 1909, working for the occultist A. E. Waite. She was paid a flat fee and got no royalties. For most of a century the deck carried his name and the publisher's but not hers. Her monogram is on every card.
VAULT-004: Made for Esigie, the king of Benin, in honour of his mother Idia, and worn at his hip during ceremonies. The row of tiny bearded heads across the top are Portuguese traders, who had recently arrived on the coast. It was taken from Benin City during the British military expedition of 1897.
VAULT-105: Bonheur went to the Paris horse market twice a week for a year and a half to sketch, and got a police permit to wear trousers so she could work there without being bothered. The finished canvas is about sixteen feet wide. Cornelius Vanderbilt bought it and gave it to the Met in 1887.
VAULT-111: Peeters was one of the very few women working as a professional painter in Flanders in the early 1600s, and one of the first anywhere to specialise in still life. Almost nothing is known about her life. In some paintings she hid tiny self-portraits in the reflections on cups and jugs.
VAULT-005: Number 43 of the eighty prints in Los Caprichos, Goya's attack on the superstition and foolishness of Spain in his day. He first planned it as the opening image. He pulled the series from sale soon after it was published in 1799, having sold only a couple of dozen sets.
VAULT-112: A joint effort: Michiel van Musscher painted the portrait, and Rachel Ruysch painted the flowers herself. She was the most successful flower painter in the Netherlands, worked into her eighties, raised ten children, and often sold for more than Rembrandt had.
VAULT-113: Merian raised caterpillars from the age of thirteen and painted insects on the plants they actually eat, with every life stage on one page. At the time plenty of educated people still thought insects grew out of mud. At fifty-two she sailed to Suriname with her daughter to study them in the rainforest.
VAULT-006: The Shahnama, or Book of Kings, is Persia's national epic, some fifty thousand couplets that Ferdowsi finished around the year 1010. Rustam is its great hero. This page comes from a small illustrated copy made about three hundred years later, when Mongol rulers of Iran were commissioning the old Persian stories for themselves.
VAULT-115: Ma Shouzhen was a famous courtesan in Nanjing, and also a poet, playwright and painter. Orchids were her signature subject. Her long attachment to the poet Wang Zhideng is part of the legend, and he wrote inscriptions on many of her paintings.
VAULT-146: Painted in Roman Egypt in coloured wax on a thin wooden panel, then bound over the face of the man's mummy. Around a thousand of these portraits survive. They are by far the largest group of painted portraits left from the ancient world.
VAULT-116: Kollwitz lived for fifty years in a working-class district of Berlin, where her husband was a doctor for the poor. Her younger son Peter was killed in the first months of the First World War. Mothers holding children, protecting them or mourning them, run through everything she made afterwards.
VAULT-007: One of the three large engravings Dürer made in 1513 and 1514 that are usually called his master prints, with Saint Jerome in His Study and Melencolia I. Every line was cut by hand into a copper plate. Nobody has settled who the knight is or whether we are meant to admire him.
VAULT-148: A wayang kulit puppet, cut from buffalo hide and mounted on horn rods. In performance a single puppeteer, the dalang, works every character and does every voice through the night, casting shadows on a lit screen. This is Bima, the strongest of the five Pandava brothers from the Mahabharata.
VAULT-103: The French Royal Academy capped its women members at four. Labille-Guiard got in on the same day in 1783 as her rival Vigée Le Brun. Two years later she showed this at the Salon: herself at the easel in a silk gown, with two students behind her. It was widely read as an argument for letting more women train.
VAULT-008: Filippo Negroli of Milan was the most admired armourer of the Renaissance. He hammered this helmet into shape from steel, in high relief, which is far harder than doing it in softer metal. It is signed and dated 1543. Armour like this was for parades and showing off, not for battle.
VAULT-104: Painted in 1789, the year the French Revolution began. Vigée Le Brun was Marie Antoinette's favourite portraitist, which made Paris dangerous for her. She left that October with her daughter and spent twelve years working her way around the courts of Europe.
VAULT-107: The woman reading is Morisot's sister Edma, who had trained as a painter alongside her and gave it up when she married. Morisot showed this at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, the only woman in the show.
LIT-229: From Akhmatova's first book, Evening, published in 1912 when she was twenty-two. The detail of the glove pulled onto the wrong hand made the poem famous in Russia almost at once.
VAULT-009: Van Gogh painted this in the summer of 1889 while living at the asylum in Saint-Rémy. He was fixated on cypresses, compared them to Egyptian obelisks, and was surprised nobody had painted them the way he saw them. He counted this among the best of his summer landscapes.
VAULT-109: Septeuil is a village west of Paris where Cassatt spent a summer, and Hélène was a child who lived there. Cassatt never married and had no children. Mothers and children became the subject she is best known for anyway.
VAULT-131: Kalighat paintings were sold as cheap souvenirs to pilgrims visiting the Kali temple in Calcutta in the nineteenth century. The painters worked fast on thin mill-made paper, with big sweeping outlines and almost no background. Modern Indian artists such as Jamini Roy later took the style as a starting point.
VAULT-110: Eva Gonzalès was the only formal pupil Édouard Manet ever took on. Unlike him she was accepted at the official Salon year after year. She died at thirty-four, shortly after giving birth, and less than a week after Manet himself.
VAULT-010: One of the last pictures Caravaggio painted, in the final months of his life. He had been on the run since killing a man in Rome in 1606. Peter, by the fire, is denying he ever knew Jesus. A maid is pointing him out to a soldier.
VAULT-114: Only two paintings by Margareta Haverman are known today. She studied with Jan van Huysum, a flower painter so secretive about his methods that he is said to have taken no other pupil. She was admitted to the French Royal Academy in 1722 and expelled not long after.
VAULT-133: Among the Bamana of Mali, Ci Wara is the half-antelope being who taught people to farm. Headdresses like this are worn on top of the head, always as a male and female pair, by young men who dance bent low over sticks in the fields to honour the best farmers.
LIT-224: Al-Mutanabbi is widely held to be the greatest poet in classical Arabic. He travelled from court to court writing poems in praise of rulers, and addressed this ode to Sayf al-Dawla of Aleppo. Its best-known line, a boast about the steed, the night and the desert, comes later in the ode than the opening shown here. By tradition a servant quoted that line back to him when he was attacked on the road in 965, and he turned to fight and was killed.
VAULT-117: Bonheur was the most famous animal painter of the nineteenth century and the first woman artist to be given the French Legion of Honour. She kept a private menagerie at her château near Fontainebleau that at various times included lions.
VAULT-012: Henry VIII set up the royal workshops at Greenwich and staffed them with German and Flemish armourers so he would not have to import the best work. A garniture is a suit with swappable parts for war and for the tournament. This one is etched and gilded all over, and the designs are attributed to Hans Holbein.
VAULT-118: Joan of Arc in her parents' garden at Domrémy, hearing the voices that tell her to go and save France. The saints float behind her in the trees. Bastien-Lepage came from the same region, Lorraine. France had just lost part of it to Germany in the war of 1870, and Joan was everywhere as a national symbol.
VAULT-119: Virginie Gautreau was an American-born Paris socialite famous for her looks. When Sargent showed this at the 1884 Salon, one jewelled strap had slipped off her shoulder. The scandal was bad enough that he repainted the strap and moved to London. He kept the painting for thirty years, then sold it to the Met and said it was probably the best thing he had done.
VAULT-013: Athens sentenced Socrates to death in 399 BCE for corrupting the young and disrespecting the gods. He could have fled and chose the hemlock instead. David took liberties. The old man slumped at the foot of the bed is Plato, who was young at the time and not actually there.
VAULT-120: In Jewish legend Lilith was Adam's first wife, who refused to obey him and left. Rossetti shows her as a modern woman combing her hair at a mirror. This is the watercolour version he painted after the oil, and it keeps the face of his first model, Fanny Cornforth, which he later painted out of the bigger canvas.
LIT-231: Alfonsina Storni was born in Switzerland and grew up in Argentina. She raised a son alone and earned her living as a teacher and journalist in Buenos Aires. This poem, from 1918, is addressed to men who demand a purity in women that they do not keep themselves.
VAULT-121: Fragonard was the great painter of flirtation and pleasure in pre-revolutionary France. Who the woman is, and what the note in her bouquet says, has been argued over for a long time. The Revolution wiped out his clients, and he died in 1806 more or less forgotten.
VAULT-039: One of seven tapestries showing the hunt of the unicorn, woven in wool, silk and metal thread. Nobody knows for certain who ordered them or what the knotted letters A and E in every panel stand for. John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought the set in the 1920s and gave it to the Met's Cloisters.
VAULT-122: For the first half of his career Redon worked almost entirely in black: charcoal drawings and lithographs of floating eyes and smiling spiders that he called his noirs. Colour only took over in his fifties. Pandora, the first woman in Greek myth, stands here with the box she has not yet opened.
VAULT-144: The room is in Hammershøi's own apartment at Strandgade 30 in Copenhagen. He painted its doors, windows and bare floors dozens of times, sometimes with his wife Ida seen from behind, often, as here, with nobody at all.
VAULT-123: Okita was a real person, a waitress at the Naniwaya teahouse near the Asakusa temple in Edo, and one of the most talked-about beauties of the 1790s. Prints like this were the pin-ups of their day. When the government banned putting such women's names on prints, artists switched to picture-puzzles that spelled them out.
VAULT-040: A lamassu stood guard at a gateway in the palace of the Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud, in what is now northern Iraq. It has five legs. From the front it stands firm, and from the side it strides forward.
LIT-225: Gibran was born in Lebanon, emigrated to the United States as a boy, and wrote The Prophet in English in New York. It was published in 1923 and has never been out of print. It has been translated into more than a hundred languages.
VAULT-147: The last of Rustam's seven trials in the Shahnama. He tracks the White Demon to its cave and kills it to free the foolish king Kay Kavus, who has been captured and blinded. The demon's blood restores the king's sight.
VAULT-046: Cornelis was one of a small group of painters in Haarlem who loved twisting, muscular nudes above everything else, and the myth of the Titans being thrown out of heaven gave him an excuse to paint dozens of them. The butterflies and dragonflies are placed to serve as fig leaves.
VAULT-149: An amo is one of the two carved posts at the front of a Māori meeting house, holding up the sloping boards of the gable. The house as a whole stands for the body of an ancestor, and the figures carved on it are named forebears of the people it belongs to.
VAULT-047: Tom Sharkey's Athletic Club was across the street from Bellows's studio in New York. Public prizefighting was illegal in the state at the time, so clubs got around it by making the boxers members for the night. Bellows painted it in fast, slashing strokes.
VAULT-126: Jeong Seon changed Korean painting by going outside and painting real Korean mountains, where earlier artists had painted imagined Chinese ones. The approach is called true-view landscape. Inwangsan is a granite peak in Seoul, near where he lived for most of his life.
VAULT-048: Painted in Naples for the Spanish viceroy, who took it home to Spain. In the legend Andrew preached from the cross for two days and asked not to be taken down. When the executioners tried to untie him, their arms froze. Caravaggio paints that moment.
VAULT-134: Shevchenko is Ukraine's national poet. He was born a serf, and his freedom was bought in 1838 by artists and writers who had seen his talent. This painting illustrates his own poem about a Ukrainian village girl seduced and abandoned by a Russian officer.
VAULT-049: Church built this sunset in his New York studio from sketches made in Maine. He finished it in 1860, months before the Civil War began, and people have read the blood-red sky as a warning ever since. There is not a single person in it.
VAULT-051: Shiva dances the universe into and out of existence inside a ring of fire. One hand holds the drum of creation, another the flame of destruction, and his foot is planted on the dwarf of ignorance. Bronzes like this were cast in southern India under the Chola kings and carried through the streets on festival days.
VAULT-150: Hei tiki are carved from pounamu, the New Zealand greenstone, which is hard enough that before metal tools it had to be ground into shape with sandstone, grit and water. They are heirlooms. Each one is passed down and is felt to gather the standing of everyone who has worn it.
VAULT-055: Homer spent the best part of two years in an English fishing village, Cullercoats, and his work changed there. Afterwards he settled on the coast of Maine and painted people who work on the sea. Here two fishermen haul a net of herring into a dory while the fleet fades into the fog behind them.
VAULT-056: Seurat spent two years on this, with dozens of sketches and studies, building the picture from small touches of unmixed colour that blend in the eye. It is about two metres by three. He showed it at the last Impressionist exhibition in 1886, when he was twenty-six, and died five years later.
LIT-226: Elias Lönnrot was a country doctor who walked through Finland and Karelia writing down songs from traditional singers. He arranged them into one long epic, published in 1835 and expanded in 1849. It became the national poem of Finland. In this section the old singer Väinämöinen makes a harp from the bones of a pike.
VAULT-057: Van Gogh's bedroom in the Yellow House in Arles. He painted it three times. This is the second version, made a year later in the asylum at Saint-Rémy after the first was damaged by damp. He wanted the colours alone to suggest rest.
VAULT-130: The same heroine as the Chicago painting: the woman who sets out at night to meet her lover. She comes from a list of eight types of women in love that goes back to an ancient Sanskrit handbook on drama. Painters in the small hill courts of the Himalayan foothills returned to these types again and again.
VAULT-064: A huge hand holds a lump of raw stone, and Adam and Eve are just starting to come out of it. God is shown as a sculptor. Rodin himself modelled in clay and plaster and left the marble carving to skilled assistants, which was normal practice and something he never hid.
VAULT-069: A Sicilian nobleman, Antonio Ruffo, ordered a painting from Rembrandt and left the subject up to him. He got Aristotle, in a gold chain, resting his hand on a bust of the blind poet Homer. The medallion on the chain shows Alexander the Great, Aristotle's pupil. When the Met bought it in 1961, it was the most expensive painting ever sold.
VAULT-070: Only about three dozen paintings by Vermeer survive. This was the first to reach America, given to the Met in 1889. A woman opens a window with one hand and holds a water pitcher with the other.
VAULT-071: Monet painted his water garden at Giverny for the last thirty years of his life, the canvases growing larger as his eyesight got worse. This is one panel of a three-part work nearly thirteen metres wide. The other two are in museums in St. Louis and Kansas City.
VAULT-153: A siphonophore looks like one animal and is actually a colony of many small ones, each with a single job, strung together and working as a body. Haeckel described thousands of sea creatures new to science. He drew them accurately, then arranged them on the page like ornaments.
VAULT-073: One of a series on the seasons that Bruegel painted in 1565 for the dining room of an Antwerp merchant. Five survive, and this is the only one outside Europe. It is late summer. Some people are cutting wheat, and some have stopped for lunch and a nap under a pear tree.
VAULT-072: Monet spent several months of 1882 at Pourville, a small fishing village on the Normandy coast, and came away with around a hundred canvases of its cliffs and beaches. He often worked on several at once, switching as the light changed.
LIT-227: Lermontov began The Demon at fourteen and kept rewriting it for ten years. The censors would not allow it to be printed in Russia, and it circulated in handwritten copies. He was killed in a duel in 1841, at twenty-six, and the poem was first published abroad.
VAULT-156: Vredeman de Vries was a Dutch designer who was obsessed with perspective. He published a manual on it in 1604 that artists and architects went on using for generations. Most of the buildings he drew were never meant to exist anywhere but on paper.
VAULT-074: One of only two pure landscapes El Greco is known to have painted. It is not an accurate view. He moved the cathedral and other buildings from their real positions and set the city under a storm sky.
VAULT-075: Cézanne painted five versions of men playing cards, using farmworkers from his family's estate near Aix as models. This is one of the larger ones. In 2011 another of the five was reportedly sold to the royal family of Qatar for more than 250 million dollars, the highest price then known for a painting.
VAULT-160: Ethiopia has been Christian since the fourth century, and its monasteries have been making books like this ever since. The text is written on parchment in Ge'ez, the old church language. Lake Tana, in the northern highlands, is dotted with island monasteries that kept their libraries safe for centuries.
VAULT-077: Painted for the opera singer Jean-Baptiste Faure, one of the first people to collect Degas seriously. The old man with the stick is Jules Perrot, a famous ballet master. The room is invented. Degas set it in the old Paris Opera house, which had burned down the year before.
LIT-444: Sei Shōnagon was a lady-in-waiting to the empress of Japan around the year 1000. The Pillow Book is her collection of lists, anecdotes and sharp opinions about court life. By her own account it began when the empress gave her a bundle of spare paper.
VAULT-076: Cézanne worked so slowly on his still lifes that the fruit sometimes rotted before he was done. Apples were his favourite because they kept. This painting once belonged to Claude Monet.
VAULT-078: Manet painted this in the summer of 1874 at Argenteuil, on the Seine outside Paris, where he was working alongside Monet and Renoir. The flat blue water with no horizon comes from Japanese prints. Mary Cassatt talked her American friends the Havemeyers into buying it.
VAULT-079: The first big canvas Gauguin painted after arriving in Tahiti in 1891. Mary and the child Jesus are Tahitian, and so is the angel hidden in the bushes. The two women with their hands together are borrowed from a photograph he owned of carvings on a Buddhist temple in Java.
VAULT-080: Rousseau worked as a toll collector on the edge of Paris and taught himself to paint. He never left France. His jungles come from the hothouses of the Paris botanical garden, the zoo, and pictures in books and magazines.
LIT-228: Pushkin wrote this in 1826, shortly after five leaders of a failed uprising against the tsar, some of them his friends, were hanged. It is based on the vision of the prophet in chapter six of the Book of Isaiah.
VAULT-081: Georges de La Tour was successful in his lifetime, then so thoroughly forgotten that his paintings were credited to other people for nearly three hundred years. A German scholar pieced his career back together in 1915. Nearly all his best pictures are lit by a single candle.
VAULT-082: A study in chalk for the face of Mary in The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne, the painting now in the Louvre that Leonardo worked on for years and never delivered. He blurred the edges with his fingers until the face seems to come out of smoke.
VAULT-167: A tughra is the official signature of an Ottoman sultan, drawn at the top of his decrees by a court calligrapher. It spells out the sultan's name, his father's name and the phrase 'ever victorious'. Each sultan had his own.
VAULT-083: A page of red chalk studies for the Libyan Sibyl on the Sistine Chapel ceiling. The sibyl is a woman, but the model was plainly a young man, probably one of Michelangelo's assistants. He redrew the left foot and its big toe several times to work out how it carries the weight.
LIT-458: Mirabai was a Rajput princess of the sixteenth century who gave herself to the worship of Krishna and refused the life expected of a royal widow. Her songs are still sung across northern India. Max Macauliffe was an Irish official in the Punjab who translated them for his history of the Sikh religion.
VAULT-084: Raphael was about twenty-one when he painted this for a convent in Perugia. The nuns are said to have asked that the baby Jesus be fully clothed. The banker J. P. Morgan bought it in 1901 for what was then the highest price ever paid for a painting.
VAULT-085: Painted for Francesco del Pugliese, a rich Florentine wool merchant and a follower of Savonarola, the friar who briefly turned the city against its own luxuries. The story is that Jerome, dying, got up from his bed to take communion one last time.
VAULT-086: Cranach was court painter to the rulers of Saxony and a close friend of Martin Luther. His workshop turned out Judiths by the dozen. She is always dressed in the latest fashion of the Saxon court, with the general's head in front of her.
VAULT-087: Painted for Cardinal del Monte, Caravaggio's first important patron, who took the young painter into his household in Rome. The boy second from the right, looking out at us, is generally thought to be Caravaggio himself.
LIT-230: José Martí led the movement for Cuban independence from Spain and spent much of his adult life in exile in New York, where these verses were published in 1891. He was killed in battle in Cuba in 1895. Lines from this poem were later set to the tune of the song Guantanamera.
VAULT-088: Rubens more or less invented the large-scale hunting picture, and this is one of the first he painted. He ran a big workshop in Antwerp, where assistants and specialists worked up his designs and he finished the parts that mattered.
VAULT-089: Not a portrait in the usual sense. The Dutch called this kind of picture a tronie: a study of a face or an expression, painted for its own sake and sold on the open market. It is a close cousin of Girl with a Pearl Earring.
VAULT-091: Thomas Cole founded what became known as the Hudson River School. This is a bend in the Connecticut River, with wild forest and a storm on the left and sunlit farmland on the right. Cole painted himself into it, at his easel, near the bottom centre.
VAULT-092: Bingham grew up in Missouri and painted life on its rivers. His own first title for this identified the pair as a French trader and his son, whose mother was Native American. What the animal chained to the front of the canoe is has been argued about for a long time. A bear cub is the usual answer.
VAULT-093: Bierstadt went west with a government survey party in 1859 and built this in his New York studio from the sketches. He named the peak after the expedition's leader, Frederick Lander, who had since died in the Civil War. It sold in 1865 for 25,000 dollars, a record at the time for an American painting.
VAULT-094: Courbet had a nude turned down by the Paris Salon in 1864 as indecent. Two years later he sent this, and it was accepted, though critics still complained about the tangled hair and the clothes left on the floor. Manet painted his own woman with a parrot the same year, fully dressed.
LIT-499: A poem by Alfonsina Storni, shown in Alice Stone Blackwell's prose translation. Blackwell was an American campaigner for women's right to vote. She also translated poetry from Armenian, Russian and Yiddish, and published an anthology of Spanish-American poets in 1929.
VAULT-090: A woman tunes her lute and looks out of the window, as if waiting for someone. The map behind her shows Europe. The paint has worn thin over the centuries, which is part of why the picture looks so soft.
VAULT-095: Manet's first success. It won an honourable mention at the Salon of 1861, when he was twenty-nine. Sharp-eyed viewers noticed that the model is left-handed and the guitar is strung for a right-handed player, so he could not actually have been playing it.
VAULT-096: The only sculpture Degas ever exhibited. The original, shown in 1881, was wax, with a real fabric tutu, a real ribbon and real hair, and critics found it ugly and disturbing. The model was Marie van Goethem, a student at the Paris Opera ballet school. The bronzes were cast after his death.
VAULT-097: In 1897 an eye infection kept Pissarro from working outdoors. He took a hotel room above the Boulevard Montmartre in Paris and painted the street below more than a dozen times, in rain, snow, sun and at night.
VAULT-098: Toulouse-Lautrec's first poster. It went up all over Paris in 1891 and made him famous more or less overnight. The dancer is Louise Weber, known as La Goulue, 'the glutton'. The silhouette in front is her partner, Valentin the Boneless.
VAULT-099: Mäda was nine. Her father, Otto Primavesi, was a banker and the main financial backer of the Vienna design workshops Klimt was close to. Klimt made a string of pencil sketches to work out the pose before settling on this one: feet apart, looking straight at you.
VAULT-100: From the same series as the Great Wave. In late summer and early autumn, the rising sun can turn Mount Fuji red for a few minutes, and that is the moment Hokusai shows. The earliest printings are much paler, and collectors call them Pink Fuji.
LIT-232: The narrator of this novel is dead and writing from the grave. He dedicates the book to the first worm that gnawed his corpse. Machado de Assis was the grandson of freed slaves, taught himself several languages, and became the first president of the Brazilian Academy of Letters.
VAULT-101: From One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, the series Hiroshige was still working on when he died in 1858. The rain is printed as hundreds of fine black lines, which was very hard to cut into a woodblock. Van Gogh copied this print in oils.
LIT-233: Rubén Darío, from Nicaragua, led the movement that renewed poetry in Spanish at the end of the nineteenth century. This short poem closes his 1905 book Songs of Life and Hope.
VAULT-193: The Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493 is a history of the world from Creation to its own day, with more than eighteen hundred woodcut pictures. It was the most heavily illustrated book yet printed. The teenage Albrecht Dürer was an apprentice in the workshop that made the woodcuts.
LIT-234: A traditional Māori chant for hauling a canoe. Tainui is one of the great voyaging canoes that, in tradition, brought the ancestors of Māori to Aotearoa. Chants like this were handed down by word of mouth and have no single author or date.
LIT-068: Christina Rossetti wrote this sonnet in 1849, while still in her teens. It was published in 1862 in her first collection, Goblin Market and Other Poems.
LIT-235: About seven thousand pages of Leonardo's notes survive, covering painting, anatomy, engineering, water, flight and much else. He wrote them from right to left in mirror script. None of it was published in his lifetime.
LIT-073: Sappho's poems filled nine books in the ancient world. One complete poem and a few hundred fragments are left. This one survives because a later writer on verse metre quoted it as an example. He did not name the author, and some scholars doubt it is hers.
LIT-236: Leonardo planned a book on painting and never finished it. After his death his pupil and heir Francesco Melzi put this one together from the notebooks. It was first printed in Paris in 1651.
VAULT-228: Robert Fludd was an English physician who tried to fit all of nature, medicine, music and religion into a single system. His huge book on the 'two worlds' was published in Germany from 1617. The engravings were made by Matthäus Merian, whose daughter was the naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian.
VAULT-230: Athanasius Kircher was a Jesuit scholar in Rome who wrote on everything from volcanoes to Egyptian hieroglyphs. This map from his book on the underground world, first published in the 1660s, shows Atlantis as a real island in the Atlantic, between Spain and America. South is at the top.
VAULT-232: Johannes Hevelius was a brewer and city councillor in Danzig who built an observatory across the roofs of his houses. His star atlas was published in 1690, three years after his death, by his wife Elisabeth, who had observed alongside him for years. Several constellations he introduced are still in use.
LIT-056: Dickinson copied many of her poems onto folded sheets and sewed them into small booklets, forty in all. They were found after her death. She gave her poems no titles, so they are known by their first lines and by the numbers editors have assigned.
LIT-237: Michelangelo wrote about three hundred poems, most of them in his sixties and seventies. This sonnet was written for his friend Vittoria Colonna. It sets out his idea that the sculptor's figure is already inside the block of marble, and the work is to remove what covers it.
LIT-094: Wuthering Heights is Emily Brontë's only novel. It came out in 1847 under the name Ellis Bell, and most early reviewers found it brutal. She died the following year, at thirty.
LIT-238: A comic sonnet Michelangelo wrote while painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. He complains to a friend about what the work is doing to his body: his neck bent back, his beard pointing at heaven, paint dripping in his face. In the margin he drew a little figure of himself reaching up to paint.
LIT-095: Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell. It was a success at once, and readers argued over whether the author was a man or a woman. This is from the chapter in which Rochester proposes.
LIT-239: Hokusai wrote this in 1834 at the back of the first volume of his One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji. In it he gives his age as seventy-five. He signed it with the name he was then using, which means the old man mad about painting. He died in 1849.
VAULT-273: Kūya was a tenth-century monk who walked the roads of Japan beating a gong and chanting the name of the Buddha Amida. The six small figures coming from his mouth are the six syllables of the chant. The sculptor, Kōshō, was a son of the great Unkei. The statue is in the Rokuharamitsu-ji temple in Kyoto.
LIT-074: This fragment survives because a Greek critic, writing centuries after Sappho, quoted it in a book on greatness in writing. The Roman poet Catullus made a famous version of it in Latin.
VAULT-282: Tao Yuanming was a poet who gave up a government post around the year 405 and went home to farm, drink and write. Chen Hongshou painted this in 1650 for a friend who had just accepted office under the new Qing dynasty. It is generally read as a hint.
LIT-240: From The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, which Blake wrote, etched and printed himself in the early 1790s. He presents the proverbs as sayings he collected while walking among the fires of Hell.
LIT-057: In her later years Dickinson rarely left her family's house in Amherst, Massachusetts. Her first editors smoothed out her dashes, capitals and rhymes. An edition that printed the poems as she wrote them did not appear until 1955.
LIT-241: More than 650 of Van Gogh's letters to his brother Theo survive. Theo died six months after Vincent. It was Theo's widow, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, who kept the letters, put them in order and published them in 1914.
LIT-096: Gilman based this story on her own experience. After the birth of her daughter she was prescribed a 'rest cure' by a leading doctor: bed, isolation and no writing. She said it nearly drove her out of her mind, and that she sent him a copy of the story.
LIT-242: Delacroix kept a journal as a young man and again from 1847 until his death in 1863. He used it to think through painting, music, books and the people he met. It was published thirty years after he died.
LIT-118: The Pillow Book opens with a list of the best time of day in each season. The longer passage here is in the translation by William George Aston, a British diplomat in Japan and one of the first Western scholars of the language. It appeared in 1899 in his history of Japanese literature.
LIT-058: Dickinson wrote this around 1872. Like nearly all her poems it was not published in her lifetime. It was first printed in 1945.
LIT-245: In 1903 Franz Kappus, a nineteen-year-old cadet at a military academy, sent Rilke his poems and asked for an opinion. Rilke, who was twenty-seven, answered with the first of ten letters. Kappus published them in 1929, three years after Rilke's death.
LIT-159: Sojourner Truth was born into slavery in New York and escaped in 1826. She gave this speech at a women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio, in 1851. The words shown here come from the report Marius Robinson printed in the Anti-Slavery Bugle a few weeks later. The better-known version, with its repeated question and Southern dialect, was published twelve years later by Frances Gage, who had presided at the convention.
LIT-246: Okakura Kakuzō wrote The Book of Tea in English, in 1906, while working at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. He used the tea ceremony to explain Japanese ideas of art and living to Western readers.
LIT-168: In August 1588, during the Armada campaign, Elizabeth went to Tilbury on the Thames to address the army gathered to resist a Spanish invasion. The text comes from a letter written about thirty-five years later by a chaplain who had been present.
VAULT-378: Elizabeth Siddal is best known as the model for Millais's Ophelia and as the wife of Dante Gabriel Rossetti. She also drew, painted and wrote poetry, and the critic John Ruskin paid her a yearly sum for her work. She died in 1862 at thirty-two.
LIT-247: A collection of advice on conduct, presented as the words of an old Egyptian vizier to his son. Ptahhotep served a king of the Fifth Dynasty, though the text as we have it was written down several centuries later. The longer passage is in Battiscombe Gunn's translation of 1906.
VAULT-385: Carlos Schwabe was a German-born Swiss artist who worked in Paris and was known for his book illustrations. Here Death comes for an old gravedigger in the form of a young woman with long green wings. It is a watercolour, in the collection of the Musée d'Orsay.
LIT-171: From the speech Emmeline Pankhurst made to the magistrate at Bow Street police court in London in October 1908. She was on trial for a handbill urging a crowd to rush the House of Commons, and was sent to prison. She printed the speech in her memoir, My Own Story.
LIT-248: Diogenes lived in Athens in the fourth century BCE, in a large storage jar, owning almost nothing. Nothing he wrote survives. What we have are stories about him, collected about five hundred years later by a writer who happened to share his name.
VAULT-402: Mucha was an unknown Czech illustrator in Paris until the end of 1894, when he designed a poster for the actress Sarah Bernhardt at short notice. She signed him to a six-year contract. This one shows her as Medea, who has just killed her children. A jeweller later made the snake bracelet for Bernhardt to wear.
VAULT-405: Bilibin illustrated a series of Russian fairy tales between 1899 and 1902, drawing on folk embroidery, wood carving and old prints. Baba Yaga is the witch of the forest, who travels in a mortar and steers with a pestle. Bilibin died in 1942 during the siege of Leningrad.
LIT-172: Lucy Parsons was a labour organiser and anarchist in Chicago for more than fifty years. She was probably born into slavery. She wrote this in 1884 for the first issue of a radical newspaper, addressing the unemployed men then walking the city's streets.
VAULT-406: Sofonisba Anguissola painted three of her younger sisters at chess when she was in her early twenties. Their father, a nobleman in Cremona, had all his daughters educated like sons. She became a painter at the Spanish court and lived to be about ninety. The painting is in Poznań, in Poland.
LIT-249: Epictetus was born a slave and was lame for most of his life. Once freed, he taught philosophy in Rome and then in Greece. He wrote nothing down. His student Arrian recorded his talks and boiled them down into this short handbook.
VAULT-415: Goncharova was a leader of the Russian avant-garde before the First World War. The repeated outlines of the rider and wheels show movement, an idea taken from Italian Futurism, and the shop signs behind him are in Cyrillic. She left Russia and spent the rest of her life in Paris, designing for the ballet. The painting is in the Russian Museum in St Petersburg.
VAULT-416: Suzanne Valadon began as an artists' model in Montmartre and posed for Renoir and Toulouse-Lautrec. She taught herself to draw, and Degas bought her work and encouraged her. Here a woman in striped trousers lies on a bed, smoking, with books at her feet. It is in the Centre Pompidou in Paris.
LIT-180: Susan B. Anthony voted in the presidential election of 1872 in Rochester, New York, and was arrested for it. Before her trial she gave this speech in every district of the county. The judge directed the jury to find her guilty and fined her a hundred dollars, which she never paid.
VAULT-420: Katsushika Ōi was Hokusai's daughter. She worked alongside him for the last twenty years of his life, and it is not known how much of his late work is partly hers. Only about ten paintings can be securely given to her. This one, with its strong lantern light and deep shadow, is in the Ōta Memorial Museum in Tokyo.
LIT-250: Seneca wrote these letters in the last three years of his life, after withdrawing from the court of the emperor Nero, whose tutor and adviser he had been. They are addressed to a younger friend, Lucilius. In 65 CE Nero ordered him to take his own life.
LIT-191: From A Few Figs from Thistles, published in 1920, which made Millay the voice of a younger generation in Greenwich Village. Three years later she won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry.
LIT-251: Erasmus said he wrote In Praise of Folly in about a week in 1509, while staying at the London house of his friend Thomas More. The Latin title puns on More's name. Folly herself delivers the speech, and churchmen and scholars are among her targets.
LIT-193: Elizabeth Barrett wrote these sonnets in secret while Robert Browning was courting her, and showed them to him only after they were married. 'The Portuguese' was his pet name for her. The title let the poems pass as translations.
LIT-252: Montaigne retired at thirty-eight to the tower of his family house near Bordeaux and spent the next twenty years writing about himself. He called the pieces essais, meaning attempts, which is where the word essay comes from. This is from the last one, on experience.
LIT-194: An oread is a mountain nymph in Greek myth. This six-line poem, published in 1914, became the standard example of Imagism, the movement for short, hard, exact poems. Hilda Doolittle signed her work H.D., on Ezra Pound's suggestion.
LIT-253: Bacon published ten essays in 1597 and kept adding to them until there were fifty-eight in 1625. He was a lawyer who rose to be Lord Chancellor of England, and lost the office in 1621 after admitting to taking bribes.
VAULT-466: From the Sanskrit play by Kalidasa. Shakuntala pretends to pull a thorn from her foot so that she can look back at the king she has fallen in love with. Ravi Varma painted Indian subjects in European oil technique. In 1894 he set up a printing press, and cheap colour prints of his gods and heroines reached homes all over India.
LIT-195: Amy Lowell came from a prominent Boston family and became the chief organiser and promoter of the Imagist poets in America. Patterns, published in 1915, is spoken by an eighteenth-century woman who has just learned her fiancé has been killed in war.
LIT-254: Baltasar Gracián was a Spanish Jesuit. This book of three hundred maxims on how to get on in the world appeared in 1647. He published without his order's permission and was eventually disciplined for it. The philosopher Schopenhauer admired the book enough to translate it into German.
LIT-192: A sonnet first published in 1920 and collected in 1923. Millay wrote in strict traditional forms about subjects, especially women's desire, that were new to them.
LIT-255: La Rochefoucauld was a French duke who spent his youth in plots and civil wars and was shot in the face in one of them. He retired to the drawing rooms of Paris, where maxims were polished as a kind of game. His were published in 1665 and revised through five editions.
LIT-196: Persuasion was the last novel Jane Austen finished. It was published a few months after her death in 1817. She was unhappy with her first ending and rewrote it, adding the letter this passage comes from. The discarded chapters are the only manuscript pages of her published novels to survive.
VAULT-502: Ryder said this came from something that happened to a waiter he knew, who bet his savings on a horse race, lost, and killed himself. He worked on the picture for years. Ryder piled up paint and varnish in ways that have not lasted well, and many of his paintings have darkened and cracked. This one is in Cleveland.
VAULT-021: Song Xu was a Ming dynasty painter known for pictures of real, named places. This leaf comes from an album of famous scenic spots in and around the city of Wuxing, now Huzhou, south of Lake Tai. He later became a Buddhist monk.
VAULT-011: The third of Dürer's three master engravings. A winged figure sits doing nothing, surrounded by the tools of geometry and building. On the wall is a square of numbers in which every row, column and diagonal adds up to 34. The two middle numbers of the bottom row give the date, 1514.
VAULT-019: Early in the Shahnama the young hero Rustam needs a horse strong enough to carry him. He tests each one by pressing down on its back, and they all buckle until he comes to the colt Rakhsh. This page was painted in India, where Persian was the language of the Muslim courts.
LIT-256: Chamfort was a celebrated wit in Paris before the Revolution, and supported it when it came. During the Terror he was threatened with a second arrest, and died in 1794 of injuries from an attempt to kill himself. A friend published the notes he left behind.
VAULT-017: On Benin plaques, size shows rank. The war chief in the centre is the largest figure and his attendants get smaller with their importance. Much of the brass came from bracelets that Portuguese merchants brought in huge quantities to trade.
VAULT-015: Leutze painted this in Germany in 1851, using the Rhine as his model for the Delaware. He hoped the example of the American Revolution would encourage German reformers after the failed uprisings of 1848. The flag shown had not yet been designed in 1776. The canvas is more than six metres wide.
VAULT-050: Sesson was a Zen monk who spent his life in the remote northeast of Japan, far from the art centres of Kyoto, and learned largely by studying Chinese paintings. The dragon and the tiger are an old pairing. The dragon brings clouds and rain, and the tiger brings the wind.
VAULT-014: Made for Henry VIII around 1544, near the end of his life, when he led his last campaign against France in person. He was in his fifties, very heavy and in poor health, and the armour is built to his size. It was made in Italy.
VAULT-026: The last of Rustam's seven trials in the Shahnama, the Persian Book of Kings. He tracks the White Demon to its cave and kills it to free the captured king. This page comes from a small illustrated copy made in Iran in the 1330s, more than three hundred years after Ferdowsi finished the poem.
VAULT-042: Moche potters on the north coast of Peru often showed warriors with the features of animals. The owl, a hunter that works at night, appears again and again in scenes of battle and sacrifice. The Moche left no writing, so their pottery is the main record of what they believed.
VAULT-044: In 1878 Muybridge set up a row of cameras along a racetrack in California, each one tripped by a thread as the horse ran past. The photographs settled an old argument by showing that a galloping horse does lift all four feet off the ground at once. This album of 1881 collects the results.
LIT-197: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. Middlemarch came out in eight parts between 1871 and 1872. This is from the closing pages, where she tells what became of each character.
VAULT-052: Hevajra is a deity of Tantric Buddhism, shown with eight heads and sixteen arms, dancing. This bronze was made around 1200 in what is now northeastern Thailand, then part of the Khmer empire of Angkor, under a king who had made Buddhism the state religion.
VAULT-016: Canova's first version of this was bought by the Pope to stand in the Vatican in place of an ancient statue that Napoleon had carried off to Paris. This is the second version, carved for a Polish countess. Perseus holds up the head of Medusa, whose gaze turned people to stone.
VAULT-034: Made in eastern Iran or Central Asia in the tenth century. The only decoration is a line of Arabic in an angular script around the rim, usually a proverb or a blessing for the owner. Bowls like this are among the earliest ceramics anywhere to be decorated with writing alone.
VAULT-062: Posada made thousands of pictures for a publisher of cheap news sheets and songbooks in Mexico City. His calaveras, skeletons going about everyday life, illustrated comic verses printed for the Day of the Dead. He died poor in 1913 and was buried in a common grave. Mexican artists rediscovered his work in the 1920s.
VAULT-045: From Animal Locomotion, published in 1887: 781 plates of people and animals in motion, photographed by Muybridge at the University of Pennsylvania with banks of cameras firing in sequence. He also built a device to project such sequences as moving pictures, a step towards cinema.
VAULT-067: A stencil for dyeing patterns onto kimono cloth. It is cut by hand from sheets of mulberry paper glued together and toughened with persimmon juice. The trade was centred on the Ise region of Japan. Stencils like this were collected in Europe in the late 1800s and influenced Art Nouveau design.
VAULT-018: Juan de Pareja was enslaved in Velázquez's household and worked as his studio assistant. Velázquez painted him in Rome in 1650 and exhibited the portrait publicly, to great praise. He signed papers to free Pareja a few months later. Pareja became a painter in his own right. The portrait is in the Metropolitan Museum.
VAULT-035: The official monogram of Suleiman the Magnificent, who ruled the Ottoman Empire from 1520 to 1566. A calligrapher drew the lines, and painters from the court workshop filled the loops with spiralling stems and tiny flowers in blue and gold. It headed a state document.
VAULT-068: Ōtsu-e were cheap folk paintings sold to travellers at the town of Ōtsu, on the main road into Kyoto. This is one of the standard subjects: a demon dressed up as a begging monk. It poked fun at religious hypocrisy. People also hung it up in the belief that it stopped babies crying at night.
VAULT-020: The head of John the Baptist on a dish was made as a sculpture on its own, for prayer and for display on his feast day, particularly in Spain and Italy. The maker of this one is not known.
VAULT-036: A page from an early Qur'an, written on parchment in the angular script called Kufic. The letters are stretched sideways and there are only a few lines to a page, so a complete Qur'an filled many volumes. The red dots are marks to guide pronunciation.
VAULT-022: Van Gogh painted more than twenty self-portraits during his two years in Paris, mostly because he could not afford to pay models. To save on canvas he painted this one on the back of an earlier picture, a study of a peasant woman peeling potatoes.
VAULT-041: The partner of the winged bull, from the same palace gateway at Nimrud in northern Iraq. The horned cap marks the figure as divine. Both were excavated in the 1840s and came to the Metropolitan Museum in 1932 as a gift from John D. Rockefeller Jr.
VAULT-023: From Dante's Inferno. Count Ugolino of Pisa was locked in a tower with his sons and grandsons and left to starve. Carpeaux made the group while a student at the French Academy in Rome, in defiance of a rule limiting students to one or two figures.
LIT-198: Katherine Mansfield was born in New Zealand and left it for good at nineteen, for London. At the Bay draws on childhood summers spent on the harbour near Wellington. She wrote it in 1921 while seriously ill with tuberculosis, and died in 1923 at thirty-four.
VAULT-024: Turner visited Venice three times, for a few weeks in all, and went on painting it for the rest of his life. He showed this at the Royal Academy in 1835. It combines buildings that cannot all be seen from one spot.
VAULT-028: Canaletto's views of Venice were bought mainly by wealthy British travellers as souvenirs of the Grand Tour. His agent was the British consul in the city. So many went to Britain that for a long time there were few in Venice itself.
VAULT-031: Exekias worked in Athens in the sixth century BCE and is generally considered the finest painter in the black-figure technique, in which figures are painted in black slip on the red clay and the details scratched through. He was a potter as well, and signed some vases as both.
VAULT-032: Euphronios was one of the first Athenian painters to master red-figure, in which the background is painted black and the figures are left in the colour of the clay. That allowed details to be drawn with a brush. In later life he ran a pottery workshop.
VAULT-033: A wine cup with a large pair of eyes on each side. When the drinker lifts it to his mouth the eyes cover his face like a mask, with the handles for ears. Cups like this were used at Athenian drinking parties.
VAULT-037: Vesalius published his great anatomy book in 1543, at the age of twenty-eight. It was the first based throughout on the dissection of human bodies. The ancient authority, Galen, had worked mostly from animals. This portrait from the book shows Vesalius himself, dissecting a forearm.
VAULT-038: In the eighth century a Spanish monk called Beatus wrote a commentary on the Book of Revelation. For the next four hundred years monasteries in Spain copied and illustrated it in flat, bright colours. This leaf comes from a copy made around 1180 at a monastery near Burgos.
LIT-258: Voltaire published Candide in 1759 without his name on it. It was banned in Paris and Geneva and sold out everywhere. This is from the last chapter, when the survivors of all its disasters settle on a small farm.
VAULT-043: One of the charcoal drawings Redon called his noirs. He worked in black for more than twenty years before he began to use colour regularly. He said black was the most essential of all colours.
VAULT-053: Delacroix visited London in 1825 and saw Shakespeare performed there. This lithograph of Macbeth and the witches was made the same year, when he was twenty-seven. He worked the image from dark to light, scraping the highlights out of the black.
VAULT-054: Édouard Detaille was the best-known French painter of soldiers of his generation. He had served in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 himself, and afterwards painted it in careful detail, down to the uniforms and equipment.
VAULT-058: Félix Vallotton was a Swiss artist in Paris who helped revive the woodcut in the 1890s. He used flat black against bare paper, with almost no shading. Here a crowd scatters as the police arrive, seen from above.
VAULT-060: In April 1834, during unrest in Paris, soldiers entered an apartment building on the rue Transnonain and killed the people inside, among them women, a child and old men. Daumier's print shows one room afterwards. It was sold to raise money for press freedom. The police seized the printing stone and all the copies they could find.
VAULT-061: John Taylor Arms was an American who trained as an architect and became one of the most exacting etchers of the twentieth century. This is the first of a series on the stone creatures of Notre-Dame in Paris, which were themselves added during the restoration of the cathedral in the 1840s.
VAULT-063: A study for the hand of one of the figures in The Burghers of Calais. Rodin modelled hands, feet and limbs separately and kept them by the hundred in drawers, to be tried on different figures or shown as works of their own.
LIT-199: From Monday or Tuesday, the only collection of short stories Virginia Woolf published in her lifetime. She and her husband Leonard printed it in 1921 at their own Hogarth Press, with woodcuts by her sister, Vanessa Bell.
VAULT-066: Gaetano Gandolfi belonged to a family of painters in Bologna. Sheets of invented heads like this, old and young, handsome and ugly, were made as exercises in character and expression, and were bought by collectors.
VAULT-059: A woodcut by Vallotton from 1896. He cut his blocks with a knife along the grain, which favours broad shapes and hard edges. His prints appeared in magazines across Europe and the United States, and were widely imitated.
VAULT-065: A caryatid is a column carved in the form of a woman, holding up a building. Rodin shows one who has collapsed under the weight but has not let go of it. He first made the figure for The Gates of Hell and later enlarged it as a work on its own.
LIT-259: Nietzsche wrote the four parts of Zarathustra between 1883 and 1885. They sold so badly that he had the last part printed privately in forty copies. In this section of the prologue Zarathustra describes to a crowd the last man, who wants only comfort.
LIT-200: Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in about six weeks in 1792. Its main argument is that women appear inferior only because they are denied education. She died in 1797, days after giving birth to the daughter who became Mary Shelley.
LIT-260: Nietzsche wrote Twilight of the Idols in little more than a week in the summer of 1888. It opens with this set of short sayings. In January 1889, before the book was published, he collapsed in Turin, and he never wrote again.
LIT-201: Sor Juana was a nun in Mexico City in the late 1600s, largely self-taught, with one of the biggest private libraries in the Americas. This poem charges men with blaming women for faults that men cause. Church authorities eventually pressed her to give up her books. She died in 1695 nursing her sisters during an epidemic.
LIT-261: Bierce wrote these mock definitions for newspapers and magazines from 1881 onwards. They were first collected in 1906 and reissued under this title in 1911. In 1913, aged seventy-one, he travelled to Mexico during the revolution and was never heard from again.
LIT-202: Li Qingzhao is generally regarded as the greatest woman poet in Chinese. In 1127 invaders took northern China and she fled south, and two years later her husband died. This lyric comes from the years that followed. In the original it opens with seven pairs of repeated syllables.
LIT-262: From Emerson's first book of essays, published in 1841. He had been a minister in Boston and resigned his pulpit. Self-Reliance argues that a person should trust their own judgement over custom, institutions and the opinions of others.
LIT-203: Ono no Komachi lived at the Japanese court in the ninth century and is counted among the six great poets of her age. Almost nothing certain is known about her life. Later legend made her a great beauty who grew old in poverty, and she is the subject of several Noh plays.
LIT-263: On 4 July 1845 Thoreau moved into a one-room cabin he had built on land belonging to his friend Emerson, beside Walden Pond in Massachusetts. He stayed two years and two months. The pond is about a mile and a half from the centre of Concord. The book came out in 1854.
LIT-204: Izumi Shikibu served at the Japanese court around the year 1000, at the same time as Murasaki Shikibu, author of The Tale of Genji. This is one of her earliest poems and her most famous. It is addressed to a Buddhist priest and asks him to light her way.
LIT-264: Juvenal's tenth satire is about the foolishness of what people pray for: power, long life, beauty. It is the source of the phrases 'bread and circuses' and 'a sound mind in a sound body'. Samuel Johnson based his poem The Vanity of Human Wishes on it.
LIT-206: Murasaki Shikibu was a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese court around the year 1000. Her real name is not known. The Tale of Genji runs to fifty-four chapters and is often called the world's first novel.
LIT-265: Hanshan means Cold Mountain, the place in eastern China where this recluse lived, and it is the only name we have for him. About three hundred poems are attributed to him. The old preface says they were collected from the rocks, trees and walls where he had written them.
LIT-207: Mirabai's best-known song. Giridhar Gopal is a name for Krishna as the cowherd who lifted a mountain. In it she says she has no one else. Her songs were passed on by singers for centuries before they were written down, so the wording varies from place to place.
LIT-266: Ryōkan was a Zen monk who lived alone in a one-room hut on a mountain in northern Japan, begging for his food and playing with the village children. The story attached to this poem is that a thief came to the hut and found nothing worth taking.
LIT-208: Rābiʿa lived in Basra, in Iraq, in the eighth century, and by tradition was a freed slave. She is remembered for teaching that God should be loved for his own sake, and not out of fear of hell or hope of paradise. Her sayings were written down by others, some of them centuries later.
LIT-205: From the Hyakunin Isshu, an anthology of one hundred poems by one hundred poets, put together around 1235. Most Japanese people know it through a card game played at New Year, in which players race to match the two halves of each poem. Izumi Shikibu is said to have written this one while ill.
LIT-209: Lal Ded was a mystic in fourteenth-century Kashmir who left her marriage and wandered as a holy woman. Her short verses were passed on by word of mouth for hundreds of years, among Hindus and Muslims alike. They are among the earliest compositions in the Kashmiri language.
LIT-269: Bashō's last poem. He fell ill on a journey and dictated it to a student in Osaka in November 1694, a few days before he died, at the age of fifty.
LIT-210: In 1373, at the age of thirty, Julian was thought to be dying and had a series of visions. She recovered and spent the rest of her life in a cell attached to a church in Norwich, thinking about what they meant. Her book is the earliest surviving work in English known to be by a woman.
LIT-270: Buson was as well known in his lifetime as a painter as he was as a poet. He lived a century after Bashō and led a movement to return haiku to Bashō's standard.
LIT-211: These lines were found after Teresa's death in 1582, written on a slip of paper she kept in her prayer book. She was a Carmelite nun who reformed her order and founded seventeen convents across Spain. The translation is by the American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.
LIT-271: Kenkō was an official at the Japanese court who became a Buddhist monk. Essays in Idleness is a collection of 243 short pieces on whatever crossed his mind. One tradition says he wrote them on scraps of paper and pasted them to the walls of his hut.
LIT-212: Phillis Wheatley was taken from West Africa as a child and sold in Boston in 1761. Her book of poems was published in London in 1773, the first by an African American. Because people doubted she could have written it, eighteen prominent Boston men signed a statement that she had.
LIT-272: Tao Yuanming held a series of minor government posts and gave up the last one after less than three months to go home and farm. His poems about that life, written around 400 CE, became a model for later Chinese poets. The longer passage is in Arthur Waley's translation of 1918.
LIT-213: Frances Harper was born free in Baltimore and became one of the best-known antislavery lecturers in the northern states. This poem was printed in an abolitionist newspaper in 1858. She went on to publish novels and poetry for another forty years.
LIT-214: Ida B. Wells was a newspaper editor in Memphis. In 1892, after three of her friends were lynched, she began investigating and reporting on lynching across the South. A mob destroyed her newspaper office while she was away, and she did not return to the city.
LIT-215: The title poem of Christina Rossetti's first collection, published in 1862 with illustrations by her brother Dante Gabriel. Two sisters are tempted by goblins selling fruit.
LIT-216: Anne Bradstreet sailed from England to Massachusetts in 1630. A book of her poems was published in London in 1650, the first by anyone living in the English colonies in America. This poem to her husband Simon was printed after her death.
LIT-276: Issa's life was hard. His mother died when he was a small child, and four of his children died in infancy. He wrote about twenty thousand haiku, many of them about flies, fleas, sparrows and other small creatures.
LIT-217: From Flame and Shadow, published in 1920. Sara Teasdale was one of the most widely read American poets of her time. In 1918 she won the prize that later became the Pulitzer Prize for poetry.
LIT-277: Tagore wrote mainly in Bengali. In 1913 he became the first writer from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Stray Birds, from 1916, is a book of some three hundred short sayings, which he wrote in English or translated from his own Bengali.
LIT-218: Emily Brontë dated this poem 2 January 1846. Her sister Charlotte described it as the last thing she ever wrote, which is not quite accurate. Emily Dickinson admired it, and it was read at Dickinson's funeral.
LIT-278: A book of short sayings Gibran published in 1926, three years after The Prophet. Gibran was born in Lebanon and emigrated to the United States as a child.
LIT-279: In 480 BCE three hundred Spartans and their allies held the pass at Thermopylae against the Persian army until they were all killed. These two lines were cut on a stone set up where they fell. The historian Herodotus recorded them. They have traditionally been credited to the poet Simonides.
LIT-280: Callimachus worked at the great library of Alexandria, where he compiled its catalogue. This short poem mourns a friend and fellow poet, Heraclitus of Halicarnassus. The English version is by William Johnson Cory, a master at Eton, from his book Ionica.
LIT-281: Anyte lived in Arcadia, in Greece, around 300 BCE. About twenty of her short poems survive. She was among the first poets to write epitaphs for animals and to describe the countryside for its own sake. W. R. Paton's translation is from the Loeb edition of the Greek Anthology.
LIT-282: Meleager came from Gadara, in what is now Jordan, and wrote in Greek. Around 100 BCE he gathered short poems by nearly fifty poets, his own included, into a collection he called the Garland. It became the core of the Greek Anthology. The word anthology means a gathering of flowers.
LIT-283: From the Gulistan, or Rose Garden, a book of stories and verses that Saadi completed in Shiraz in 1258. For centuries it was the first book students of Persian read. These lines, on all human beings as limbs of one body, are among the most quoted in the language.
LIT-284: Kabir was a weaver in the city of Benares in the fifteenth century. He was brought up in a Muslim family, attacked the rituals of Hindus and Muslims alike, and is honoured today by both, as well as by Sikhs. This English version comes from the selection Rabindranath Tagore translated in 1915.
LIT-287: Basava was a minister to a king in twelfth-century Karnataka, in southern India, and the founder of a movement that rejected caste and temple ritual. His vachanas, 'sayings', are short prose poems in plain Kannada. P. G. Halkatti spent years in the early 1900s collecting them from palm-leaf manuscripts.
LIT-288: Three collections of a hundred Sanskrit verses each are attributed to Bhartṛhari: one on love, one on worldly conduct and one on giving up the world. This is from the third. Legend makes him a king who left his throne, though nothing reliable is known about him.
LIT-289: Leopardi wrote L'Infinito in 1819, at twenty-one, in the small hill town of Recanati where he grew up. He had spent his teens studying in his father's library and had damaged his health and eyesight doing it. The poem is fifteen lines long.
LIT-290: This song comes from Hölderlin's novel Hyperion, whose second volume appeared in 1799. Brahms later set it for chorus and orchestra. From 1807 until his death thirty-six years later Hölderlin lived in a tower room in Tübingen, looked after by the family of a carpenter who admired his work.
LIT-291: From Heine's Book of Songs, published in 1827, which became the most popular book of German poetry of the century. Composers have set its poems to music thousands of times.
LIT-292: From Verlaine's first book, published in 1866 when he was twenty-two. In June 1944 the BBC broadcast the opening lines of this poem to tell the French Resistance that the Allied invasion was about to begin.
LIT-293: Apollinaire wrote this after the end of his relationship with the painter Marie Laurencin. The Mirabeau bridge crosses the Seine in the west of Paris, on his way home from her. When the poem was collected in 1913 he removed all the punctuation, as he did throughout the book.
LIT-294: A long letter Wilde wrote to Lord Alfred Douglas in early 1897, during the last months of his two-year prison sentence. A shortened version was published in 1905, five years after his death.
LIT-295: Wilde wrote this in France after his release from prison in 1897. It was published under his cell number, C.3.3. The poem is about a soldier who was hanged at Reading Gaol while Wilde was a prisoner there. It was the last thing he wrote.
LIT-296: W. E. B. Du Bois was the first Black American to earn a doctorate from Harvard. The Souls of Black Folk, published in 1903, is a collection of essays on Black life in America after slavery. This opening chapter introduces his idea of 'double consciousness'.
LIT-297: This poem won first prize in a magazine contest in 1925. It became the title poem of Hughes's first book the following year. It describes a blues pianist playing on Lenox Avenue in Harlem and borrows the rhythm of the music.
LIT-298: Whitman added this poem to the second edition of Leaves of Grass in 1856. The Brooklyn Bridge had not been built, and the ferry was how people crossed between Brooklyn and Manhattan. He addresses the people who will make the same crossing long after he is dead.
LIT-299: Rilke began the Duino Elegies in January 1912 at Duino Castle, on the Adriatic coast near Trieste, where he was a guest. He said the first line came to him as he walked on the cliffs in a strong wind. It took him ten years to finish the cycle.
LIT-300: In Attar's poem, the birds must cross seven valleys to reach their king. Astonishment, or bewilderment, is the sixth. Attar was a pharmacist in the city of Nishapur in northeastern Iran. He is thought to have died when the Mongols sacked it in 1221.
LIT-301: Imruʾ al-Qais was a prince of an Arab tribe in the century before Islam, known as 'the wandering king'. His ode is the first of the seven 'hanging poems', which tradition says were displayed at Mecca. Its opening, in which the poet stops to weep at an abandoned campsite, set the pattern for Arabic poetry for centuries.
LIT-302: ʿAntara was the son of an Arab chief and an enslaved African woman. By tradition he was treated as a slave until he won his freedom by his courage in battle. His love for his cousin ʿAbla runs through his poetry. He later became the hero of a long popular romance.
LIT-303: Labīd was one of the poets of the seven 'hanging odes' of pre-Islamic Arabia. He lived long enough to become a Muslim, and is said to have given up composing poetry afterwards.
LIT-304: Al-Khansāʾ is the most famous woman poet in Arabic. Nearly all her poems are laments for her two brothers, Ṣakhr and Muʿāwiya, who were killed in tribal fighting before the coming of Islam. Tradition says the Prophet Muhammad heard her recite and admired her.
LIT-305: Abu Nuwas lived in Baghdad around 800, at the court of the caliph Harun al-Rashid. He is best known for poems in praise of wine, which broke with the desert themes of older Arabic poetry. He turns up as a comic character in the Thousand and One Nights.
LIT-306: Al-Maʿarrī, from a town in northern Syria, lost his sight to smallpox as a small child. He was a sceptic about religion, never married, and ate no meat. Ameen Rihani, who translated these verses, was a Lebanese-American writer.
LIT-309: Ibn Arabi was born in Muslim Spain and became one of the most influential mystics in Islam. This book of love poems was inspired by a young woman he met in Mecca. When critics said the poems were too worldly he wrote a commentary explaining each one in spiritual terms.
LIT-311: Rudaki, who lived around 900, is regarded as the first major poet of the Persian language. According to an old story, the ruler of Bukhara had stayed away from home for years, and his courtiers asked Rudaki to help. He sang these lines about Bukhara, and the ruler rode for home without stopping to put on his boots.
LIT-313: The story of Qays, who loves Layla so much that he loses his mind and is called Majnun, 'the madman', came from Arabia. Nizami turned it into a long Persian poem in 1188, and his version became the standard one. James Atkinson's English translation was published in 1836.
LIT-314: The Haft Paykar, or Seven Beauties, tells how King Bahram Gur visits seven princesses, one on each day of the week, in seven domed pavilions of different colours. Each tells him a story. The black dome is the first, on Saturday.
LIT-317: Muhammad Iqbal wrote this long poem in Persian in 1915. It argues that the self should be strengthened, and should not be dissolved as some mystical traditions teach. Iqbal is honoured as the national poet of Pakistan. R. A. Nicholson, who had known him at Cambridge, translated it in 1920.
LIT-318: The stories of the Nights were gathered over centuries from Indian, Persian and Arabic sources. In the frame tale, Shahrazad tells the king a story each night and stops before the end, so that he will let her live another day. Husain Haddawy's translation of 1990 follows Muhsin Mahdi's edition of the oldest surviving manuscript, a Syrian one of the fourteenth century.
LIT-319: A spirit exiled far from his home in the Himalayas asks a passing rain cloud to carry a message to his wife, and describes the route it must take across India. Kālidāsa is the most celebrated poet in classical Sanskrit. Arthur Ryder, who translated it, taught Sanskrit at Berkeley.
LIT-320: Jayadeva wrote the Gīta Govinda in eastern India in the twelfth century. It tells of the love, quarrel and reunion of the god Krishna and the cowherd Radha, and is still sung in temples. The longer passage here is Edwin Arnold's English version of 1875, which is a free one.
LIT-322: The Therīgāthā, or Verses of the Elder Nuns, is a collection of poems by the first Buddhist women, kept in the Pali scriptures. It is often described as the oldest known anthology of writing by women.
LIT-323: In Buddhist tradition, Kisāgotamī's child died and she carried the body from house to house asking for medicine. The Buddha told her to bring a mustard seed from a home where no one had died. She could not find one, understood, and became a nun.
LIT-324: Ambapālī was a famous courtesan in the city of Vesālī. She gave her mango grove to the Buddha and his followers and later became a nun. In her poem she goes through her body part by part, comparing what it was with what age has made it.
LIT-325: The Tirukkuṛaḷ is a Tamil book of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love. Nothing certain is known about its author, and estimates of its date vary by several centuries. It is among the most widely translated works from India.
LIT-328: Tukārām was a shopkeeper from a village near Pune in western India, and the best-loved poet-saint in the Marathi language. His songs are sung every year by pilgrims on the long walk to the temple at Pandharpur.
LIT-329: Qu Yuan was a minister of the state of Chu who was slandered and sent into exile. In this dialogue a fisherman asks why he will not bend with the times. Tradition says Qu Yuan drowned himself in a river, and the Dragon Boat Festival is held in his memory.
LIT-330: One of the first poems Chinese children learn by heart. It is four lines of five characters each. The translation comes from The Jade Mountain, a 1929 English version of the standard anthology of Tang poetry, made by an American poet and a Chinese scholar working together.
LIT-331: Wei Yingwu wrote this while serving as governor of Chuzhou, in eastern China. He held a series of provincial posts and was known for quiet poems about landscape. The translation is from The Jade Mountain.
LIT-332: In 816 Bai Juyi was serving in a minor post far from the capital after being demoted. One night on the river he heard someone playing the lute on a nearby boat. She turned out to be a former entertainer from the capital, and he wrote this long poem about the meeting.
LIT-333: Liu Zongyuan was a high official who backed a reform movement that failed in 805. He was sent away from the capital and spent the rest of his life in remote southern posts. He wrote this poem in exile. It is twenty characters long.
LIT-337: More than nine thousand of Lu You's poems survive. He lived when northern China was under foreign rule and never stopped hoping to see it won back. Herbert Giles, who translated this, was professor of Chinese at Cambridge.
LIT-342: The Kokinshū, compiled in 905, was the first anthology of Japanese poetry made by order of an emperor. Ki no Tsurayuki, its chief editor, wrote this preface in Japanese at a time when serious prose was written in Chinese. It is the first major statement of what Japanese poetry is for.
LIT-343: Fujiwara no Teika was the most influential poet and critic of medieval Japan, and the compiler of the Hyakunin Isshu, the collection of a hundred poems by a hundred poets. This is the poem of his own that he chose to include.
LIT-344: Shiki reformed the haiku in the 1890s and gave it the name it now goes by. He had tuberculosis of the spine, was confined to bed for his last years and died at thirty-four. He was very fond of persimmons. The poem names Hōryū-ji, a temple near Nara, which he visited in 1895.
LIT-352: The Kebra Nagast, 'The Glory of Kings', was written down in Ethiopia in the fourteenth century. It tells how the Queen of Sheba visited Solomon, and how their son Menelik brought the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia. Ethiopian emperors traced their line to him until 1974. E. A. Wallis Budge of the British Museum translated it in 1922.
LIT-353: A song from ancient Egypt, performed by a harpist at funeral feasts. It is unusual because it doubts the afterlife. No one, it says, has come back to tell us how the dead are, so enjoy the day. It survives in copies made around 1300 BCE.
LIT-354: A clay cylinder written in Babylon for the Persian king Cyrus after he took the city in 539 BCE. It gives his own account of the conquest and says he restored temples and sent displaced peoples home. It was found in 1879 and is in the British Museum.
