LIT-355: Hammurabi ruled Babylon in the eighteenth century BCE. His 282 laws are carved on a stone pillar found in 1901 and now in the Louvre. In the prologue he names the gods who called him to rule and states his purpose, which is that the strong should not harm the weak.
LIT-358: The Popol Vuh is the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala. It was written down in the K'iche' language in the 1550s, and survives in a single copy made by a Spanish friar around 1700. Lewis Spence's 1908 version is a retelling in English, not a direct translation. In this episode the lords of the underworld put to death Hunhun-Ahpu, the father of the hero twins, and his brother.
LIT-359: The Kumulipo is a Hawaiian creation chant of more than two thousand lines, which traces the royal family back to the beginning of the world. Queen Liliʻuokalani translated it into English in 1895 while she was held prisoner in her own palace, after the overthrow of the Hawaiian kingdom.
LIT-360: Sitting Bull was a leader and holy man of the Hunkpapa Lakota. After the defeat of Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876 he took his people to Canada, and returned to surrender in 1881. He was killed in 1890 during an attempt to arrest him. His speeches survive only as others recorded and translated them.
LIT-361: Old Joseph was a chief of the Nez Perce in the Wallowa Valley of Oregon, who refused to sign the treaty of 1863 that gave the valley away. These words were reported by his son, Chief Joseph, in an account of his people's history published in an American magazine in 1879.
LIT-364: From Martí's Simple Verses of 1891, and one of the first poems Cuban children learn. It is eight lines long. He offers the same white rose to a true friend and to the one who has wronged him.
LIT-365: Omar Khayyam was known in his own time as a mathematician and astronomer. Edward FitzGerald's very free English version of the quatrains attributed to him came out in 1859 as an anonymous pamphlet and did not sell. It was marked down to a penny, discovered by a group of poets, and became one of the most popular poems in English.
LIT-366: The hero of this novel, Des Esseintes, shuts himself up in a house outside Paris and devotes himself to rare sensations. In this chapter he has a live tortoise's shell set with jewels. The book became a handbook for the decadent writers of the 1890s. It is the 'yellow book' that corrupts Dorian Gray in Wilde's novel.
LIT-367: From The Flowers of Evil, published in 1857. Within weeks Baudelaire and his publisher were prosecuted for offending public morals. They were fined, and six poems were banned from the book. The ban was not lifted in France until 1949.
LIT-368: The opening piece of Illuminations, Rimbaud's book of prose poems. He had given up writing altogether by about the age of twenty-one. The book was published in 1886 without his knowledge, while he was working as a trader in East Africa.
LIT-370: Mallarmé wrote this in 1865, at twenty-three. He was teaching English at a school in a small provincial town, had a wife and a baby daughter, and was struggling to write. The poem is about wanting to leave everything and sail away.
LIT-372: Tristan Corbière came from Brittany and published one book, in 1873, at his own expense. Nobody noticed it. He died two years later, at twenty-nine. Paul Verlaine made him known in 1884 in a set of essays on poets he called 'accursed'.
LIT-373: Aloysius Bertrand is credited with inventing the prose poem. He died poor in 1841, and Gaspard of the Night was published the year after. Baudelaire named it as a model for his own prose poems. In 1908 Maurice Ravel wrote three piano pieces based on it, the last of them on Scarbo, a goblin who appears at night.
LIT-377: Wilde wrote Salomé in French, in Paris, in 1891. A London production starring Sarah Bernhardt was banned the next year, because the law did not allow biblical characters on stage. The English translation is credited to Lord Alfred Douglas. Wilde was unhappy with it and revised it himself.
LIT-378: From Swinburne's Poems and Ballads of 1866. The book caused such an outcry over its sensuality and its attitude to religion that the publisher withdrew it. Proserpine is the Roman queen of the underworld. The poem imagines death as rest and nothing more.
LIT-379: A sonnet from The House of Life, the sequence Rossetti worked on for decades. In 1862 he buried the only manuscript of many of his poems in the coffin of his wife, Elizabeth Siddal. Seven years later he had the grave opened to get them back, and published them in 1870.
LIT-380: Tennyson published The Lady of Shalott in 1832 and revised it heavily for the version of 1842, which is the one usually read. In this part Lancelot rides by and she turns from her mirror to look at him. The Pre-Raphaelite painters returned to the poem again and again.
LIT-381: De Quincey first took opium, as laudanum, for toothache while a student in 1804. His account of the pleasures and then the horrors of addiction appeared in a London magazine in 1821 without his name, and made him famous.
LIT-382: A vampire story by the Irish writer Sheridan Le Fanu, published in 1872, twenty-five years before Dracula. The vampire is a young woman, Carmilla, who becomes the guest and close companion of the girl who tells the story.
LIT-383: Bram Stoker was the business manager of a London theatre and wrote in his spare time. Dracula is told entirely through diaries, letters and newspaper cuttings. He never visited Transylvania and worked from books and maps. This is from Jonathan Harker's journal, on his arrival at the castle.
LIT-384: Arthur Machen was a Welsh writer of supernatural fiction. This short novel, about an experiment on the brain that lets a woman see the god Pan, was attacked as morbid and indecent when it came out in 1894. Later horror writers have counted it among the best ever written.
LIT-385: The King in Yellow is a book of stories from 1895, linked by an imaginary play of the same name that drives anyone who reads it mad. Cassilda's Song is presented as a fragment of that play. Chambers went on to write popular romances, and this early book is the one that has lasted.
LIT-386: Two men canoeing down the Danube camp on an island among willow bushes, and gradually sense that something there is aware of them. Blackwood based it on a canoe trip he had made himself. H. P. Lovecraft considered it the finest supernatural story in English.
LIT-387: Lord Dunsany was an Irish peer. In his first book, published in 1905 at his own expense, he invented a complete set of gods with their own creation story.
LIT-388: Lovecraft wrote this story in 1926 and it was printed in the magazine Weird Tales in 1928. Almost all his work appeared in cheap pulp magazines. He died in poverty in Providence, Rhode Island, in 1937, and his reputation was made after his death.
LIT-390: E. T. A. Hoffmann was a judge in Berlin by day and wrote tales of the uncanny at night. The Sandman, about a student haunted by a figure from his childhood who falls in love with a mechanical doll, is the starting point of Freud's essay on the uncanny and of the ballet Coppélia.
LIT-391: Annette von Droste-Hülshoff came from a noble family in Westphalia and is regarded as the most important woman poet in German of the nineteenth century. She wrote this at a castle on Lake Constance. In it a woman stands on a tower in a storm and wishes she had the freedom of a man.
LIT-392: Else Lasker-Schüler was a leading figure among the Expressionist poets and artists of Berlin before the First World War. She was Jewish and fled Germany in 1933. She died in Jerusalem in 1945. This translation is from an anthology of German poetry published in New York in 1923.
LIT-393: Georg Heym wrote visions of cities overrun by demons, fire and war in the two years before 1912. In January of that year he drowned while skating on a frozen river near Berlin, trying to save a friend who had fallen through the ice. He was twenty-four.
LIT-394: Georg Trakl was an Austrian poet who trained as a pharmacist. In 1914 he served as a medical officer on the Eastern Front, and after one battle was left alone to care for some ninety badly wounded men. He died in a military hospital a few weeks later, at twenty-seven.
LIT-396: Kafka wrote In the Penal Colony in two weeks in October 1914, while he was also working on The Trial. It was published in 1919, one of the few works he allowed into print in his lifetime. An officer shows a visitor a machine that carves the sentence into the condemned man's body.
LIT-397: Kierkegaard published Either/Or in 1843 under an invented editor's name, not long after breaking off his engagement to Regine Olsen. The book opens with these short paragraphs, presented as the papers of a young man who lives for pleasure. The longer passage is in Lee Hollander's translation of 1923.
LIT-398: A tale Andersen published in 1847. A scholar's shadow detaches itself, goes out into the world, grows rich, and comes back to make the scholar its servant.
LIT-400: Rosalía de Castro wrote in both Galician and Spanish. Her books helped bring Galician back to life as a literary language after centuries in which it was hardly written. The day her first Galician book was published is now a public holiday in Galicia. This translation is from Thomas Walsh's Hispanic Anthology of 1920.
LIT-401: A poor copying clerk in St Petersburg saves for months to buy a new overcoat, and it is stolen on the first night he wears it. Gogol published the story in 1842. A remark often attributed to Dostoevsky says that all later Russian writers came out from under it.
LIT-402: From a letter Chekhov wrote in October 1888 to Alexei Suvorin, a newspaper publisher in St Petersburg and for many years his closest correspondent. Chekhov was twenty-eight. That same month the Academy of Sciences had awarded him the Pushkin Prize.
LIT-522: In his reminiscences, the writer S. Shchukin records this as advice Chekhov gave him about a story. It is one of several recorded wordings of the principle now called Chekhov's gun. Chekhov made the same point in a letter of November 1889.
LIT-403: Blok wrote this in October 1912. It is eight lines long, and the second half mirrors the first. It belongs to a group of poems he called Dances of Death. Blok was the leading poet of the Russian Symbolists.
LIT-404: Andrei Bely was the pen name of Boris Bugaev, a poet and novelist of the Russian Symbolist movement, best known for his novel Petersburg. This translation comes from an anthology of modern Russian poetry published in New York in 1921.
LIT-405: Tsvetaeva wrote this in October 1915, during the First World War, when she was twenty-three. She left Russia after the Revolution, lived in poverty in Prague and Paris, and returned to the Soviet Union in 1939. She died in 1941.
LIT-406: Paul Laurence Dunbar was the son of parents who had been enslaved in Kentucky. He was working as an elevator operator in Dayton, Ohio, when his poems first drew attention. He became known for poems in dialect and also wrote in standard English, as here. He died at thirty-three.
LIT-407: The title poem of Georgia Douglas Johnson's first book, published in 1918. For decades her house in Washington, D.C. was a weekly meeting place for Black writers, among them Langston Hughes and Jean Toomer.
LIT-408: Alice Dunbar-Nelson was a teacher, journalist and campaigner for civil rights and women's suffrage. She wrote this in 1918, during the First World War. A woman at her sewing thinks of the men at the front and of the work she is not permitted to do there.
LIT-409: Fenton Johnson was a poet and editor in Chicago. This prose poem appeared in 1919 in a magazine of experimental verse.
LIT-410: Claude McKay was born in Jamaica and moved to the United States in 1912. He wrote this sonnet in the summer of 1919, when white mobs attacked Black neighbourhoods in cities across the country. It was published in a radical magazine that July.
LIT-411: From Cane, published in 1923, a book that mixes poems, stories and a play. Jean Toomer wrote it after spending a few months as acting head of a school for Black students in rural Georgia. He published little after it.
LIT-412: From Color, Countee Cullen's first book, published in 1925 while he was still a student. It is a sonnet. He lists hard things he can believe God has reasons for, and ends with the one that puzzles him most.
LIT-413: Zitkala-Ša was a Yankton Dakota writer and musician. At eight she left her mother's home for a missionary boarding school in Indiana. She described what happened there in a series of articles for the Atlantic Monthly in 1900. She later led a national organisation campaigning for Native American rights.
LIT-414: Pauline Johnson was the daughter of a Mohawk chief and an Englishwoman, and grew up on the Six Nations reserve in Ontario. This poem dates from 1892, the year a reading in Toronto made her name. She spent the next seventeen years touring Canada, the United States and England as a performer.
LIT-416: Juana de Ibarbourou, from Uruguay, published her first book in 1919. It was an immediate success across the Spanish-speaking world. Ten years later, at a public ceremony in Montevideo, she was given the title 'Juana of America'.
LIT-417: Gabriela Mistral was a schoolteacher in Chile when these sonnets won a national poetry prize in 1914. She wrote them after the death of a man she had loved. In 1945 she became the first Latin American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
LIT-421: Pu Songling failed the civil service examinations again and again and spent his life as a tutor in a provincial family. Over decades he wrote nearly five hundred tales of ghosts, fox spirits and strange events. They were passed around in manuscript and printed fifty years after his death. Herbert Giles translated them in 1880.
LIT-425: Akutagawa wrote Rashōmon in 1915, when he was a twenty-three-year-old student, basing it on a twelfth-century tale. Kurosawa's film of 1950 takes its title and its ruined gate from this story. The plot of the film comes from another Akutagawa story.
LIT-426: Lu Xun had studied medicine in Japan and gave it up to write. A Madman's Diary appeared in 1918 in a reform magazine. It was written in everyday spoken Chinese at a time when literature used the classical language, and is generally counted as the first modern Chinese short story. The title is borrowed from Gogol.
LIT-427: José Rizal, a doctor and novelist, wrote this poem in his cell the night before the Spanish authorities executed him in Manila on 30 December 1896. He hid it in a small alcohol stove, which he gave to his sister. It had no title and no signature.
LIT-428: Kartini was the daughter of a Javanese nobleman. From the family home, where custom kept her secluded, she wrote letters in Dutch to friends in the Netherlands about education and freedom for Javanese girls. She died in 1904 at twenty-five, days after giving birth. Her birthday is a national day in Indonesia.
LIT-429: Toru Dutt grew up in Calcutta and spent four years in France and England. She wrote in English and French and translated from Sanskrit. She died of tuberculosis in 1877, at twenty-one. The poem remembers a tree in the family garden and the brother and sister she had played under it with, both already dead.
LIT-430: Olive Schreiner wrote The Story of an African Farm in her early twenties, while working as a governess on remote farms in South Africa. It was published in London in 1883 under a man's name. This passage is a tale told by a passing stranger, about a hunter who spends his life climbing after the bird of truth.
LIT-431: In 416 BCE Athens demanded that the small neutral island of Melos join its side in the war against Sparta. Thucydides, an Athenian general turned historian, sets out the negotiation as a dialogue. The Melians refused. The Athenians took the island, killed the men and enslaved the women and children.
LIT-432: La Rochefoucauld's book grew from about three hundred maxims in 1665 to over five hundred in the edition of 1678, the last published in his lifetime. He revised the maxims from one edition to the next.
LIT-434: Han Fei was a prince of the small state of Han. According to the ancient historian Sima Qian he had a stammer, and so put his arguments in writing. He made his points with short, pointed stories. The longer passage is in Herbert Giles's translation of 1923.
LIT-435: Zhuangzi is, with Laozi, one of the two founding writers of Daoism. His book teaches through jokes, tall stories and imaginary conversations. In this chapter the god of the Yellow River, proud of his autumn floodwaters, reaches the sea for the first time.
LIT-436: Xunzi was a Confucian philosopher of the third century BCE. Against the earlier thinker Mencius, he argued that people are born selfish, and that goodness has to be learned through education and ritual. His students included Han Fei, the Legalist philosopher, and Li Si, who became chief minister of the Qin state.
LIT-443: Eduard Douwes Dekker was a Dutch colonial official in Java who resigned in 1856 in protest at the treatment of the Javanese. His novel, published under the name Multatuli, shocked the Netherlands and led in time to reforms. The story of the young villager Saïdjah and his love Adinda is told inside the novel.
LIT-448: Ferdowsi finished the Shahnama in 1010, after some thirty years of work. In its closing lines he speaks of his age and poverty and of the fame the poem will bring him. A famous legend says the sultan paid him far less than he had promised, and that a proper reward arrived as the poet's coffin was being carried out of the city.
LIT-449: One of the best-known poems by Hafez. In its opening lines he offers to give away the cities of Samarkand and Bukhara for the mole on his beloved's cheek. Iranians still open his collected poems at random to tell fortunes. The longer passage here is the translation Gertrude Bell published in 1897, long before her career in the politics of the Middle East.
LIT-455: Sarojini Naidu was born in Hyderabad and published three books of poems in English between 1905 and 1917. She then gave most of her time to the independence movement. She was the first Indian woman to serve as president of the Indian National Congress, and later the first woman to govern an Indian state.
LIT-456: From the second of Bhartṛhari's three collections of a hundred verses, the one on conduct in the world. It deals with learning, fools, money, friendship and how to behave around the powerful. B. Hale Wortham's translation was published in 1886.
LIT-467: Ibn Battuta left Morocco in 1325, aged twenty-one, and travelled for nearly thirty years, as far as China. He dictated his account when he got home. Taghaza was a salt-mining settlement in the Sahara that he passed through in 1352 on his way to Mali. He reports that its houses were built of blocks of salt.
LIT-469: Liliʻuokalani was the last monarch of Hawaii. She was overthrown in January 1893. In 1897, when a treaty to annex the islands to the United States was signed in Washington, she filed this protest with the State Department. She printed it the following year in her book Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen.
LIT-471: Geronimo dictated the story of his life in 1905 and 1906, in Apache, through an interpreter. He was then in his late seventies and had been a prisoner of war of the United States for nearly twenty years. Publishing the book required the permission of President Roosevelt.
LIT-474: Marcus Garvey, born in Jamaica, founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association, which by the early 1920s claimed millions of members around the world. He was convicted of mail fraud, and wrote this message to them as he entered the federal prison in Atlanta in February 1925. He was released and deported in 1927.
LIT-476: Bolívar wrote this letter in Kingston, Jamaica, in September 1815. He was in exile after the collapse of the Venezuelan republic. Replying to an English resident of the island, he sets out why Spanish America would win its independence and what kind of governments it would need.
LIT-477: Harriet Jacobs escaped slavery in North Carolina by hiding for seven years in a crawl space under the roof of her grandmother's house, before getting away to the North in 1842. She published her story in 1861 under the name Linda Brent. For a century many readers assumed it was fiction, until a scholar proved otherwise in the 1980s.
LIT-478: Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1849. She went back about thirteen times and led some seventy people to freedom. She could not read or write. Her words were taken down by Sarah Bradford for a biography published in 1869 to raise money for her.
LIT-479: These sayings head the chapters of Following the Equator, Mark Twain's account of the round-the-world lecture tour he undertook at about sixty to pay off his debts after going bankrupt. They are presented as the work of a character from one of his novels.
LIT-480: From The Black Riders, Stephen Crane's first book of poems, published in 1895, the same year as The Red Badge of Courage. He was twenty-three. The poems have no titles, no rhyme and no regular metre, and many readers at the time did not consider them poems.
LIT-481: From War Is Kind, Crane's second book of poems, published in 1899. He had worked as a war correspondent in Greece and Cuba. He died of tuberculosis the following year, at twenty-eight.
LIT-482: James Weldon Johnson was the principal of a school in Jacksonville, Florida. He wrote these words for a celebration of Lincoln's birthday in 1900, and his brother Rosamond wrote the music. Five hundred schoolchildren sang it. It spread from school to school across the South and became known as the Black national anthem.
LIT-483: Angelina Weld Grimké taught English in Washington, D.C. She was the great-niece of two famous white abolitionists, the Grimké sisters. This poem appeared in 1927 in an anthology of Black poets. 'Tenebris' is Latin for 'in darkness'.
LIT-484: Nella Larsen was the daughter of a Danish mother and a father from the Danish West Indies. She worked as a nurse and a librarian. Quicksand, published in 1928, was her first novel. She wrote one more, then stopped publishing and went back to nursing.
LIT-485: From Spoon River Anthology, published in 1915, in which more than two hundred people buried in the graveyard of a small Illinois town each speak their own epitaph. Masters, a Chicago lawyer, based Lucinda Matlock on his grandmother.
LIT-486: Vachel Lindsay walked hundreds of miles across the United States, trading printed copies of his poems for meals and a bed. He performed his poems as chants. This one is from a collection published in 1914.
LIT-487: William Carlos Williams was a family doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey, for more than forty years, and wrote between seeing patients. The Great Figure records a fire engine passing in the street in New York. His friend Charles Demuth turned it into a painting, I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold.
LIT-488: Marianne Moore first published this poem in 1919 and went on revising it for nearly fifty years. One version runs to about thirty lines. In her collected poems of 1967 she cut it to three.
LIT-489: Wallace Stevens worked for an insurance company in Hartford, Connecticut, and rose to be a vice-president. He composed poems in his head on the walk to the office. His first book, Harmonium, came out in 1923, when he was forty-three.
LIT-490: Thirteen short sections, each a different way of seeing the same bird. Stevens wrote the poem in 1917 and included it in Harmonium, his first book. He said the sections were not meant as epigrams or ideas. They were meant as sensations.
LIT-491: José Asunción Silva, from Colombia, wrote this poem after the death of his sister Elvira in 1891. Its long, uneven lines were new in Spanish and were widely imitated. In 1895 he lost most of his unpublished work in a shipwreck. He died the next year, at thirty.
LIT-492: An essay published in 1900 by the Uruguayan writer José Enrique Rodó, addressed to the young people of Latin America. Using the figures of Ariel and Caliban from Shakespeare's Tempest, it urges them to value the life of the mind over material success. It was read across the continent for decades.
LIT-495: Amado Nervo was a Mexican poet who spent much of his life abroad as a diplomat. His late poems, calm and religious in tone, were enormously popular. When he died in Uruguay in 1919 his body was brought home by a naval escort, and huge crowds attended the funeral.
LIT-496: The title poem of César Vallejo's first book. It was printed in Lima in 1918 and held back for months while he waited for a preface that never arrived. He left Peru in 1923, lived in poverty in Paris, and died there in 1938.
LIT-498: Oswald de Andrade published this manifesto in São Paulo in 1928. Its argument is that Brazil should treat European culture the way the Tupi people were said to have treated their enemies: eat it, digest it and turn it into something of its own. The play on Hamlet is in English in the original.
LIT-001: Coleridge published the Ancient Mariner in 1798 in Lyrical Ballads, the book he made with Wordsworth. The two planned the poem together on a long walk. It was Wordsworth who suggested that the mariner should kill an albatross and be pursued for it.
LIT-003: Book twelve of the Odyssey takes Odysseus past the Sirens and between the monster Scylla and the whirlpool Charybdis. The longer passage is in the plain prose translation made in 1900 by Samuel Butler, the Victorian novelist. He also argued, in a separate book, that the poem had been written by a woman.
LIT-004: The spirit Ariel sings this to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned in the shipwreck. The Tempest, first performed in 1611, was probably the last play Shakespeare wrote alone. The phrase 'sea-change' comes from this song.
LIT-005: Arnold probably wrote Dover Beach around 1851, about the time of his honeymoon, which included a stay at Dover. He did not publish it until 1867. It is his best-known poem.
LIT-006: Bashō wrote this in 1689 on the five-month journey through northern Japan that he recorded in The Narrow Road to the Deep North. He was standing on the coast looking across to Sado, an island to which emperors and priests had been exiled.
LIT-008: In the graveyard, a gravedigger hands Hamlet the skull of Yorick, who was the court jester when Hamlet was a child. Hamlet was written around 1600. It is Shakespeare's longest play.
LIT-009: Macbeth speaks these lines when he is told that his wife is dead, with an enemy army closing in on his castle. The play was written around 1606, soon after a Scottish king, James I, came to the English throne.
LIT-011: Poe published this story in 1842. A prince seals himself and a thousand friends inside an abbey to wait out a plague, and gives a costume ball. Earlier that year Poe's wife Virginia had shown the first signs of the tuberculosis that killed her.
LIT-012: Nezahualcóyotl ruled the city of Texcoco, beside the Aztec capital, in the fifteenth century, and is remembered as a poet, lawgiver and builder. The poems under his name were written down after the Spanish conquest, so it is not certain which are his. Daniel Brinton's English version of 1887 was made from a Spanish translation.
LIT-013: From the King James Bible, the English translation made by about fifty scholars at the order of King James I and published in 1611. This verse describes the last of the four horsemen who appear when the seals are opened in the Book of Revelation.
LIT-015: From Beyond Good and Evil, which Nietzsche published in 1886 at his own expense after his publisher turned it down. It sold just over a hundred copies in its first year. The fourth part of the book is made up of short sayings like this one.
LIT-016: Rilke wrote The Panther in Paris, around 1902. The sculptor Rodin had urged him to work as a craftsman does, by looking closely at things. The panther was one of the animals kept in the Jardin des Plantes. It is the earliest of the poems collected in his New Poems.
LIT-019: Near the end of the Book of Job, God answers Job's complaints from a whirlwind by describing the creatures he has made. Leviathan, the great sea monster, is the last of them. The translation is the King James Version of 1611.
LIT-020: Miyamoto Musashi was a swordsman who, by his own account, fought more than sixty duels and never lost. In 1643 he withdrew to a cave in the south of Japan and wrote this book on strategy. He finished it a few weeks before his death in 1645. The Book of the Void is the last and shortest of its five parts.
LIT-021: Jia Dao was a Buddhist monk who gave up his vows to try for a government career. He was known for agonising over single words. A story about him hesitating between 'push' and 'knock' in a line gave Chinese its everyday word for weighing one's words.
LIT-022: Macbeth is on his way to murder King Duncan, who is asleep as a guest in his castle. He sees a dagger in the air in front of him and cannot tell whether it is real.
LIT-023: The best-known story in the Shahnama. The hero Rostam meets a young warrior on the battlefield and kills him, and learns too late that it is his own son, Sohrab. James Atkinson's English version was published in 1832. Matthew Arnold based his poem Sohrab and Rustum on the same story.
LIT-024: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, written around the year 1000. It was badly scorched in a library fire in 1731. In this passage Beowulf finds an ancient sword made by giants and kills Grendel's mother with it. The blade then melts away.
LIT-025: Milton was completely blind by the time he wrote Paradise Lost. He composed it in his head, mostly at night, and dictated it in the morning to whoever was at hand. It was published in 1667. He sold the rights for five pounds, with more to follow if it sold.
LIT-026: The Bhagavad Gita is a conversation between the warrior Arjuna and his charioteer, the god Krishna, on the eve of a battle. In chapter eleven Arjuna asks to see Krishna as he really is, and is terrified by what he sees. The Gita is part of the vast Sanskrit epic, the Mahabharata.
LIT-027: Blake never published this poem. It comes from a notebook of fair copies he made around 1803, and first appeared in print in 1863, thirty-six years after his death.
LIT-028: Dante was exiled from Florence in 1302 on political charges and never went back. He wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, and in Italian, when serious works were written in Latin. Canto three takes him through the gate of Hell. In the last canto he reaches Satan, frozen in ice at the centre of the earth.
LIT-029: In Attar's twelfth-century poem the birds of the world set out to find their king, the Simorgh. Thirty of them reach the end of the journey, and in Persian the name Simorgh can be read as thirty birds. The longer passage is from Edward FitzGerald's much shortened and very free version, Bird Parliament, published in 1889, six years after his death.
LIT-030: Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome from 161 to 180. He wrote these notes in Greek, for himself alone, much of it while commanding the army on the Danube frontier. He gave them no title. How they survived to be copied is not known.
LIT-031: The Art of War is a short book in thirteen chapters, traditionally credited to a general called Sun Tzu who lived around 500 BCE. Its central idea is that the best commander wins before the fighting starts. It has been studied by soldiers in East Asia for more than two thousand years.
LIT-032: In 756 a rebel general captured the Chinese capital. Du Fu was caught and held in the occupied city, apart from his family. He wrote this poem there the following spring. It is eight lines long, and is one of the most famous poems in Chinese.
LIT-033: In book eighteen of the Iliad, Achilles learns that his friend Patroclus has been killed by Hector. He resolves to go back to the fighting, although his mother Thetis has told him that his own death must follow soon after Hector's. Later in the book the god Hephaestus makes him new armour, including a shield that shows cities at peace and at war.
LIT-035: Swift was the dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin. He published this pamphlet in 1729 without his name. In the calm voice of an economist, it proposes that the poor of Ireland solve their problems by selling their babies as food for the rich. It is aimed at English policy in Ireland and at the people who wrote such proposals.
LIT-036: Frost published this nine-line poem in a magazine in 1920 and included it in his book New Hampshire in 1923. That book won him the first of his four Pulitzer Prizes.
LIT-037: The poem that opens The Flowers of Evil. Baudelaire lists the vices he shares with his reader and names boredom as the worst of them. T. S. Eliot borrowed its last line for The Waste Land.
LIT-038: One of the best-known stanzas in Edward FitzGerald's English version of the Rubáiyát, first published in 1859. The image of a hand that writes and moves on echoes the story of the writing on the wall in the Book of Daniel.
LIT-039: Li Bai is one of the two most celebrated poets of Tang dynasty China, with his friend Du Fu. Wine and the moon run through his work. A popular legend, with no historical basis, says he drowned when he leaned out of a boat, drunk, to embrace the moon's reflection.
LIT-043: Byron wrote this in the summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva. A huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia the year before had filled the atmosphere with ash, and across Europe that summer was cold, dark and wet. Mary Shelley began Frankenstein in the same house party.
LIT-044: Bashō wrote this at Hiraizumi in northern Japan in 1689. Five hundred years earlier it had been the capital of a powerful family, and the place where the hero Yoshitsune and his last followers were killed. Bashō records that he sat down there and wept.
LIT-045: The best-known speech in English drama. Hamlet weighs whether it is better to endure life or end it, and decides that fear of what comes after death is what keeps people going. The play was written around 1600.
LIT-046: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets were published in 1609, possibly without his agreement. Most of the first 126, including this one, are addressed to a young man. Who he was is not known.
LIT-047: Lear has given his kingdom to two of his daughters and been turned out of doors by both. In this scene he is on an open heath in a storm at night, with only his Fool beside him, shouting at the weather.
LIT-048: On the morning of his assassination, Caesar's wife begs him to stay at home because of bad omens. This is his answer. The play was written in 1599 and was one of the first staged at the new Globe theatre.
LIT-049: Richard returns from Ireland to find his army gone and his cousin in rebellion, and sits down on the ground to talk about how kings die. The play shows a king being deposed, which made it dangerous. In 1601 supporters of the Earl of Essex paid for a performance the day before their uprising against Elizabeth I.
LIT-050: Keats wrote his great odes in the spring and summer of 1819, when he was twenty-three. No single urn has been identified as the one in the poem. He seems to have combined vases and marbles he had seen in the British Museum and in books of engravings.
LIT-051: A friend Keats was living with in Hampstead said that Keats wrote this in one morning in the spring of 1819, sitting under a plum tree in the garden where a nightingale had nested. His younger brother Tom had died of tuberculosis a few months before.
LIT-052: Keats wrote this ballad in April 1819 in the middle of a long letter to his brother and sister-in-law in America. He took the title, which means the beautiful lady without pity, from a medieval French poem.
LIT-053: Keats wrote this sonnet in January 1818, at twenty-two. He had trained as a surgeon and had nursed his mother through tuberculosis, so he knew the disease well. He died of it in Rome three years later, at twenty-five.
LIT-055: Whitman wrote this after the assassination of Abraham Lincoln in April 1865. It is in regular rhyme and metre, unlike nearly everything else he wrote, and it was the most popular of his poems in his lifetime. He came to resent being asked for it.
LIT-059: The last complete poem Poe wrote. It was published in a New York newspaper two days after his death in October 1849. His wife Virginia, whom he had married when she was thirteen, had died of tuberculosis two years before.
LIT-060: Published in March 1849, the year Poe died. He reworked it from a much earlier poem of his own, written when he was eighteen.
LIT-061: Tennyson wrote Ulysses in October 1833, within weeks of hearing that his closest friend, Arthur Hallam, had died suddenly at twenty-two. He said it expressed his need to go forward and face life. The old hero who cannot stay at home comes from Dante more than from Homer.
LIT-062: On 25 October 1854, in the Crimean War, a misunderstood order sent about six hundred British light cavalry straight down a valley at Russian guns. Tennyson, then Poet Laureate, read the report in The Times and wrote the poem in a few minutes. It was in the newspapers six weeks after the battle.
LIT-063: Tennyson published The Kraken in 1830, when he was twenty. The kraken is a giant sea monster from Scandinavian legend. In the poem it sleeps on the sea bed until the end of the world.
LIT-064: Donne wrote his Holy Sonnets around 1609, and like nearly all his poems they circulated only in handwritten copies. They were printed in 1633, two years after his death. By then he had been famous for a decade as the dean of St Paul's Cathedral and the greatest preacher in London.
LIT-065: In late 1623 Donne fell dangerously ill with a fever. While recovering he wrote a set of meditations on the stages of the illness. This one begins with the sound of a church bell tolling for someone else's death. It is the source of two famous phrases, about no man being an island and about for whom the bell tolls.
LIT-066: Marvell was a member of Parliament for Hull and had worked alongside Milton in Cromwell's government. Almost none of his poems were printed while he was alive. They were published in 1681, three years after his death, by his housekeeper, who claimed to be his widow.
LIT-067: Herrick was a country vicar in Devon. He lost his parish during the English Civil War for his loyalty to the king, and in 1648 published his life's work, more than a thousand short poems, in a single volume. This is the best known.
LIT-069: Hopkins was a Jesuit priest who wrote this in 1885 while teaching in Dublin, isolated and deeply depressed. It is one of a group known as the terrible sonnets. He published almost nothing. A friend brought out his poems in 1918, twenty-nine years after his death.
LIT-070: The only book Rimbaud saw through the press himself. He wrote it in 1873, at eighteen, and finished it in the weeks after his lover, the poet Verlaine, shot him in the wrist in Brussels. He could not pay the printer, and nearly all the copies sat in a warehouse until 1901.
LIT-071: One of the short prose poems Baudelaire wrote in his last years. They were collected after his death in 1867 under the title Paris Spleen. He said he wanted a prose that was musical without metre or rhyme.
LIT-072: Villon was a university graduate and a thief, and is regarded as the leading French poet of the fifteenth century. By tradition he wrote this ballad while under sentence of hanging. In January 1463 the sentence was changed to ten years' banishment from Paris. Nothing is known of him after that.
LIT-075: Catullus's brother died and was buried near Troy, on the far side of the sea from Rome. Catullus made the journey to the grave and wrote these ten lines. The Latin words that end the poem, meaning hail and farewell, have been quoted ever since.
LIT-076: In book six of the Aeneid, Aeneas goes down into the underworld to meet the ghost of his father. Virgil died in 19 BCE with the poem not quite finished, and is said to have asked for it to be burned. The emperor Augustus ordered it published.
LIT-077: A song from the chorus of Sophocles's Antigone, first staged in Athens around 441 BCE. It lists what human beings have mastered: the sea, the earth, animals, speech, cities. Only death has no cure. The longer passage is in the translation Storr made for the Loeb Classical Library in 1912.
LIT-078: Gilgamesh, grieving for his friend and afraid of dying, meets Siduri, who keeps a tavern at the edge of the world. She tells him to go home and enjoy his life. Her speech survives on a clay tablet of about 1800 BCE. It was left out of the later standard version of the epic.
LIT-079: The speaker of Ecclesiastes calls himself Qoheleth, usually translated 'the Preacher' or 'the Teacher'. Tradition identified him with King Solomon, though the book was written many centuries after Solomon's time. The English is the King James Version of 1611.
LIT-080: The opening lines of the Masnavi, Rumi's poem of some twenty-five thousand couplets. A reed flute, cut from the reed bed, cries out to return to it. Rumi lived in Konya, in what is now Turkey, and began dictating the poem to a disciple around 1258.
LIT-082: Tagore wrote this poem in Bengali and translated it into English prose himself. The English Gitanjali was published in London in 1912 with an introduction by W. B. Yeats, and it won Tagore the Nobel Prize the following year. India was then under British rule.
LIT-084: Wang Wei was a poet, painter and musician, and a devout Buddhist. This is one of twenty short poems about places on his country estate. It is four lines of five characters each, and is among the most translated poems in Chinese.
LIT-085: Issa wrote this in 1819 after the death of his daughter Sato from smallpox. She was a little over a year old. Buddhist teaching compares the world to dew because it does not last.
LIT-086: Dostoevsky published Notes from Underground in 1864, the year his first wife and his brother both died. The narrator is a retired minor official in St Petersburg, forty years old, who has shut himself away to argue with the world.
LIT-087: A story told by one brother to another inside The Brothers Karamazov. Christ returns to earth in Seville at the height of the Spanish Inquisition, and the old Grand Inquisitor has him arrested. Dostoevsky finished the novel in November 1880 and died less than three months later.
LIT-088: Crime and Punishment appeared in monthly instalments through 1866. In 1849 Dostoevsky had himself been sentenced to death for belonging to a political discussion group. He was led out to be shot, reprieved at the last moment, and sent to a prison camp in Siberia for four years.
LIT-089: A whole chapter of Moby-Dick in which the narrator, Ishmael, tries to explain why the whiteness of the whale frightens him more than anything else about it. He runs through polar bears, albino people, ghosts, snow and the Milky Way.
LIT-090: Melville published this story in a magazine in 1853, without his name, two years after Moby-Dick had failed. A Wall Street lawyer hires a quiet copying clerk, who one day politely declines to do what he is asked, and goes on declining.
LIT-091: Joseph Conrad was Polish, and English was his third language. In 1890 he took a job as captain of a river steamer in the Congo, then the private colony of the king of Belgium. What he saw there became this short novel, published in 1899.
LIT-093: A short parable that Kafka published separately in 1915. It also appears in The Trial, where a priest tells it to the main character. Kafka asked for his unpublished manuscripts, The Trial among them, to be burned after his death. His friend Max Brod published them.
LIT-097: Poe published this story in January 1843 in a new magazine edited by a friend, and was paid ten dollars for it. The narrator insists throughout that he is perfectly sane.
LIT-098: Published in 1846, and one of the last stories Poe wrote. During carnival, a man leads an acquaintance who has insulted him down into his family's wine cellars, promising a taste of a rare sherry.
LIT-099: By his family's account, the central scenes came to Stevenson in a nightmare. He wrote a draft in three days, burned it after his wife criticised it, and wrote the whole story again in another few days. It was published in January 1886 and sold forty thousand copies in six months.
LIT-100: The Picture of Dorian Gray first appeared in an American magazine in 1890, after the editor had cut passages he thought improper. Wilde expanded it into a book the next year. In 1895 passages from it were read out against him in court. In this chapter the painter sees what has become of his portrait.
LIT-101: The diary of a minor St Petersburg clerk who becomes convinced that dogs are writing letters to each other and that he is the rightful king of Spain. As he gets worse, the dates at the top of the entries stop making sense. Gogol published it in 1835.
LIT-102: The chapter with the windmills. Cervantes had been a soldier, lost the use of his left hand in a sea battle, and spent five years as a captive in Algiers. He published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605, in his late fifties. The longer passage is in John Ormsby's translation of 1885.
LIT-104: Euripides entered Medea in the drama competition at Athens in 431 BCE, and it came last of three. The longer passage here is in the verse translation by Gilbert Murray, professor of Greek at Oxford. His translations of the Greek plays were staged in London in the early 1900s.
LIT-105: Euripides wrote The Bacchae at the end of his life, at the court of the king of Macedon. It was staged in Athens after his death and won first prize. The god Dionysus comes to Thebes in disguise, and the young king who refuses to honour him is torn apart by his own mother.
LIT-106: The first play of the Oresteia, the only trilogy of Greek tragedies to survive complete. It was staged in 458 BCE. Aeschylus had fought the Persians at Marathon. The epitaph on his grave mentions the battle and says nothing about his plays.
LIT-107: Aristotle treated this play as the model of what a tragedy should be. When it was first staged in Athens, it won only second prize. Oedipus sets out to find the killer of the previous king so as to end a plague, and the trail leads to himself.
LIT-108: The last hour of Faustus, who sold his soul to the devil for twenty-four years of knowledge and power. Marlowe was the most successful playwright in London before Shakespeare. He was stabbed to death in 1593, at twenty-nine, in a house in Deptford, in a quarrel said to be over the bill.
LIT-109: Webster based this play on a real case. Around 1510 an Italian duchess, a young widow, secretly married her steward and had children with him. Her brothers, one of them a cardinal, had her killed. In this scene her murderers come for her.
LIT-110: The Spanish Tragedy, staged in the late 1580s, set the fashion for plays of revenge on the London stage. It has a ghost, a play within the play and a hero who may or may not be mad, all of which reappear in Hamlet. Kyd was arrested and tortured in 1593 and died the following year.
LIT-111: A single line from Seneca's tragedy Phaedra, on small griefs and great ones. Seneca's plays may have been written to be read aloud to guests, and may never have been staged. They were the main model for tragedy when English playwrights took it up fifteen centuries later.
LIT-112: The first sonnet of a group of twelve that Nerval published in 1854. He had suffered several mental breakdowns, and died in Paris in January 1855. Eliot's poem The Waste Land quotes a line of it near the end.
LIT-113: A Latin poem in six books setting out the teaching of the Greek philosopher Epicurus: that everything is made of atoms, that the soul dies with the body, and that there is therefore nothing to fear. It was lost for centuries. One copy turned up in a German monastery in 1417.
LIT-114: Pascal was a mathematician and physicist. He was planning a defence of Christianity when he died in 1662, at thirty-nine, and left about a thousand notes for it on loose sheets of paper. His family and friends published a selection in 1670. Editors have been rearranging them ever since.
LIT-115: Schopenhauer published his main work in 1818, when he was thirty, and it was ignored for more than thirty years. He lived alone in Frankfurt with a succession of poodles. A book of essays in 1851 finally brought him readers, and by his death in 1860 he was famous.
LIT-116: The best-known passage in the Zhuangzi, a Daoist book of the fourth and third centuries BCE. It takes up only a few lines at the end of the second chapter. Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, and wakes unable to say which of the two is the dreamer.
LIT-117: Cao Xueqin came from a family that had been rich and close to the emperor and then lost everything. He wrote this novel in poverty and left it unfinished when he died in the 1760s. It was first printed in 1791, with an ending supplied by another hand. The longer passage is in the 1892 translation by Henry Bencraft Joly, a British consular official.
LIT-119: Kamo no Chōmei was a court poet in Kyoto who became a Buddhist monk at fifty and went to live in a hut ten feet square in the hills. In this short book of 1212 he looks back on the disasters he had seen in the capital: fire, whirlwind, famine and earthquake. Then he describes the hut.
LIT-120: Heraclitus wrote a single book, around 500 BCE, and it is lost. About a hundred and thirty sentences from it survive because later writers quoted them. Even in the ancient world he was nicknamed 'the Obscure'. This fragment says the world is an ever-living fire.
LIT-121: A hymn from the tenth and latest book of the Rigveda, the oldest scripture of India. It asks what existed before there was anything, and how creation began. It ends by suggesting that perhaps even the highest god does not know. The longer passage here is in Ralph Griffith's translation, published in the 1890s.
LIT-122: Ezekiel was a priest among the Jews deported to Babylon in the early sixth century BCE. His book opens with this vision by a river there: four winged creatures, wheels within wheels covered in eyes, and a throne above them. Later Jewish mystics built a whole tradition of contemplation on it.
LIT-123: One of the most commented-on verses in the Qur'an. It compares the light of God to a lamp set in a niche. For centuries it has been written on the glass lamps that hang in mosques. The longer passage is in John Medows Rodwell's translation of 1861.
LIT-124: One of the short, early chapters of the Qur'an, dating from Muhammad's first years of preaching in Mecca. It has eleven verses and describes the Day of Judgement, when people will be scattered like moths and the mountains will be like tufts of wool.
LIT-125: The Song of Songs is a collection of love poetry in the Hebrew Bible. It does not mention God. Jewish and Christian readers have traditionally taken it as a picture of the love between God and his people. The English is the King James Version.
LIT-126: John of the Cross was a Spanish friar who worked with Teresa of Ávila to reform the Carmelite order. In 1577 friars opposed to the reform seized him and held him for nine months in a tiny cell in Toledo. He escaped through a window. This poem dates from soon afterwards.
LIT-127: One of the shortest and best-known Buddhist scriptures. In its most widely used Chinese version it has only about 260 characters. It is chanted daily in temples across East Asia.
LIT-128: The opening poem of the Poetic Edda. A seeress, questioned by the god Odin, tells the history of the world from its creation to its destruction at Ragnarök and its rebirth. The main manuscript was written in Iceland around 1270. It was kept in Denmark for three centuries and returned to Iceland in 1971.
LIT-129: A boy called Nachiketa is sent by his angry father to the house of Death. Death is away, and to make up for keeping a guest waiting he grants the boy three wishes. For the third the boy asks what happens to a person after they die.
LIT-131: The Tao Te Ching is a book of eighty-one short chapters, about five thousand Chinese characters in all. Legend says Laozi wrote it at the request of a border guard, then rode off west and was never seen again. The longer passage is in James Legge's translation of 1891.
LIT-133: The first part of the Popol Vuh tells how the gods made the earth and then tried several times to make people. Those made of mud dissolved, and those made of wood had no minds. The ones who lasted were made of maize. This English text is Lewis Spence's retelling of 1908.
LIT-134: A spell from the Egyptian Book of the Dead. It was often carved on a stone scarab laid over the heart of the mummy. In it the dead person asks their own heart not to testify against them when it is weighed in the judgement hall. The Papyrus of Ani is in the British Museum.
LIT-135: The Babylonian creation epic is named after its opening words. In the fourth tablet the young god Marduk kills Tiamat, the sea, and splits her body in two to make the sky and the earth. It was recited each year at the New Year festival in Babylon. The longer passage is in Leonard King's translation of 1902.
LIT-136: Meister Eckhart was a Dominican friar who preached in German to ordinary congregations in the Rhineland in the early 1300s. Late in life he was put on trial for heresy. He died before the verdict. In 1329 the Pope condemned twenty-eight statements taken from his work.
LIT-139: The opening of the Hebrew Bible, in the English of the King James Version, published in 1611. That translation was made by about fifty scholars working in six committees, and it drew heavily on William Tyndale's version of eighty years earlier.
LIT-140: Psalm 23 is traditionally credited to King David, who was a shepherd as a boy. It is the most widely known of the hundred and fifty psalms, and is read at funerals in both Jewish and Christian traditions. The English is the King James Version.
LIT-141: In 586 BCE the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and deported much of its population. This psalm is spoken by the exiles, who sit by the rivers of Babylon and are asked by their captors to sing. It has been set to music many times.
LIT-142: The prophet Elijah has fled into the desert from Queen Jezebel, who wants him dead, and hides in a cave on Mount Horeb. A wind, an earthquake and a fire pass by. God is in none of them. Then comes what the King James Version calls a still small voice.
LIT-143: Isaiah's account of the vision in the Temple that made him a prophet, in about 740 BCE. He sees winged seraphim around God's throne, and one touches his lips with a burning coal. The seraphim's threefold cry of holy passed into both Jewish and Christian worship.
LIT-144: From the prologue to the Gospel of John, the last of the four gospels to be written. Where the others begin with Jesus's birth or baptism, John begins before creation. The English is the King James Version.
LIT-145: From a letter Paul wrote around 54 CE to the Christian community he had founded in the Greek city of Corinth. Mirrors at that time were made of polished bronze, and gave a dim, imperfect image. Corinth was known for making them.
LIT-146: A Latin hymn about the Day of Judgement, written in the thirteenth century and traditionally credited to a Franciscan friar. For centuries it was sung at every Catholic funeral mass. Its plainchant melody has been quoted by composers from Berlioz to Rachmaninoff and in many film scores.
LIT-147: The closing lines of a short Buddhist scripture. A copy printed in China in 868 and found in a sealed cave at Dunhuang is the oldest dated printed book in the world. It is in the British Library. The longer passage is in William Gemmell's English version of 1912, made from the Chinese translation of about 400 CE.
LIT-148: Tradition says these two verses are what the Buddha said at the moment of his enlightenment. He addresses the builder of the house, meaning the craving that leads to rebirth, and tells him that the house will not be built again.
LIT-149: A poem in Coptic from the Nag Hammadi library, a set of early Christian and Gnostic books that farmers found buried in a jar in Egypt in 1945. A female voice describes herself in a long chain of opposites. Nothing is known about who wrote it, or for whom.
LIT-150: Thin sheets of gold, inscribed in Greek and folded into the graves of initiates in Greece and southern Italy from around 400 BCE. They give the dead person directions for the underworld: which spring to avoid, which to drink from, and what to say to the guardians. The longer passage is in Gilbert Murray's translation of 1903.
LIT-151: Linji was a Chinese Zen master who died in 866. He taught with shouts, blows and startling statements meant to knock students out of fixed ideas. The school named after him became the largest in Chinese Zen. In Japan it is known as Rinzai.
LIT-152: A Tibetan text read aloud beside the dying and the dead to guide them through the forty-nine days between one life and the next. Tradition says it was composed in the eighth century, hidden, and rediscovered in the fourteenth. The English title was chosen by its first Western editor in 1927, by analogy with the Egyptian book.
LIT-154: A short text credited to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus. The oldest known versions are in Arabic, from around the eighth or ninth century, and it reached Europe in Latin in the twelfth. Alchemists treated it as the foundation of their art. Isaac Newton made his own English translation.
LIT-155: The Zafarnama, 'Letter of Victory', is a letter in Persian verse from Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, to the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. He wrote it in 1705, after losing his four sons and most of his followers. It accuses the emperor of breaking an oath sworn on the Qur'an.
LIT-156: Frederick Douglass had escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1838. In 1852 the Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society of Rochester, New York, asked him to give their Fourth of July address. He chose to speak on the fifth. About six hundred people heard it.
LIT-157: Lincoln gave this speech on 4 March 1865, with the Civil War almost won. It is about seven hundred words long. He declines to blame the South alone and suggests the war was a judgement on the whole country for slavery. He was shot forty-one days later.
LIT-158: Lincoln spoke for about two minutes at the dedication of a military cemetery at Gettysburg, four and a half months after the battle. The main speaker of the day, Edward Everett, had just spoken for two hours. Everett wrote to Lincoln the next day to say that Lincoln had done it better.
LIT-160: In 399 BCE Socrates, aged seventy, was tried in Athens before a jury of five hundred citizens for impiety and corrupting the young. 'Apology' here means a speech in defence. Plato was at the trial. How closely his version follows what Socrates actually said is not known.
LIT-161: In October 1859 John Brown led a raid on the federal armoury at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to start an uprising of enslaved people. He was captured, tried and sentenced to hang. He made this statement to the court without notes. He was executed a month later.
LIT-162: Danton was one of the leaders of the French Revolution. In the spring of 1794 his former allies had him arrested and condemned. He was guillotined on 5 April. Witnesses reported that he told the executioner to show his head to the crowd afterwards, since it was worth seeing.
LIT-163: Eugene Debs, the leader of the American Socialist Party, was convicted in 1918 for a speech opposing the First World War. He made this statement before being sentenced to ten years. In 1920 he ran for president from his prison cell and received nearly a million votes.
LIT-164: In 1877 Chief Joseph and about seven hundred Nez Perce, most of them women, children and the old, fought their way more than a thousand miles towards Canada to avoid being forced onto a reservation. The army stopped them forty miles from the border. His words were translated and written down by an army officer, and scholars are unsure how exact the record is.
LIT-165: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who tried to unite the tribes from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico against the loss of their land. In 1810 he met the governor of Indiana Territory at Vincennes and argued that the land belonged to all the tribes together, so no single tribe could sell it. He was killed in battle in 1813.
LIT-166: Calgacus led the tribes of northern Scotland against a Roman army in about 83 CE. This speech before the battle was written by the Roman historian Tacitus, whose father-in-law commanded the Roman side.
LIT-167: At the end of the first year of the war between Athens and Sparta, the Athenian leader Pericles spoke at the public funeral of the dead. He used the occasion to describe what Athens stood for. The text is the historian Thucydides's version. Pericles died of the plague two years later.
LIT-169: Patrick Henry gave this speech in a church in Richmond, Virginia, in March 1775, urging the colony to arm against Britain. Nobody wrote it down. The text we have was reconstructed forty-two years later by his biographer, from the memories of men who had been there.
LIT-170: Roosevelt gave this speech at the Sorbonne in Paris in April 1910, a year after leaving the presidency, on his way home from a long safari in Africa. One paragraph, about the man in the arena, is the part that is remembered.
LIT-173: William Jennings Bryan was thirty-six and a former congressman from Nebraska. At the Democratic convention in Chicago in 1896 he spoke for farmers and debtors against tying the dollar to gold. The delegates went wild, and nominated him for president the next day. He lost the election.
LIT-174: In 63 BCE Cicero was consul of Rome and learned that a senator, Catiline, was plotting to seize power. He delivered this attack in the Senate with Catiline sitting there. The other senators moved away from Catiline's bench. He left Rome that night.
LIT-175: Demosthenes spent more than a decade warning the Athenians that King Philip of Macedon meant to rule all of Greece. This speech, from 341 BCE, is usually considered the strongest of the series. Philip defeated Athens three years later. Charles Rann Kennedy's translation dates from 1852.
LIT-176: On 20 April 1653 Cromwell lost patience with what was left of the Parliament that had fought the Civil War, went to the chamber, and had soldiers clear it. No one recorded his exact words. The versions that circulate were put together later from several accounts.
LIT-177: William Pitt the Elder made this speech in 1763, opposing a tax on cider that would have let officials enter private houses. No full text survives. The passage about the poor man's cottage, which the king himself may not enter, was preserved by a later writer.
LIT-178: In 1898 the novelist Émile Zola published an open letter to the president of France on the front page of a Paris newspaper. It accused the army of framing a Jewish officer, Alfred Dreyfus, for treason and covering it up. Zola was convicted of libel and fled to England. Dreyfus was cleared in 1906.
LIT-179: Giordano Bruno was a former friar who taught that the universe is infinite and contains countless worlds. The Roman Inquisition held him for seven years and condemned him as a heretic. A witness reported what he said to his judges on hearing the sentence. He was burned in Rome on 17 February 1600.
LIT-181: Robert Emmet led a rising against British rule in Dublin in July 1803, which collapsed within hours. He was tried in September, spoke from the dock after the verdict, and was executed the next day, at twenty-five. Several versions of the speech were printed, and they differ.
LIT-182: In 1924 two wealthy Chicago teenagers, Leopold and Loeb, admitted killing a fourteen-year-old boy. Their lawyer, Clarence Darrow, had them plead guilty and then argued before the judge for three days against the death penalty. They were sentenced to life in prison.
LIT-183: In 324 BCE, at Opis on the Tigris, Alexander announced he was sending his older Macedonian soldiers home, and the army mutinied. This is the speech he is said to have made to them. It was written by the historian Arrian more than four hundred years later. The longer passage is in Edward Chinnock's translation of 1884.
LIT-184: On 20 April 1814, after abdicating, Napoleon said goodbye to the soldiers of his Old Guard in the courtyard of the palace of Fontainebleau, embraced their general and kissed their flag. He then left for exile on the island of Elba. He was back in France within a year.
LIT-185: In the summer of 1849 a French army crushed the short-lived Roman Republic. On 2 July Garibaldi addressed his volunteers in St Peter's Square. He told them he could offer no pay and no rest, and listed the hardships he could offer. About four thousand followed him out of the city.
LIT-186: Toussaint Louverture was born into slavery and became the leader of the revolution in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, now Haiti. In 1802 the French seized him by a trick and shipped him to France. He died in a fortress in the mountains the following April. Haiti declared its independence eight months later.
LIT-187: Brutus has allowed Mark Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral, on condition that he does not blame the killers. Antony keeps to the letter of it. In a few minutes, by praising Brutus over and over, he turns the Roman crowd against him.
LIT-188: Red Jacket was the leading orator of the Seneca nation. In 1805 a missionary from Boston came to the Seneca at Buffalo Creek and asked to preach among them. This is the reply. Red Jacket asks why, if there is only one true religion, the white people disagree so much about it.
LIT-190: Balzac died in Paris in August 1850, five months after marrying the Polish countess he had courted by letter for eighteen years. Victor Hugo gave the address at his grave in the Père Lachaise cemetery.
LIT-501: Dickens published this in weekly instalments in 1859, in a magazine he had just launched himself. It is set in London and Paris around the French Revolution. He leaned heavily on Thomas Carlyle's history of the Revolution, which he claimed to have read hundreds of times.
LIT-502: Anna Karenina came out in instalments in a Russian magazine through the 1870s. Constance Garnett learned Russian in her thirties and went on to translate around seventy volumes, including works by Tolstoy, Dostoevsky and Chekhov. For decades, hers was the English that readers knew them in.
LIT-504: Eliot wrote most of this in his early twenties. It sat unpublished for years until Ezra Pound pushed the editor of Poetry magazine in Chicago to print it in 1915. The Italian epigraph comes from Dante's Inferno.
LIT-506: The last story in Dubliners. Joyce wrote it in 1907 while living in Trieste. The book took years longer to appear, held up by publishers and printers who were nervous about what was in it, and finally came out in 1914.
LIT-507: From Through the Looking-Glass, where Alice finds it printed backwards and has to hold it up to a mirror. Carroll had written the first verse years earlier for a magazine he made at home to amuse his family. 'Chortle' and 'galumph' were invented here and are now in the dictionary.
LIT-508: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, after the Medici returned to power in Florence and he was sacked, tortured and sent to live on his farm. He hoped it would get him a job. It did not, and the book was only printed in 1532, five years after he died.
LIT-509: The Analects were put together by Confucius's students and their students after his death. This is the very first line. The longer passage here is in the translation by James Legge, a Scottish missionary in Hong Kong who became Oxford's first professor of Chinese.
LIT-510: The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses that tradition says were spoken by the Buddha. It is among the most widely read of all Buddhist texts. Max Müller's translation from the Pali appeared in 1881 in the Sacred Books of the East, the series he edited at Oxford.
LIT-511: Goethe worked on Faust, off and on, for about sixty years. Part One came out in 1808. The longer passage is in the 1870 translation by Bayard Taylor, an American travel writer and poet, who kept the metres and rhymes of the German.
LIT-512: The Poetics is thought to be Aristotle's lecture notes. This passage is his definition of tragedy. A second part, on comedy, is lost.
LIT-513: From the second part of Rilke's New Poems, 1908. He had spent time in Paris working as secretary to the sculptor Rodin, who taught him to look at objects long and hard. The torso is an ancient Greek fragment in the Louvre.
LIT-514: Brooke wrote this at the end of 1914, in the first months of the First World War. He died the following April, aged twenty-seven, of blood poisoning from an insect bite on his way to Gallipoli. He is buried on the Greek island of Skyros.
LIT-515: Horace addresses this to a woman called Leuconoe, and tells her to stop asking astrologers how long she has left. The famous phrase is a farming one. 'Carpe' means to pluck or pick, the way you would fruit.
LIT-516: From Gypsy Ballads, the 1928 book that made Lorca famous across Spain. Eight years later, in the first weeks of the Spanish Civil War, he was shot by Nationalist forces near Granada. His body has never been found.
LIT-517: Pessoa wrote as dozens of invented poets, each with his own biography, style and opinions. He called them heteronyms. This poem, about the poet as a faker, he signed with his own name. When he died in 1935 he left a trunk holding more than twenty-five thousand pages, most of them unpublished.
LIT-518: Kipling said the poem was inspired by Leander Starr Jameson, who led a disastrous raid in South Africa and took the consequences quietly. Two lines from it are written over the players' entrance to Centre Court at Wimbledon.
LIT-519: From Songs of Experience, 1794. Blake lived in London nearly all his life. He did not send his books to a printer. He etched the words and pictures onto copper plates himself, printed them at home, and coloured each copy by hand with his wife Catherine.
LIT-520: Byron wrote this in June 1814, the morning after a London party where he had seen his cousin's wife, Anne Wilmot, in a black mourning dress covered in spangles. It was published the next year with music, as one of his Hebrew Melodies.
LIT-521: Burns spent his last years collecting and patching up old Scottish songs, and said he took this one down from a country singer. How much is his and how much is older is hard to say. It was written to be sung.
VAULT-526: Mondrian painted this in 1930. Besides black and white, the only colours in it are red, blue and yellow. It is very similar to his Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow of the same year.
LIT-523: Hölderlin published this poem in 1804. Two years later he was committed to a clinic in Tübingen, and from 1807 he lived in a tower room in the town for the rest of his life.
LIT-524: Ghalib lived in Delhi and wrote in Urdu and Persian. He was a poet at the court of the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and lived through the uprising of 1857. This is the opening couplet of one of his best-known ghazals.
LIT-525: Yamamoto Tsunetomo was a retainer of the Nabeshima lords of Saga, in southern Japan. After his lord died he became a Buddhist monk. A younger samurai wrote down his talk over several years, and the collection was finished around 1716.
LIT-526: Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332. He wrote the Muqaddimah in 1377 as the introduction to a history of the world. It sets out how societies form, grow strong and decline. He later served as a judge in Cairo.
LIT-527: Kleist published this short dialogue in December 1810 in a Berlin newspaper he edited. In it a dancer argues that puppets move with more grace than people, because they have no self-consciousness. Kleist died the following year at thirty-four.
LIT-528: The first of ten short dream pieces Sōseki published in a Tokyo newspaper in 1908. A dying woman asks the dreamer to bury her and wait at her grave. Sōseki had left his post at Tokyo Imperial University the year before to write full time.
LIT-529: Lautréamont was the pen name of Isidore Ducasse, who was born in Montevideo to French parents. He finished Les Chants de Maldoror in Paris in 1869 and died the next year at twenty-four. The Surrealists took up the book in the 1920s, and this sentence became one of their touchstones.
LIT-530: Hildegard was the abbess of a convent on the Rhine. She set down her visions in three books; this passage comes from the last, the Book of Divine Works, which she finished in her seventies. She also composed music and wrote on medicine.
LIT-531: Yu Xuanji lived in the Tang capital Chang'an in the ninth century. She was a concubine and later a Daoist nun. About fifty of her poems survive.
LIT-532: Apollinaire printed this poem with its letters running down the page like rain. It appeared in a magazine in 1916 and in his book Calligrammes in 1918, the year he died. It is shown here as a plain line, not in its shape.
LIT-533: Wordsworth wrote the poem in 1804. It draws on a walk he took with his sister Dorothy beside Ullswater in April 1802, which she described in her journal. It was first published in 1807, and he added a stanza when he revised it in 1815.
LIT-534: Dickinson wrote the poem around 1861. It was first printed in 1891, five years after her death, in the second series of her Poems, edited by Thomas Wentworth Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd. The text here follows that edition, which changed some of her wording and punctuation.
LIT-536: Bashō composed this haiku in 1686 in Edo, now Tokyo. It is the most widely known haiku in Japanese. This English version is by Lafcadio Hearn, from an essay on frogs in his book Exotics and Retrospectives, published in 1898.
LIT-537: Hardy dated the poem 31 December 1900. It was first printed in The Graphic on 29 December 1900 under the title By the Century's Deathbed, and collected in Poems of the Past and the Present in 1901.
LIT-538: Fog appeared in Chicago Poems, published in 1916, the book that made Sandburg's name. He was working as a newspaperman in Chicago at the time. He later won three Pulitzer Prizes, two for poetry and one for his biography of Abraham Lincoln.
LIT-539: Chaucer began The Canterbury Tales around 1387 and left it unfinished when he died in 1400. Its pilgrims are riding from Southwark to the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury. The text is in Middle English, from W. W. Skeat's edition for the Clarendon Press.
LIT-540: Ovid finished the Metamorphoses around 8 CE, the year the emperor Augustus banished him from Rome to Tomis on the Black Sea. The poem fills fifteen books and tells about 250 myths of transformation. This passage comes from Book VIII.
LIT-541: Cavafy published the poem in 1911. He lived most of his life in Alexandria, where he worked as a clerk in a government irrigation office. The title comes from Plutarch's account of the night before Mark Antony's defeat. E. M. Forster printed this translation in 1923, which helped bring Cavafy to English readers.
LIT-542: The poem was first published in Poetry magazine in April 1913. Pound wrote that it began with faces he saw on leaving a train at La Concorde station in Paris, and that he cut it down from a thirty-line draft over about a year. It is a standard example of Imagism.
LIT-543: The poem was first printed in The Dial in January 1920 and collected in Tulips and Chimneys in 1923. William F. Cody, the showman known as Buffalo Bill, had died in January 1917. The spacing follows the 1923 book.
LIT-544: Lawrence wrote the poem while living at Taormina in Sicily, where he stayed from 1920 to 1922. It was printed in The Dial in July 1921 and collected in Birds, Beasts and Flowers in 1923. The passage shown is the end of the poem.
LIT-545: Swann's Way, the first volume of In Search of Lost Time, was published in 1913 at Proust's own expense after several publishers turned it down. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation appeared in 1922, the year Proust died.
LIT-546: Madame Bovary ran as a serial in the Revue de Paris in 1856. Flaubert was tried for offending public morals early in 1857 and acquitted, and the novel came out as a book that year. Eleanor Marx-Aveling, a daughter of Karl Marx, made this first English translation in 1886.
LIT-547: The Social Contract was published in Amsterdam in 1762. It was condemned in Geneva, Rousseau's birthplace, the same year. G. D. H. Cole's translation was first issued in 1913.
LIT-548: This is a ghazal from the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, the collection of lyric poems Rumi composed in Konya after he met the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz in 1244. R. A. Nicholson published this translation in 1898. The passage shown is the first half of the poem.
LIT-549: Yeats wrote the poem in London in 1888 and published it in the National Observer in December 1890. Innisfree is a small uninhabited island in Lough Gill, County Sligo, where he spent much of his childhood.
LIT-550: Written in 1891 and published in 1892, the poem is addressed to Maud Gonne. It is a free adaptation of a sonnet by the sixteenth-century French poet Pierre de Ronsard.
LIT-551: Yeats wrote the poem in 1926, when he was sixty-one. It opens The Tower, his collection of 1928. He had seen Byzantine mosaics at Ravenna in 1907 and in Sicily in 1925.
LIT-552: Hughes wrote the poem in 1920 on a train crossing the Mississippi, on his way to visit his father in Mexico. It was published in The Crisis in June 1921 and collected in The Weary Blues in 1926.
LIT-553: The poem was first published in The Crisis in December 1922. It was collected in The Weary Blues in 1926, Hughes's first book.
LIT-554: Mrs Dalloway was published by the Hogarth Press in May 1925. The novel follows Clarissa Dalloway through a single day in London in June 1923 as she prepares to give a party. Woolf's working title was The Hours.
LIT-555: War and Peace was published in full in 1869. In this passage Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, called Andrew in this translation, lies wounded on the field at Austerlitz, the battle of 2 December 1805 in which Napoleon defeated the Russian and Austrian armies. The translation is by Louise and Aylmer Maude.
LIT-556: The Bell Jar, Plath's only novel, was published in London in January 1963 under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas, a month before her death. It did not appear in the United States until 1971.
LIT-557: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings was published in 1969 and is the first of Angelou's seven autobiographies. It covers her childhood and adolescence in Stamps, Arkansas, in St. Louis and in California.
LIT-558: Giovanni's Room was published in 1956. Baldwin wrote it while living in France, where he had moved in 1948. Knopf, the publisher of his first novel, turned the book down, and it was issued by Dial Press.
LIT-559: Thomas recorded the piece in New York in 1952 for Caedmon Records. It grew out of a radio talk he gave for the BBC in 1945. It was published as a book after his death in November 1953.
LIT-560: Neruda's memoirs were published in 1974, the year after his death, under the Spanish title Confieso que he vivido. Hardie St. Martin's English translation appeared in 1977. Neruda received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
