LIT-561: The short prose piece Borges y yo was collected in El hacedor in 1960. James E. Irby's translation appeared in Labyrinths, the New Directions selection of 1962 that helped establish Borges's reputation in English.
LIT-562: A Shropshire Lad was published in 1896, partly at Housman's own expense, after a publisher had turned it down. Housman was then professor of Latin at University College London. The book sold slowly at first and became widely read during the Boer War and the First World War.
LIT-563: The Age of Innocence was published in 1920 and is set in the New York society of the 1870s in which Wharton grew up. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, making her the first woman to win the prize for the novel.
LIT-564: The Sun Also Rises was published by Scribner's in October 1926. It draws on a trip Hemingway made with friends to the festival of San Fermín in Pamplona in July 1925. These are the last lines of the book.
LIT-565: The Sound and the Fury was published in October 1929. Its four sections follow the decline of the Compson family of Mississippi, and the second is narrated by Quentin Compson on a day in June 1910. Faulkner received the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1949.
LIT-566: The poem dates from 1915 and appeared in the second edition of Mandelstam's first book, Stone, in 1916. The catalogue of ships is the long list of Greek forces in Book II of the Iliad. Mandelstam was arrested in 1938 and died that December in a transit camp near Vladivostok.
LIT-567: Nineteen Eighty-Four was published in June 1949. Orwell wrote most of it on the Scottish island of Jura while seriously ill with tuberculosis, and he died in January 1950. The line is a slogan of the ruling Party in the novel.
LIT-568: Le Mythe de Sisyphe was published in Paris in 1942, during the German occupation. Justin O'Brien's English translation appeared in 1955. This is the last sentence of the essay. Camus received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.
LIT-569: Huis clos was first staged in Paris in May 1944, at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier. Three people find themselves shut in a room together after their deaths. This English translation is by Stuart Gilbert.
LIT-570: L'Innommable was published in French in 1953, and Beckett's own English version followed in 1958. These are the closing words of the novel, the last of the three that began with Molloy. Beckett received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.
LIT-571: East of Eden was published in 1952 and is set largely in the Salinas Valley of California, where Steinbeck was born. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962.
LIT-572: The Catcher in the Rye was published in July 1951 and is Salinger's only novel. These are its last lines. He published no new work after 1965.
LIT-573: Lolita was first published in Paris in 1955 by the Olympia Press, after American publishers had declined it. The American edition followed in 1958. Nabokov, who was born in St Petersburg, wrote the novel in English.
LIT-574: On the Road was published in 1957. Kerouac typed a full draft in three weeks in April 1951, on a continuous roll of paper about 120 feet long.

LIT-706: Stevenson published Requiem in his collection Underwoods in 1887. He died in Samoa in 1894 and was buried on Mount Vaea above his house. The poem is on a bronze plaque on his tomb.
LIT-707: Wilde wrote De Profundis in Reading Gaol between January and March 1897, as a long letter to Lord Alfred Douglas. He was serving two years with hard labour. His friend Robert Ross published a shortened version in 1905, five years after Wilde's death, and it opens with these lines.
LIT-708: The Grand Inquisitor is a story told by Ivan Karamazov to his brother Alyosha in Book V of The Brothers Karamazov. In it Christ returns to Seville during the Spanish Inquisition and is arrested, and the aged cardinal speaks to him in his cell. The novel was serialised in 1879 and 1880; Constance Garnett's translation appeared in 1912.
LIT-709: Van Gogh wrote to the younger painter Émile Bernard from Arles in 1888. The two had met in Paris and exchanged letters and sketches. This English text is from Anthony M. Ludovici's 1912 selection, made from a German edition of the letters.
LIT-710: Van Gogh moved to Arles in the south of France in February 1888 and wrote often to his brother Theo, an art dealer in Paris who supported him. This extract is from Anthony M. Ludovici's 1912 English selection of the letters.
LIT-711: Van Gogh painted outdoors around Arles through 1888, often in the strong north wind of the region. He reported on the work in letters to his brother Theo in Paris. This extract is from Anthony M. Ludovici's 1912 English selection.
LIT-712: Émile Bernard was a French painter fifteen years younger than Van Gogh. Van Gogh's letters to him were among the first to be published, in the 1890s. This extract is from Anthony M. Ludovici's 1912 English selection.
LIT-713: Leonardo planned a treatise on painting and filled notebooks with drafts for it, written in mirror script. This passage opens his argument that painting ranks above poetry. Jean Paul Richter published the notebooks with an English translation in 1883.
LIT-714: This fragment is on a sheet now in the British Library's Codex Arundel, a bound collection of Leonardo's loose papers. The text breaks off, and the gaps marked in it are in the manuscript. Jean Paul Richter published it with an English translation in 1883.
LIT-715: Leonardo studied the flight of birds for years and drew designs for a flying machine. Jean Paul Richter, who published the notebooks with an English translation in 1883, read this note as referring to that machine. No flight is recorded.
LIT-716: Michelangelo sent this sonnet to the painter and biographer Giorgio Vasari in 1554, when he was nearly eighty and working on St Peter's in Rome. John Addington Symonds published his rhymed English translation of the sonnets in 1878.
LIT-717: Dürer spent 1505 to 1507 in Venice, where he painted an altarpiece for the German merchants of the city. He wrote a series of letters from there to his friend Willibald Pirckheimer, a scholar in Nuremberg.
LIT-718: Whistler gave this lecture at Prince's Hall in London on 20 February 1885, at ten in the evening. He repeated it at Cambridge and Oxford and reprinted it in The Gentle Art of Making Enemies in 1890.
LIT-719: Whistler painted the Thames at dusk in a series he called Nocturnes during the 1870s. He gave this lecture at Prince's Hall in London on 20 February 1885 and reprinted it in The Gentle Art of Making Enemies in 1890.
LIT-720: William Morris was a designer, poet and socialist who ran a firm making wallpaper, textiles and furniture. He gave this lecture to the Birmingham Society of Arts and School of Design on 19 February 1880. It was printed in Hopes and Fears for Art in 1882.
LIT-721: Morris gave this address to the Birmingham Society of Arts and School of Design on 19 February 1879. It was printed in Hopes and Fears for Art in 1882, a collection of five of his lectures.
LIT-722: Kandinsky was a Russian painter working in Munich when he wrote this book in German. It was published at the end of 1911, the year he helped found the Blue Rider group. M. T. H. Sadler's English translation appeared in 1914.
LIT-723: These are the first lines of the book Kandinsky published in Munich at the end of 1911. He painted some of the first abstract pictures in European art in the same years. M. T. H. Sadler's English translation appeared in 1914.
LIT-724: Walter Pater was a fellow of Brasenose College, Oxford. His Studies in the History of the Renaissance came out in 1873. He removed this conclusion from the second edition in 1877 and restored it, slightly changed, in 1888.
LIT-725: The Decay of Lying is a dialogue between two speakers, Vivian and Cyril, named after Wilde's sons. It first appeared in the magazine The Nineteenth Century in January 1889 and was revised for the book Intentions in 1891. Vivian is speaking here.
LIT-726: The Critic as Artist is a dialogue between two speakers, Gilbert and Ernest. It first appeared in two parts in The Nineteenth Century in July and September 1890, and was collected in Intentions in 1891. Gilbert is speaking here.
LIT-727: Joshua Reynolds was the first president of the Royal Academy of Arts in London. He gave fifteen discourses to its students between 1769 and 1790. This is from the second, delivered at the prize-giving on 11 December 1769.
LIT-728: The critic Paul Gsell wrote down his conversations with Rodin at the sculptor's studios in Meudon and Paris and published them in French in 1911. Rodin was seventy. This passage closes the first chapter, where Gsell has challenged him about copying nature.
LIT-729: Louis Sullivan was a Chicago architect whose firm built some of the first steel-framed office towers, among them the Wainwright Building in St. Louis. This essay appeared in Lippincott's Magazine in March 1896. The phrase is often shortened to form follows function.
LIT-730: Robert Henri was an American painter and a leader of the group known as the Ashcan School. He taught for many years in New York, where his students included Edward Hopper and George Bellows. His student Margery Ryerson compiled this book from his notes, letters and talks, and it was published in 1923.
LIT-731: The Nature of Gothic is a chapter in the second volume of The Stones of Venice, published in 1853. Ruskin was the leading English art critic of his time. William Morris reprinted the chapter as a separate book at his Kelmscott Press in 1892.
LIT-732: Keats was twenty-two when he wrote this letter to his two brothers from Hampstead in late December 1817. The phrase negative capability appears nowhere else in his writing. Charles Wentworth Dilke, named in the passage, was a friend and neighbour.
LIT-733: Benjamin Bailey was an Oxford student of theology and a close friend of Keats. Keats wrote to him on 22 November 1817 while finishing his long poem Endymion. The first Book he mentions is the first book of that poem.
LIT-734: Keats's brother George emigrated to America with his wife Georgiana in 1818. Keats wrote them long journal letters, adding to each over weeks. This passage is from the one he kept from February to May 1819, the spring in which he wrote most of his odes.
LIT-735: Whitman published the first edition of Leaves of Grass himself in Brooklyn in July 1855. It held twelve untitled poems and this prose preface, and did not carry his name on the title page. He dropped the preface from later editions.
LIT-736: Lyrical Ballads, by Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, first appeared without a preface in 1798. Wordsworth added one to the second edition, dated 1800, and enlarged it in 1802. He was living at Grasmere in the Lake District.
LIT-737: Shelley wrote this essay in Italy in 1821 as a reply to The Four Ages of Poetry by his friend Thomas Love Peacock. It was not printed in his lifetime. Mary Shelley published it in 1840, eighteen years after his death.
LIT-738: The Poet is the first essay in Emerson's Essays: Second Series, published in Boston in 1844. Emerson had been a Unitarian minister before he became a lecturer and essayist in Concord, Massachusetts. Walt Whitman later sent him a copy of the first Leaves of Grass.
LIT-739: Henry James wrote this essay in reply to a lecture on fiction given by the novelist Walter Besant in London in April 1884. It appeared in Longman's Magazine in September 1884. James reprinted it in his book Partial Portraits in 1888.
LIT-740: Joseph Conrad was born in Poland, served for years as a merchant seaman and wrote in English, his third language. He wrote this preface for his third novel, a sea story serialised in the New Review in 1897. It was printed at the end of the serial rather than in the first book edition.
LIT-741: Stevenson published this essay in the Fortnightly Review in April 1881, two years before Treasure Island came out as a book. It was collected after his death in Essays in the Art of Writing in 1905.
LIT-742: Poe published this essay in Graham's Magazine, a Philadelphia monthly, in April 1846. In it he claims to set out, step by step, how he wrote The Raven, which had appeared the year before.
LIT-743: Woolf first published a version of this essay as Modern Novels in the Times Literary Supplement in April 1919. She revised it under this title for The Common Reader, published by the Hogarth Press in 1925, the same year as Mrs Dalloway.
LIT-744: Alexei Pleshcheyev was a poet and the literary editor of the journal Severny Vestnik, which printed several of Chekhov's long stories. Chekhov was twenty-eight and still practising as a doctor. Constance Garnett's English translation of the letters appeared in 1920.
LIT-745: Chekhov's grandfather was a serf who bought his family's freedom, and his father kept a grocery shop in Taganrog. Alexei Suvorin was the owner of the newspaper Novoye Vremya and Chekhov's publisher. Constance Garnett's English translation of the letters appeared in 1920.
LIT-746: Wollstonecraft travelled through Scandinavia in the summer of 1795 with her infant daughter and a maid, on business for the American merchant Gilbert Imlay. She published twenty-five letters from the journey in London in 1796. It was the last book she issued in her lifetime.
LIT-747: Margaret Fuller edited The Dial, the Transcendentalist magazine, and published an early version of this work there in 1843 as The Great Lawsuit. The expanded book came out in New York in 1845, while she was literary critic of the New-York Tribune. She died in a shipwreck off Fire Island in 1850.
LIT-748: Marx and Engels wrote the Manifesto in German for the Communist League, and it was printed in London in February 1848. Samuel Moore's English translation, revised by Engels, was published in 1888 and became the standard English text. These are its last lines.
LIT-749: The first women's rights convention in the United States met at Seneca Falls, New York, on 19 and 20 July 1848. Elizabeth Cady Stanton drafted this declaration for it on the model of the Declaration of Independence. One hundred people signed it, sixty-eight women and thirty-two men.
LIT-750: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration in Philadelphia on 4 July 1776. Thomas Jefferson wrote the draft as one of a committee of five, and Congress edited it before the vote. Jefferson was thirty-three.
LIT-751: Thomas Paine was an English-born writer who had come to Philadelphia in 1774. The first number of The Crisis was printed in the Pennsylvania Journal on 19 December 1776, during the retreat of Washington's army across New Jersey. He issued thirteen numbered Crisis papers in all, the last in 1783.
LIT-752: Dorothy Wordsworth kept this journal at Dove Cottage in Grasmere, where she lived with her brother William. On 15 April 1802 the two walked along the shore of Ullswater. William wrote his poem on the daffodils two years later.
LIT-753: Samuel Pepys was a naval administrator who kept a diary in shorthand from 1660 to 1669. The Great Fire began in a baker's house in Pudding Lane early on Sunday 2 September 1666 and burned for four days. Pepys watched it that evening from the south bank of the Thames.
LIT-754: Beethoven wrote this letter to his brothers Carl and Johann in October 1802 at Heiligenstadt, a village outside Vienna, when he was thirty-one and losing his hearing. He never sent it. It was found among his papers after his death in 1827.
LIT-755: This letter in pencil was found in Beethoven's desk after his death in 1827. It gives the day and month but no year, and it does not name the woman. Later research dated it to July 1812, when Beethoven was at the spa of Teplitz in Bohemia; who she was is still argued over.
LIT-756: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in London on 24 November 1859, more than twenty years after his voyage on the Beagle. These are the last sentences of the first edition. In the second edition, in 1860, he added the words by the Creator after breathed.
LIT-757: Murasaki Shikibu served at the Heian court as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi, whom this translation calls Queen Akiko. Her diary covers the years 1008 to 1010. She is the author of The Tale of Genji. This English version by Annie Shepley Omori and Kochi Doi was published in Boston in 1920.
LIT-758: Napoleon married Josephine de Beauharnais in Paris on 9 March 1796 and left two days later to command the French army in Italy. He was twenty-six. He wrote this letter from his headquarters at Marmirolo during the siege of Mantua, after she had joined him briefly in Milan.
LIT-759: Mozart was twenty-one and travelling with his mother in search of a court post when he wrote this from Mannheim. It is his greeting to his father Leopold, in Salzburg, for Leopold's name-day and birthday. Lady Wallace's English translation of the letters appeared in 1865.
LIT-760: Martin Luther was a friar and professor of theology at Wittenberg. He published this short treatise in November 1520, in Latin and in German, with an open letter to Pope Leo X. He was excommunicated in January 1521.
LIT-761: Thoreau began his journal on 22 October 1837, two months after graduating from Harvard, when he was twenty. The person asking the question is generally taken to be Ralph Waldo Emerson, his neighbour in Concord. He kept the journal for the rest of his life, and it was published in fourteen volumes in 1906.
LIT-762: Thomas Wentworth Higginson was a writer and abolitionist who had published advice to young authors in the Atlantic Monthly in April 1862. Dickinson, then thirty-one, sent him this unsigned note with four poems and her name on a card in a separate envelope. They wrote to each other until her death in 1886.
LIT-763: Higginson met Dickinson for the first time at her family's house in Amherst on 16 August 1870, after eight years of letters. He wrote down what she said in a letter to his wife that evening and printed it in the Atlantic Monthly in 1891. The words are hers as he reported them.
LIT-764: Ben Jonson published this song in The Forest, part of his collected Works of 1616. Jonson was an English playwright and poet, a contemporary of Shakespeare. The poem was later set to a tune that is still sung.
LIT-765: Thomas Wyatt was a courtier and diplomat under Henry VIII. He died in 1542, and this poem was first printed in 1557 in the anthology known as Tottel's Miscellany. Wyatt is credited with bringing the sonnet into English.
LIT-766: Christopher Marlowe was an English playwright and poet who died in 1593. This pastoral lyric was first printed in 1599, after his death, and in a fuller version in the anthology England's Helicon in 1600. Walter Raleigh wrote a well-known reply to it.
LIT-767: Robert Burns wrote this song in December 1791 and sent it to Agnes McLehose, who was about to sail for Jamaica. It was published in the Scots Musical Museum in 1792. It is written in Scots.
LIT-768: Emily Brontë wrote this poem in 1845. It was published in 1846 in Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell, the volume the three Brontë sisters issued under pen names. Emily Brontë died in 1848, a year after her novel Wuthering Heights appeared.
LIT-769: Christina Rossetti wrote this poem in 1848, when she was eighteen. It was published in 1862 in Goblin Market and Other Poems, her first commercially published collection.
LIT-770: This is the fourteenth of the forty-four Sonnets from the Portuguese, which Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote during her courtship with Robert Browning in 1845 and 1846. The sequence was published in 1850.
LIT-771: Gaius Valerius Catullus was a Roman poet of the late Republic, born in Verona. About twenty-five of his poems concern a woman he calls Lesbia. This is the fifth poem in the surviving collection of his work.
LIT-772: This two-line epigram is poem 85 in the collection of Catullus, a Roman poet who died around 54 BCE. In Latin it opens with the words Odi et amo. It is a single elegiac couplet.
LIT-773: The Amores are three books of love elegies by the Roman poet Ovid, his earliest published work. Many of them are addressed to a woman he calls Corinna. This is the fifth elegy of the first book.
LIT-774: Francesco Petrarca, known in English as Petrarch, was an Italian poet and scholar who lived from 1304 to 1374. His Canzoniere gathers 366 poems, most of them about a woman he calls Laura. This sonnet is number 61 in the collection.
LIT-775: Sappho lived on the Greek island of Lesbos around 600 BCE. Most of her poetry survives only in fragments. This one, known as fragment 16, was recovered in the twentieth century from a papyrus found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt.
LIT-776: The Georgics is a poem in four books about farming, by the Roman poet Virgil. It was completed around 29 BCE. The second book deals with trees and vines and closes with a passage in praise of country life, from which this comes.
LIT-777: The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon, is a book of love poetry in the Hebrew Bible. It is traditionally attributed to King Solomon. The wording here is that of the King James Version of 1611.
LIT-778: La Vita Nuova is an early work by Dante Alighieri that joins poems and prose to tell of his love for Beatrice. It was written in Florence in the 1290s. This sonnet, which begins Tanto gentile in Italian, is one of its poems. The translation is by the painter and poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti, first published in 1861.
LIT-779: Hafez was a Persian poet who lived in Shiraz in the fourteenth century. His collected poems are known as the Divan. This English version is by Gertrude Bell, the British traveller and writer, from her Poems from the Divan of Hafiz, published in 1897.
LIT-780: This is the last poem in Gertrude Bell's Poems from the Divan of Hafiz, published in 1897. Hafez was a Persian poet of fourteenth-century Shiraz. Lines from this ghazal are carved on his tomb in Shiraz.
LIT-781: Li Bai was a Chinese poet of the Tang dynasty who lived from 701 to 762. Ezra Pound made this English version from the notes of the scholar Ernest Fenollosa and published it in Cathay in 1915. Cathay gives the poet's name in its Japanese form, Rihaku.
LIT-782: John Keats wrote this letter to Fanny Brawne from College Street, Westminster; it is postmarked 13 October 1819. The two became engaged that year. Keats died of tuberculosis in Rome in February 1821, and his letters to her were first published in 1878.
LIT-783: Sara Teasdale was an American poet born in St. Louis in 1884. This poem appeared in her collection Rivers to the Sea in 1915 and again in Love Songs in 1917. Love Songs won the Columbia Poetry Prize in 1918, the award that later became the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.
LIT-784: Gitanjali is a book of devotional songs that Rabindranath Tagore translated into English prose from his own Bengali. It was published in London in 1912 with an introduction by W. B. Yeats. Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.
LIT-785: Kabir was a fifteenth-century poet and weaver of Varanasi whose songs are sung by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs. Rabindranath Tagore translated one hundred of them into English, assisted by Evelyn Underhill, and published them as Songs of Kabir in 1915. This is the fifty-second.
LIT-786: D. H. Lawrence published this poem in Look! We Have Come Through! in 1917, a sequence about the first years of his life with Frieda Weekley, whom he married in 1914. The book places the poem at Icking, in Bavaria. Gloire de Dijon is a variety of yellow climbing rose.
LIT-787: John Clare was the son of a farm labourer in Helpston, Northamptonshire, and became known in the 1820s as a poet of rural life. He wrote this poem during his years in the Northampton asylum, where he lived from 1841 until his death in 1864. It was not printed in his lifetime.
LIT-788: John Clare grew up in Helpston, Northamptonshire, and worked as a farm labourer. Emmonsail's Heath, also written Emmonsales, lay near the village. Bumbarrel is a local name for the long-tailed tit.
LIT-789: John Clare wrote this poem in the Northampton asylum, where he spent the last twenty-three years of his life and went on writing. He had made his name in 1820 with Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery. Many of his poems are close observations of birds.
LIT-790: Amy Lowell published this poem in Pictures of the Floating World in 1919. Lowell was an American poet from Brookline, Massachusetts, and a leading figure in the Imagist movement. Her love poems of these years are generally understood to be addressed to her companion, the actress Ada Dwyer Russell.
LIT-791: This poem comes from Amy Lowell's Pictures of the Floating World, published in 1919. The book takes its title from the Japanese word ukiyo-e, the name for woodblock prints of everyday life. Lowell won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1926, the year after her death.
LIT-792: Gerard Manley Hopkins was an English Jesuit priest. He wrote this poem in 1881 after a visit to Inversnaid, on the east shore of Loch Lomond in Scotland. Almost none of his poetry was printed in his lifetime; his friend Robert Bridges published it in 1918.
LIT-793: Hopkins wrote this poem in 1879, when he was a priest in Oxford, after a row of poplars along the Thames at Binsey was cut down. The edition prints it with the subtitle felled 1879. It was first published in 1918, twenty-nine years after his death.
LIT-794: William Wordsworth wrote this poem in the spring of 1798, when he was living at Alfoxden in Somerset. It was published later that year in Lyrical Ballads, the collection he issued with Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
LIT-795: John Keats wrote this sonnet on 30 December 1816 in a timed contest with his friend Leigh Hunt, each writing on the same subject. It was published in 1817 in Poems, his first book. Keats was twenty-one.
LIT-796: This is one of the few poems by Emily Dickinson printed in her lifetime. It appeared without her name in the Springfield Republican in 1866 under the title The Snake. The wording here follows the 1891 Poems, Second Series, whose editors regularised her punctuation and kept that title.
LIT-797: Song of Myself opened the first edition of Leaves of Grass, which Walt Whitman published at his own expense in Brooklyn in 1855. He revised the book for the rest of his life. This is the beginning of the sixth of the fifty-two sections in the final edition.
LIT-798: Thoreau gave Walking as a lecture many times from 1851 onward. He prepared it for print in his last months, and it appeared in the Atlantic Monthly in June 1862, a month after his death in Concord, Massachusetts.
LIT-799: John Muir was born in Scotland in 1838 and came to California in 1868. In the summer of 1869 he went into the Sierra Nevada with a flock of sheep and kept a journal. He published it in 1911 as My First Summer in the Sierra; this is from the entry for June 6.
LIT-800: This passage comes from My First Summer in the Sierra, which John Muir published in 1911 from the journal he kept in 1869. It falls in the entry for July 27, written near Lake Tenaya. Muir helped found the Sierra Club in 1892 and was its first president.
LIT-801: Samuel Taylor Coleridge wrote Frost at Midnight in February 1798 at his cottage in Nether Stowey, Somerset. The poem is addressed to his infant son Hartley, asleep beside him. These are its last ten lines.
LIT-802: Charles Darwin sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836. His account of the voyage was first published in 1839 and revised in 1845. This passage comes from the last chapter, where he looks back over the journey.
LIT-803: Richard Jefferies was an English nature writer, born on a small farm near Swindon in Wiltshire in 1848. The Story of My Heart, published in 1883, is his spiritual autobiography. It begins on a hill of the Wiltshire downs that he climbed as a young man. He died in 1887, aged thirty-eight.
LIT-804: Gilbert White was the curate of Selborne, a village in Hampshire, where he recorded the local wildlife for decades. The Natural History of Selborne, published in 1789, is made up of his letters to two fellow naturalists. This one, to Daines Barrington, is dated May 20, 1777.
LIT-805: Edward Thomas made the train journey behind this poem on 24 June 1914, when his express stopped briefly at Adlestrop station in Gloucestershire. He wrote the poem in January 1915. Thomas was killed at the Battle of Arras in April 1917, and the poem was published that year.
LIT-806: Edward Thomas was a literary critic and prose writer who began writing poems in late 1914, encouraged by his friend Robert Frost. He wrote more than 140 poems before he was killed at Arras in April 1917. This one appeared in his Poems of 1917, published after his death.
LIT-807: Thomas Hardy placed this poem last in Moments of Vision, the collection he published in 1917 at the age of seventy-seven. Hardy lived at Max Gate, near Dorchester in Dorset. He died in 1928.
LIT-808: Robert Frost published this poem in North of Boston, his second book, which came out in London in 1914 and in New York the following year. Frost had farmed in Derry, New Hampshire, before moving his family to England in 1912.
LIT-809: Mary Austin published The Land of Little Rain in 1903. Its sketches describe the desert country between the Sierra Nevada and Death Valley; she lived for years in the Owens Valley, on its western edge. This is the opening of the first sketch.
LIT-810: Du Fu lived from 712 to 770 and is counted among the greatest poets of the Tang dynasty. He wrote this poem late in life, while travelling by boat down the Yangtze. The translation is from The Jade Mountain, the 1929 English version of the anthology Three Hundred Poems of the Tang Dynasty.
LIT-811: Wang Wei was a Tang dynasty poet, painter and court official who lived in the eighth century. He was a devout Buddhist and kept a country estate in the Zhongnan mountains south of the capital, Chang'an. The translation is from The Jade Mountain, published in 1929.
LIT-812: This poem by the Tang dynasty poet Wang Wei is included in Three Hundred Poems of the Tang Dynasty, an anthology compiled in the eighteenth century. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu translated the whole anthology into English as The Jade Mountain, published in New York in 1929.
LIT-813: Titus Lucretius Carus wrote On the Nature of Things, a Latin poem in six books that sets out the philosophy of Epicurus. It opens with this address to Venus as the power that brings living things into being. William Ellery Leonard's English verse translation was published in 1916.
LIT-814: In the Book of Job, a righteous man who has lost everything demands an answer from God. In chapter 38 God answers him out of the whirlwind with a series of questions about the making of the world. The wording is that of the King James Version of 1611.
LIT-815: Shelley wrote The Mask of Anarchy in Italy in September 1819, after news reached him of the Peterloo Massacre, in which cavalry charged a crowd at a reform meeting in Manchester. He sent it to Leigh Hunt for publication, but Hunt held it back and it was not printed until 1832, ten years after Shelley's death.
LIT-816: Shelley wrote this sonnet in Italy late in 1819. The king of the first line is George III, who died the following January. The poem was first published by Mary Shelley in her 1839 edition of his Poetical Works.
LIT-817: Byron wrote the Dedication to Don Juan in Venice in 1818. It attacks the poet laureate Robert Southey and the foreign secretary Lord Castlereagh, who had earlier served as chief secretary for Ireland. The Dedication was left out when the first cantos were published in 1819 and was printed after Byron's death.
LIT-818: In April 1655 troops of the Duke of Savoy killed members of the Waldensian Protestant community in the valleys of Piedmont. John Milton, then a secretary in Oliver Cromwell's government, wrote this sonnet in response. It was published in his Poems of 1673.
LIT-819: Siegfried Sassoon served as an infantry officer on the Western Front and was decorated for bravery. In July 1917 he made a public statement against the continuation of the war and was sent to Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh. This poem was published in Counter-Attack and Other Poems in 1918.
LIT-820: Sassoon wrote this poem in March 1917 at Rouen, a base town behind the British lines in France. Staff officers in the British army wore scarlet tabs on their collars. The poem appeared in Counter-Attack and Other Poems in 1918.
LIT-821: William Lloyd Garrison printed these words in the first issue of his abolitionist newspaper The Liberator, published in Boston on 1 January 1831. He was twenty-five. The paper appeared weekly for thirty-five years, until slavery was abolished in the United States in 1865.
LIT-822: Ida B. Wells was a journalist born into slavery in Mississippi in 1862. After three of her friends were lynched in Memphis in 1892 she began investigating lynchings across the South. The Red Record, published in Chicago in 1895, sets out statistics and case reports for the years 1892 to 1894.
LIT-823: Wilfred Owen retells the story of Abraham and Isaac from Genesis 22 in this poem, written in 1918. Owen was killed in action on 4 November 1918, one week before the Armistice. The poem was first published in the 1920 Poems, edited by Siegfried Sassoon.
LIT-824: Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century BCE. In this passage God speaks through the prophet and rejects the worship of a people who neglect justice. The wording is that of the King James Version of 1611.
LIT-825: In the sixth canto of the Purgatorio, the poet Sordello embraces Virgil on learning that they both come from Mantua. Dante then breaks off the story to denounce the Italy of his own day, torn by wars between and within its cities. Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in exile from Florence. Longfellow's translation was published in 1867.
LIT-826: Emma Goldman was born in 1869 in Kovno, in the Russian Empire, and emigrated to the United States in 1885. She became a leading anarchist speaker and writer. This essay began as a lecture and was published in 1910 in Anarchism and Other Essays. She was deported to Russia in 1919.
LIT-827: Carl Sandburg published this poem in Chicago Poems in 1916, his first major collection. Sandburg was born in Galesburg, Illinois, in 1878, the son of Swedish immigrants. When the book appeared he was working as a newspaper reporter in Chicago and had earlier been an organiser for the Social Democratic Party in Wisconsin.
VAULT-555: Van Gogh made this in September 1889 at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy, in the south of France. He had entered the asylum as a voluntary patient that May and stayed for a year. The sheet is painted in thinned oils over chalk on pink paper.
VAULT-556: Adeline Ravoux was the 13-year-old daughter of Arthur Ravoux, who kept the inn at Auvers-sur-Oise, north of Paris, where Van Gogh rented a room from May 1890. He painted her in the last months of his life. He died at the inn that July.
VAULT-557: Van Gogh painted this in the autumn of 1889 while he was a patient at the psychiatric hospital near Saint-Rémy, in southern France. His doctor allowed him to work outdoors. It shows men repairing the pavement of a village street under large plane trees, a scene he described in a letter to his brother Theo.
VAULT-558: This is one of the series Monet painted in 1890 and 1891 of the wheat stacks in a field beside his house at Giverny. The stacks stood fifteen to twenty feet high. In May 1891 he showed fifteen of the canvases together at the Galerie Durand-Ruel in Paris.
VAULT-559: Monet made twelve paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare, a railway station in Paris, in 1877. This one shows the glass and iron train shed, with steam from the locomotives rising under the roof.
VAULT-560: Rembrandt painted this in 1631, when he was about twenty-five. It is a character study and not a commissioned portrait: the man wears a gold chain, a steel gorget and a plumed beret from the artist's collection of costumes. The sitter is not identified. He was once thought to be Rembrandt's father, and he posed for the artist more than once.
VAULT-561: This print is from One Hundred Views of Famous Places in Edo, the last large series Hiroshige designed. It shows a room at the end of a moon-viewing party, with ships on Edo Bay under the autumn moon. Edo is now Tokyo. Hiroshige died in 1858, the year after this design was published.
VAULT-562: Goya made this print by 1818, in the years after the war between Spain and Napoleon's France. It is an aquatint, a way of etching areas of tone into a copper plate. It shows a huge figure sitting at the edge of a landscape and looking back over his shoulder.
VAULT-563: The boy was a son of the Count of Altamira, who ordered portraits of his family from Goya in the 1780s. He stands in a red suit holding a pet magpie on a string. The bird has the painter's calling card in its beak, three cats watch it, and a cage of finches sits on the floor. Manuel was born in 1784 and died in 1792.
VAULT-564: This is a tapestry cartoon, a full-size painting made as a guide for weavers. Goya designed tapestries for the Spanish royal residences, and this one belonged to a series for the dining room of the Royal Palace of El Pardo, outside Madrid.
VAULT-565: Dürer engraved this plate in Nuremberg in 1504. Adam holds a branch with a tablet that gives the artist's name, his city and the year in Latin. Dürer had been studying the proportions of the human body, and many drawings for the two figures survive.
VAULT-566: This pen drawing of a grazing steer is one of Dürer's earliest studies of an animal, made about 1496. The date 1508 on the sheet was added by another hand and is wrong. Dürer was born in Nuremberg, trained as a goldsmith in his father's shop and then with the painter Michael Wolgemut.
VAULT-567: Degas drew his friend and fellow painter Édouard Manet about 1868. He made several drawings and etchings of Manet in the 1860s. Both men were born in Paris, two years apart.
VAULT-568: Degas made this in 1877 by drawing in pastel over a monotype, a single print taken from an inked plate. The plate is one of the widest he ever used. The view takes in the dancers on stage and the tops of the instruments in the orchestra pit.
VAULT-569: Degas worked on this painting between 1879 and 1886. It shows a woman in a hat shop holding a hat, with others displayed on stands beside her. Hat making was then a respected trade for women in Paris, and Degas returned to the subject several times.
VAULT-570: This canvas, about six feet wide, shows four dancers tying their shoes. It may be one dancer seen from four sides. Degas painted it about 1895 and put in the circles in the foreground with his thumb.
VAULT-571: Hortense Fiquet met Cézanne in Paris in 1869 and married him in 1886. He painted her more than two dozen times. This is one of four portraits that show her in the same red dress, made between 1888 and 1890.
VAULT-572: Cézanne painted this still life about 1893. The table edge does not line up from one side of the cloth to the other, and the bottle leans. It was the first of his works to enter the Art Institute of Chicago.
VAULT-573: L'Estaque is a fishing village on the Mediterranean coast just west of Marseille. Cézanne painted more than a dozen views of the bay from there during the 1880s. This one, from about 1885, looks over the roofs of the village and across the water to the hills.
VAULT-574: Mont Sainte-Victoire rises east of Aix-en-Provence, the town where Cézanne was born and died. He painted it again and again in the last twenty years of his life. He made this view about 1904 from a small road leading out of Aix, with two umbrella pines in front of the mountain.
VAULT-575: Fire destroyed most of the Houses of Parliament in London on the night of 16 October 1834, and crowds watched from the banks of the Thames. Turner was among them. He showed two paintings of the fire in 1835. The other is in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
VAULT-576: Flüelen is a small town at the southern end of Lake Lucerne in Switzerland. Turner travelled to Switzerland in the summers between 1841 and 1845 and made a group of finished watercolours from those trips. This one is dated 1845, six years before he died.
VAULT-577: Blake painted this watercolour about 1803 to 1805 for Thomas Butts, a London civil servant who bought his work for many years. It illustrates chapter 10 of the Book of Revelation. Saint John sits writing on the island of Patmos while an angel stands over him with one foot on the sea and one on the land.
VAULT-578: Fernando Niño de Guevara was made a cardinal in 1596 and Inquisitor General of Spain in 1599. He later became archbishop of Seville. El Greco painted him about 1600 in Toledo, where the artist had lived since 1577.
VAULT-579: El Greco was born on Crete, worked in Venice and Rome, and settled in Toledo in 1577. He painted this subject many times, and several versions survive. Christ is shown alone and close up, wearing the crown of thorns and looking upward.
VAULT-580: This was the central painting of the high altarpiece of the church of Santo Domingo el Antiguo in Toledo. The altarpiece was El Greco's first major commission in Spain, and he painted this canvas between 1577 and 1579. The Virgin rises on a crescent moon above the apostles gathered at her empty tomb.
VAULT-581: El Greco trained on Crete as a painter of icons. In the late 1560s he moved to Venice and then to Rome before settling in Toledo. He painted this Crucifixion there between about 1600 and 1610.
VAULT-582: The man in the top hat is William Tom Warrener, an English painter who was a friend of Toulouse-Lautrec in Paris. He is shown talking with two women at the Moulin Rouge, the Montmartre dance hall that opened in 1889. Lautrec painted this in 1892 as a study for a colour lithograph of the same title.
VAULT-583: The Cirque Fernando was a circus in Montmartre, in Paris. A trick rider is about to stand on her horse and jump through a paper hoop held by a clown, while the ringmaster follows with a whip. Toulouse-Lautrec painted this in 1887 and 1888, when he was in his early twenties.
VAULT-584: The child is Schiele's nephew, the son of his sister Gertrude and the painter Anton Peschka. Schiele drew him in 1916 with no background, wrapped in a patterned cloth. Schiele died two years later, aged twenty-eight, in the influenza pandemic.
VAULT-585: Munch painted this in 1893, the year of his first version of The Scream. A girl in a nightgown stands in a dark room and looks out at the city through the window.
VAULT-586: Munch's sister Sophie died of tuberculosis when he was thirteen. He painted her on her sickbed several times under the title The Sick Child and made prints of the subject between 1894 and 1896. This lithograph shows only her head against the pillow. It was printed in Paris by Auguste Clot.
VAULT-587: The man on the shore is Munch's friend Jappe Nilssen, an art critic, at Åsgårdstrand, a fishing village south of Oslo. Munch cut the design in heavily grained wood in 1896 and let the grain show in the print. He coloured the impressions by hand, so each one is different.
VAULT-588: This colour lithograph is from the years when Munch worked between Norway, Berlin and Paris and turned many of his subjects into prints. It shows a woman with long red hair, seen to the waist, looking straight ahead.
VAULT-589: The model is Victorine Meurent, who also posed for Manet's Olympia and Luncheon on the Grass. She stands in a pink dressing gown beside a grey parrot on a perch, holding a small bunch of violets. Manet showed the painting at the Paris Salon of 1868.
VAULT-590: Berthe Morisot was a painter who exhibited with the Impressionists. She married Manet's brother Eugène in 1874. This is one of two portraits Manet painted of her in winter clothes about 1871 or 1872, and he kept it for the rest of his life.
VAULT-591: Marguerite Charpentier was the wife of the Paris publisher Georges Charpentier and held a salon attended by writers and artists. Renoir painted her in 1878 with her daughter Georgette, who sits on the family dog, and her son Paul, who is dressed like his sister, as was usual for small boys. The painting was shown at the Salon of 1879.
VAULT-592: In 1892 the French state asked Renoir for a painting for the Musée du Luxembourg, the museum for living artists in Paris. He painted this subject several times. The version the state bought is now in the Musée d'Orsay, and this is another of them.
VAULT-593: Renoir painted this in 1881 on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant on the Seine at Chatou, west of Paris. The two models were not sisters. The painting was shown at the seventh Impressionist exhibition in 1882.
VAULT-594: Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg were acrobats at the Cirque Fernando in Paris. They hold oranges that the audience has thrown to them as gifts. Renoir set them in the circus ring but painted them in his studio in 1879.
VAULT-595: A parade was the free show that performers gave outside a circus tent to draw in a paying crowd. Seurat painted this one in 1887 and 1888. It was his first night scene, lit by gas lamps, and he showed it at the Salon des Indépendants in Paris in 1888.
VAULT-596: This is Seurat's last full study for A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, the large painting now in the Art Institute of Chicago. La Grande Jatte is an island in the Seine on the edge of Paris. He painted the study in 1884 and showed the finished picture at the eighth Impressionist exhibition in 1886.
VAULT-597: This small oil sketch on a wood panel is one of many studies Seurat made for Bathers at Asnières, the large painting now in the National Gallery in London. The painting shows men resting and bathing on the bank of the Seine at Asnières, an industrial suburb of Paris. Seurat was in his early twenties.
VAULT-598: Gauguin stayed with Vincent van Gogh in Arles, in the south of France, for about nine weeks at the end of 1888. This is one of seventeen canvases he finished there. It shows women of the town walking in the public garden across from Van Gogh's house. The mistral is the strong cold wind of the region.
VAULT-599: Gauguin painted this at Pont-Aven in Brittany in 1889. It shows a woman with red hair throwing herself into a green sea. He exhibited it that year at the Café Volpini in Paris, in a show he organised with his friends beside the World's Fair.
VAULT-600: Rodin modelled this figure in 1880 or 1881 and planned for it to stand with a figure of Eve on either side of The Gates of Hell, his bronze doors for a museum in Paris that was never built. The pose draws on Michelangelo, whose work he had studied in Italy in 1876. This bronze was cast in 1910.
VAULT-601: In 1891 the Société des Gens de Lettres, the French writers' society, asked Rodin for a monument to the novelist Honoré de Balzac, who had died in 1850. This terracotta is one of his studies from that year. Rodin worked on the monument for seven years, and the society refused the finished figure in 1898.
VAULT-602: This is Rodin's earliest surviving life-size figure, modelled in Brussels in 1875 and 1876. The model was a young Belgian soldier, Auguste Neyt. The figure first held a spear, which Rodin removed. It looked so lifelike that he was falsely accused of casting it from the model's body.
VAULT-603: The Generalife is the summer palace and garden beside the Alhambra in Granada, Spain. Sargent painted this watercolour there in 1912. The woman at the easel is his sister Emily, who was also a painter, with two companions watching her work.
VAULT-604: The couple are the painters Wilfrid and Jane Emmet de Glehn, friends who travelled with Sargent. Jane is at her easel beside a fountain in the gardens of the Villa Torlonia at Frascati, near Rome. Sargent painted it in 1907, the year he gave up most of his portrait commissions to paint outdoors.
VAULT-605: Homer spent 1881 and 1882 in Cullercoats, a fishing village on the north-east coast of England. He painted this watercolour in 1883, after he had returned to the United States. A fisherwoman walks along the shore in a strong wind, with boats behind her inside the sandbar.
VAULT-606: Homer painted this in 1865, in the months after the American Civil War ended. A former Union soldier cuts wheat with a scythe. His army jacket and canteen lie on the ground at the lower right. Homer had covered the war as an illustrator for Harper's Weekly.
VAULT-607: Homer did not take up watercolour until he was thirty-seven. He painted in the Bahamas, Bermuda, Cuba and Florida on winter trips late in his life. This sheet, from 1899, shows a man lying on a beach beside the wreck of his boat after a storm.
VAULT-608: Homer lived at Prouts Neck on the coast of Maine from 1883 until his death in 1910. The Atlantic surf there was his main subject in those years. He worked on this painting from 1900 to 1903 and began it as a watercolour.
VAULT-609: Whistler went to Venice in 1879 with a commission from the Fine Art Society in London for a set of etchings. He had just been made bankrupt after his libel case against the critic John Ruskin. This plate shows palaces on a canal at night. He varied the film of ink left on the plate, so impressions differ.
VAULT-610: Southampton Water is an inlet of the English Channel on the south coast of England. Whistler painted it at nightfall in 1872. He called his night scenes Nocturnes, a word borrowed from music, and made a series of them in the 1870s.
VAULT-611: Cassatt was born in Pennsylvania and lived in France for most of her life. She began using pastel in the 1870s. This drawing, from 1901, shows a mother and child, a subject she returned to throughout her career.
VAULT-612: This is one of ten colour prints Cassatt made in 1890 and 1891, after she saw a large exhibition of Japanese woodblock prints in Paris. A woman, a nursemaid and a baby ride in a horse-drawn omnibus across the city. Cassatt was born in Pennsylvania and worked in France.
VAULT-613: Utamaro designed this print about 1793 for a series that sorts women into types of character by their looks. He was known for half-length pictures of women seen close up. The background of this impression is printed with pink mica, and only two impressions from the series have it.
VAULT-614: Utamaro designed this triptych of woodblock prints about 1796 or 1797. Women and children chase fireflies beside a stream on a summer evening, using fans to catch them and a small cage to hold them.
VAULT-615: These five sheets are surimono, prints ordered privately and not sold in shops. Kuniyoshi designed them about 1830. They show women gathering shellfish at low tide, with ten poems by members of a poetry club across the top.
VAULT-616: A pastel made about 1903. Redon worked for years almost only in black and white, in charcoal, lithography and etching, and took up pastel and colour in the 1890s. Here a sailboat carries two figures across a sea and sky of coloured cloud.
VAULT-617: A pastel showing the head of Orpheus, the poet and musician of Greek myth, with a mountain rising behind it. Redon returned to the subject several times in different media. Another version of this pastel, now in the Musée Fabre in Montpellier, was shown at the Armory Show in 1913.
VAULT-618: A small panel in tempera and gold showing the angel Gabriel telling the Virgin Mary that she will bear the son of God. Botticelli painted it in Florence about 1490. It came to the museum with the Robert Lehman Collection in 1975.
VAULT-619: A red chalk study for one of the twenty seated male nudes, known as ignudi, on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome. Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512 and worked out the figures in drawings before painting each section. The back of the sheet carries more figure studies for the ceiling.
VAULT-620: A small drawing of a bear in silverpoint, a technique in which a metal stylus marks specially prepared paper. Leonardo made it about 1482 to 1485, around the time he moved from Florence to Milan. It is part of the Robert Lehman Collection.
VAULT-621: The story comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses: Venus tries to hold back her lover Adonis from the hunt, where a boar will kill him. Titian and his workshop painted the composition several times. One version was sent to Philip of Spain in 1554 and is now in the Prado; this one dates from the 1550s.
VAULT-622: Calabazas was a jester at the court of Philip IV of Spain. He is shown full length, as court sitters were, holding a paper pinwheel and a miniature portrait of a woman. Velázquez was painter to the king from 1623 and painted several of the court's jesters and dwarfs.
VAULT-623: Rubens painted himself with his second wife, Helena Fourment, and their son Frans in a garden about 1635. He had married Helena in Antwerp in 1630, four years after the death of his first wife, Isabella Brant. Frans was born in 1633.
VAULT-624: Two men stand on a wooded slope looking at a crescent moon and the evening star. Friedrich painted the subject more than once; the first version, of 1819, is in Dresden. This one was painted about 1825 to 1830.
VAULT-625: A woodcut of 1803 showing a woman seated between two leafless trees, with a spider web and thistles. Friedrich drew the design, and the block was cut by his brother Christian, a joiner. It is one of a small number of woodcuts made from his drawings.
VAULT-626: The scene comes from Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe. Rebecca is carried off from the burning castle of Front-de-Boeuf by two slaves acting for the Templar knight Bois-Guilbert. Delacroix showed the painting at the Paris Salon of 1846.
VAULT-627: The subject comes from The Giaour, a poem Lord Byron published in 1813, in which a Venetian fights the Turk Hassan to avenge his lover. Delacroix painted it in 1826 and returned to the poem in later pictures. He did not visit North Africa until 1832.
VAULT-628: Courbet's three sisters, Zoé, Zélie and Juliette, give alms to a young girl who is herding cattle in a valley near Ornans, the town where he was born. He showed the painting at the Paris Salon of 1852.
VAULT-629: A plate from Piranesi's series of invented prison interiors, first published in Rome about 1749 to 1750. This impression is from the first state of the plate. Piranesi reworked the plates heavily and reissued the series in 1761 with two more added.
VAULT-630: Plate 10 of the Carceri, Piranesi's series of etchings of imaginary prisons. He had trained in architecture and stage design, and the spaces are invented, not drawn from real prisons. The series first appeared in Rome about 1749 to 1750.
VAULT-631: A view of a hillside path and the houses of L'Hermitage at Pontoise, northwest of Paris, where Pissarro settled in 1866. He painted it in 1867 and showed it at the Paris Salon of 1868. Pissarro was born on the Caribbean island of Saint Thomas.
VAULT-632: Two tall, narrow panels painted in Bruges in the 1430s. One shows the Crucifixion before a distant Jerusalem; the other shows Christ in judgment above the earth, the sea and hell. They were transferred from wood to canvas in the 19th century, and the museum bought them in 1933 from the Hermitage in what was then Leningrad.
VAULT-633: A small portrait of the Dutch scholar Desiderius Erasmus, who died in 1536. Holbein first painted him in Basel in 1523, and portraits of this later type date from about 1532. Holbein spent his last years in England as painter to Henry VIII.
VAULT-634: Cole visited Niagara Falls in May 1829 and painted this autumn view the following year. He left out the factories, overlooks and hotels that already stood around the falls. Cole was born in England and is regarded as the founder of the Hudson River School of landscape painting.
VAULT-635: A view in the Adirondack Mountains of New York, painted in 1838. Cole sketched the scene in early summer and painted it in the studio in autumn colours, with two Indigenous men in the foreground. Schroon Mountain was his own name for the peak, which is officially Hoffman Mountain.
VAULT-636: A pen and ink drawing for an edition of Alexander Pope's poem The Rape of the Lock, published in London by Leonard Smithers in 1896. It shows the heroine, Belinda, at her dressing table. Beardsley died of tuberculosis in 1898, aged 25.
VAULT-637: A colour lithograph of Isolde, the heroine of the medieval romance of Tristan and Isolde, raising a cup. It was issued in 1895 by the British art journal The Studio as an extra for its readers. Beardsley died of tuberculosis three years later, aged 25.
VAULT-638: A long handscroll in cursive script, written about 1095. The text is an account of two officials of the state of Zhao, taken from the Records of the Grand Historian by Sima Qian. Huang Tingjian was a poet and official and is counted among the four great calligraphers of the Song dynasty.
VAULT-639: A handwritten copy of the Qur'an made in Ottoman Turkey. It is dated 1268 in the Islamic calendar, which is 1851 to 1852. The pages are written in ink and decorated with colour and gold, and the book keeps a leather binding.
VAULT-640: A hanging scroll of calligraphy by Musō Soseki, a Zen monk of the Rinzai school. The line he wrote comes from the Diamond Sutra. Musō was an adviser to emperors and shoguns, a garden designer, and the founding abbot of Tenryūji in Kyoto.
VAULT-641: Yueshan was a Chan Buddhist monk from Fujian in China who emigrated to Japan. He took a post at Manpukuji, the head temple of the Ōbaku school of Zen, and later became its seventh abbot. The rounded, fused strokes are typical of Ōbaku calligraphy.
VAULT-642: A book cover made in Iran in the 18th century. It is pasteboard and leather, painted and sealed under lacquer. Painted lacquer covers had been used on Persian books since the late 15th century.
VAULT-643: A leather binding made in Istanbul between 1460 and 1500, in the first decades of Ottoman rule there. The outer covers carry panels of Qur'anic inscription, interlace and a central medallion. The inner covers are leather openwork laid over coloured paper, and a flap on the back cover folds over to protect the page edges.
VAULT-644: A book printed in Venice by Aldus Manutius in December 1499. It tells of Poliphilo's search for his beloved Polia through a dream of ruins, gardens and processions. The text is attributed to Francesco Colonna, a Dominican friar, and the designer of its woodcuts is not known.
VAULT-645: A wallpaper pattern designed by William Morris about 1890 and printed from carved wooden blocks in distemper colours. Morris designed more than fifty wallpapers for his firm, Morris & Co. The firm's papers were printed by Jeffrey & Co. in London.
VAULT-646: A printed cotton furnishing fabric designed by William Morris in 1875. That year his decorating firm, founded in 1861 as Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co., was reorganised as Morris & Co. Textiles were among the firm's most profitable goods.
VAULT-647: A printed pattern design by the Austrian designer Dagobert Peche, dated about 1915. Peche joined the Wiener Werkstätte, the Vienna design workshops, in 1915 and worked there until his death in 1923. The museum names F. O. Schmidt of Vienna as the manufacturer.
VAULT-648: A panel from a scenic wallpaper showing views of the city of Lyon. It was printed in colour from woodblocks in Paris by the firm of Sauvinet between 1821 and 1825. Scenic wallpapers were sold as sets of panels that joined to form a continuous landscape around a room.
VAULT-649: Morris designed Marigold in 1875. It was first meant for wallpaper and was one of the few of his patterns sold as both wallpaper and fabric; it was also printed on linoleum. This length of cotton was printed in the 20th century.
VAULT-650: An engraving of a censer, the vessel swung on chains to burn incense in church. Schongauer worked in Colmar on the Upper Rhine and was the son of a goldsmith. The print shows the object in full detail, as a goldsmith's design would.
VAULT-651: An engraving of about 1490 in which young men dance among thorned vines around a lady at the centre, with two musicians. The dance may be a morris dance, which was popular at courts of the time. Ornament prints like this one gave other craftsmen motifs to copy.
VAULT-652: An engraving of about 1470 by a Netherlandish printmaker known only by his mark, a letter W with a key. He engraved ten leaf ornaments in all. According to the museum, this is the only known impression of the oak leaf, and the other nine also survive in single impressions.
VAULT-653: One of twelve handscrolls recording the Kangxi Emperor's tour of southern China in 1689. Wang Hui was called to Beijing to direct the project and led a team of painters. This scroll, the third, follows the route from the city of Ji'nan to Mount Tai.
VAULT-654: A panel from the base of an altarpiece painted in 1445 for the church of San Domenico in Siena. On the left God sets in motion the universe, shown as the earth ringed by coloured circles. On the right an angel drives Adam and Eve out of the garden.
VAULT-655: A deck of fifty-two hand-painted playing cards made in the southern Netherlands about 1475 to 1480. The four suits are marked with hunting gear: dog collars, hound tethers, game nooses and hunting horns. It is the only complete deck of illuminated ordinary playing cards known from the 15th century.
VAULT-656: A watercolour of a single named tulip, made about 1645 for a tulip book, an album growers used to show buyers their flowers. The striped petals, which made a bulb more valuable, were caused by a virus. Holsteyn was one of many Dutch artists who specialised in botanical subjects.
VAULT-657: A hand-coloured engraving from The Botanical Magazine, the illustrated journal of garden plants that William Curtis founded in London in 1787. Sydenham Edwards drew most of its plates in its first decades. This plate was published in 1806.
VAULT-658: A watercolour study of the arcade of the Doge's Palace in Venice. Ruskin made it in the winter of 1849 to 1850, when he was in the city measuring and drawing its buildings. That work went into his book The Stones of Venice, published from 1851 to 1853.
VAULT-659: A diagram from the Plan of Chicago, the scheme for rebuilding the city that Daniel Burnham and Edward Bennett prepared for the Commercial Club of Chicago and published in 1909. This sheet marks a proposed system of circuit roads in coloured ink on a printed map.
VAULT-660: An architects' drawing of the LaSalle Street front of the Rookery, an office building in Chicago designed by the firm of Daniel Burnham and John Wellborn Root. The building was completed in 1888 and still stands. The sheet is a hectograph, an early way of copying drawings in coloured inks.
VAULT-661: A leaded glass and bronze lamp made by Tiffany Studios in New York by 1906, with dragonflies around the rim of the shade. The design is attributed to Clara Driscoll, head of the firm's Women's Glass Cutting Department, who designed most of its lamps. Louis Comfort Tiffany approved the patterns as artistic director.
VAULT-662: A colour stencil print of 1899 by the Austrian designer Koloman Moser. Moser was a founding member of the Vienna Secession in 1897. In 1903 he and the architect Josef Hoffmann founded the Wiener Werkstätte, the Vienna design workshops.
VAULT-663: A book of ornament published in London in 1856 by the architect and designer Owen Jones. Its colour plates, printed by chromolithography, set out patterns from many periods and cultures, and the text states his principles of design. Jones had earlier devised the colour scheme for the interior of the Crystal Palace in 1851.
VAULT-664: A Gospel lectionary, a book of the Gospel readings arranged in the order they are read through the church year. It was made in Constantinople about 1100, written on parchment with painted portraits of the evangelists and gold. It is named for Mary and Michael Jaharis, whose gift helped the museum buy it in 2007.
VAULT-665: A letter N cut from a choirbook, painted in tempera and gold on vellum. The museum dates it to the 18th or 19th century and thinks it may be French. Choirbooks were made large so that a group of singers could read from one copy.
VAULT-666: A page from a small one-volume Latin Bible made in Oxford about 1230 to 1240. The initial P opens Paul's letter to Philemon and shows the saint with a sword and a book. William de Brailes is one of the few English illuminators of the period known by name; the museum gives this leaf to his circle.
VAULT-667: A page cut from a one-volume Latin Bible made in England about 1225 to 1250. The initial I, formed of a beast and a serpent, opens the Book of Ruth. The Bible has traditionally been linked to Glastonbury Abbey and later belonged to the antiquary Roger Gale, who died in 1744.
VAULT-668: An uchikake is a formal outer robe worn open, without a sash, over a kimono. This one was made in Japan in the 19th century, in the late Edo or the Meiji period. It is silk satin embroidered in silk and painted with gold, with a red silk lining dyed with safflower.
VAULT-669: A kosode is a robe with small wrist openings, the garment from which the modern kimono developed. This one was made in Japan in the 19th century, in the late Edo or the Meiji period. It is silk satin patterned with gold-wrapped thread and lined with safflower-dyed silk.
VAULT-670: A pair of six-panel folding screens showing the Thirty-Six Poetic Immortals, a group of Japanese poets chosen by the courtier Fujiwara no Kintō in the 11th century. The screens were made in the early 17th century in the studio of Kano Takanobu, a son of the painter Kano Eitoku.
VAULT-671: Hōchū painted these waves on a folding fan. A later owner took the paper off its ribs and mounted it as a hanging scroll. Hōchū, who died in 1819, modelled his work on the painter Ogata Kōrin.
VAULT-672: A book of twenty-four etched ornamental letters published in 1627. Lucas Kilian was an engraver in Augsburg and a member of a family of engravers and print publishers there.
VAULT-673: A plate from An Alphabet, the first of several sets of prints Nicholson made for the London publisher William Heinemann. He cut the images as woodblocks, issued first in a small hand-coloured edition, and they were then published in large editions as colour lithographs.
VAULT-674: The etched title page to a set of prints of insects and other small creatures. Hollar was born in Prague in 1607 and spent much of his working life in England, where he died in 1677. He made close to three thousand etchings on subjects from costume and portraits to buildings and maps.
VAULT-675: The title page to a set of ten etchings, made about 1769, that picture an imaginary journey to the moon and the lives of the people there. Morghen drew on earlier books about lunar travel, among them The Man in the Moone by Bishop Francis Godwin. He worked as an engraver in Naples.
VAULT-676: A quilt with a pattern of roses, made about 1830 to 1835 by Letticia Keziah Vernon, who lived from 1795 to 1852. The museum places its making in Virginia, Tennessee or Missouri. It was given in memory of the donor's mother.
VAULT-677: A quilt pieced from silk, velvet, ribbon and lace by Louisa Joiner of Watertown, New York, between about 1887 and 1900. Her initials are on a panel at the lower right. Little is known about her beyond her marriage to a captain who sailed the Great Lakes. Crazy quilts are named for their irregular scraps set in no fixed pattern.
VAULT-678: A linen quilt embroidered in silk, made in Ottoman Turkey in the 1600s or 1700s. Its pomegranates framed by serrated leaves follow motifs from court silks. Most of the dark brown thread of the stems has worn away, showing the ink outlines drawn on the linen.
VAULT-679: A stained glass window made about 1880 by the American painter John La Farge. He developed opalescent glass for windows and took out a patent for it in 1880. The window was made for the Newport, Rhode Island, house of the collector Henry G. Marquand.
VAULT-680: A pen and wash drawing by the French artist Jean Cousin the Younger, made as a design for a stained glass window. Its subject is Aaron, the brother of Moses and first high priest in the Hebrew Bible. Cousin worked in Paris, as did his father of the same name. The drawing is undated.
VAULT-681: A fragment of a Byzantine floor mosaic in marble and glass, made between 500 and 550 and restored in modern times. The woman is Ktisis, a figure who stands for the act of founding or generous giving. She holds a measuring rod.
VAULT-682: A stone mosaic from the fifth century, made in the Eastern Mediterranean, probably Syria. It was once part of a larger floor in a wealthy family home in the Roman Empire. A handler leads a giraffe against a ground of scallop-shaped semicircles.
VAULT-683: A disk covered in turquoise and shell mosaic, made by Mixtec artists of northern Oaxaca, Mexico, between 1400 and 1500. Such mosaics were a Mixtec specialty, and Mixtec artists also worked in the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan. The disk records historical events through calendar and mythological imagery.
VAULT-684: A panel from the floor of an early Byzantine church in northern Syria, made in the late 400s or early 500s. Adam and Eve share the fruit and cover themselves with large leaves. A Greek inscription above them refers to the verse in Genesis.
VAULT-685: A floor mosaic from the Eastern Roman Empire, made in the 300s. A tigress carries one cub on her back and faces two more. Tigers appear far less often in Roman art than lions, leopards or bears. The panel holds more than ten thousand small cut stones.
VAULT-686: A panel of glazed tiles made in Iran between 1640 and 1650, under the Safavid dynasty. The colours were kept apart in the kiln by the cuerda seca method, in which a greasy line separates the glazes. The scene shows figures at leisure in a garden.
VAULT-687: A stonepaste tile made in Ottoman Turkey about 1578. Its flowers and Chinese-style cloud bands are painted in several colours under a clear glaze. Tiles of this kind were made at Iznik for the walls of mosques and palaces.
VAULT-688: A parchment page from a Qur'an copied in southern Spain in the 1200s or 1300s. It carries verses from the Chapter of Light in the script used in Islamic Spain and North Africa. Vowels are marked in red and other signs in blue to guide reading aloud.
VAULT-689: A lacquered wooden box for cosmetics, made in Japan in the first half of the fifteenth century, during the Muromachi period. The chrysanthemums are built up in gold and silver powder sprinkled onto wet lacquer, a technique called maki-e. The fittings are gilt bronze.
VAULT-690: A Japanese lacquer writing box from the 1800s. The lid shows two Portuguese traders in ballooning trousers and a Jesuit priest in a long robe. Portuguese ships first reached Japan in the 1540s, and pictures of the foreigners stayed in use as decoration long afterwards. Designs of this kind are called nanban.
VAULT-691: A lacquer box made in Japan in the 1400s to hold the tools of calligraphy. It still has its inkstone and water dropper. The lid is decorated in sprinkled gold and silver with pine, bamboo and camellia, plants of late winter and early spring.
VAULT-692: An ink drawing on paper from an album of sketches made in China in the 1200s, during the Southern Song dynasty. It belongs to a group on the theme of clearing the mountains, in which divine soldiers fight evil spirits shown as animals and half-human creatures. The text the scenes were based on is lost.
VAULT-693: An engraving coloured by hand with gold, from a set of fifty made in Ferrara before 1467. The engraver's name is unknown. Scholars generally think the set was a teaching tool that laid out the order of the cosmos, rising from the beggar through the muses, liberal arts, virtues and planets to God. The five groups are lettered E, D, C, B and A.
VAULT-694: A page from an anthology of Persian poetry compiled by Muhammad ibn Badr al-Din Jajarmi. The manuscript is dated 741 in the Islamic calendar, or 1340 to 1341. Only one chapter of the book was illustrated, and its pages are now divided among several collections.
VAULT-695: A privately issued woodblock print made in Japan for the New Year of 1866. The twelve zodiac animals are printed in a brass-dust pigment so that they read as gold silhouettes. The tiger, the animal of 1866, comes first, at the far right. Surimono were often exchanged at New Year.
VAULT-696: A woodcut star chart of the northern sky, published in Nuremberg in 1515 with a companion map of the southern sky. Dürer drew the constellation figures, working with the astronomers Johannes Stabius and Conrad Heinfogel. The twelve signs of the zodiac run around the edge.
VAULT-697: A pair of griffins carved in pink Verona limestone in Emilia, northern Italy, between 1150 and 1175. A griffin has the features of an eagle and a lion. Such figures guarded church portals and choir screens. One of this pair holds a knight between its paws and the other a calf.
VAULT-698: A small prayer book painted in Paris about 1324 to 1328 by the illuminator Jean Pucelle. It was made for Jeanne d'Evreux, the third wife of King Charles IV of France. Pucelle painted the figures mostly in shades of grey, a technique called grisaille.
VAULT-699: A book of hours painted between 1405 and about 1409 for Jean, Duke of Berry, a son of King John II of France and a great collector of manuscripts. The painters were the brothers Paul, Herman and Jean de Limbourg, who came from Nijmegen. They later began the Très Riches Heures for the same patron.
VAULT-700: A book of hours painted in Flanders about 1500, in the workshops of Bruges and Ghent. Its first owner was Queen Isabella of Castile, who backed the first voyage of Columbus. The painter is known only by a name taken from another of his books.
VAULT-701: A book of hours made in Paris about 1404, written with a quill on vellum and painted with gold. It belonged to Charles III of Navarre, called the Noble, who probably used it at his castle of Olite in northern Spain. The lead painter is known only by a name scholars gave him.
VAULT-702: An ink drawing made in Ottoman Turkey between about 1550 and 1570, mounted with a painted and gilded border. The long, curling, feathery leaves give their name to the saz style, which was used across Ottoman court art in the sixteenth century.
VAULT-703: A dragon in wrought iron with moving joints, made in Japan about 1880. The Myochin were a line of armourers. When demand for armour fell away, metalworkers of the school turned their skills to jointed iron animals of this kind.
VAULT-704: A mask of wood, raffia and feathers made by a Chokwe artist in Angola or the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the middle or later nineteenth century. The chihongo is the male counterpart of the female mwana pwo mask. Its headdress, red colour, beard and filed teeth mark wisdom, leadership and rank.
VAULT-705: A painted wooden mask from Burkina Faso, made in the early to middle 1900s, possibly by a Bwa-style maker. Its horns and muzzle identify it as a bush buffalo. Among the Bwa, such masks represent protective spirits of the bush and are danced in the dry season at initiations, funerals and harvest celebrations. The right horn was once broken and repaired.
VAULT-706: A painted wooden mask made by a Kuba-style carver in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in the middle or later 1800s. Among the Bushoong, the central Kuba group, bwoom is one of three masks that act out the founding of the Kuba kingdom. Eagle feathers were added to it for performances.
VAULT-707: A parchment leaf painted in Spain about 1180. It comes from a copy of the commentary on the Book of Revelation written in the eighth century by the monk Beatus of Liébana. The upper scene shows Christ enthroned among angels. Below, an angel tells Saint John to write the book.
VAULT-708: A woodcut from the Apocalypse, the set of fifteen prints Dürer published in Nuremberg in 1498. It illustrates the riders of the sixth chapter of the Book of Revelation, usually named Conquest, War, Famine and Death. Dürer was in his late twenties when the book appeared.
VAULT-709: Painted scenes from a copy of the Apocalypse, the last book of the New Testament, made in Lorraine about 1295. Many illustrated copies of the text were produced in northern Europe after 1240, especially in England. The painters in Lorraine followed English models.
VAULT-710: A mandala painted on cloth in Nepal about 1100. At the centre is the Buddhist deity Chakrasamvara with his consort Vajravarahi. A mandala is a diagram of the palace and realm of an enlightened being, used as an aid in meditation.
VAULT-711: A mandala painted on cloth in Tibet in the late fourteenth century. The female Buddhist deity Jnanadakini sits at the centre of a square palace with four gates, surrounded by attendant figures. Paintings like this served as guides for meditation.
VAULT-712: A painting on silk made in Japan in the fifteenth century. It belongs to a type devoted to the Kasuga Shrine in Nara, where deer are held to be messengers of the gods. By tradition one of the shrine's deities arrived there riding a deer.
VAULT-713: A mandala painted on cloth in central Tibet about 1375. It shows the palace of the Buddhist deity Nairatma, who dances at the centre. The outer ring holds eight cremation grounds, places where practitioners went to overcome the fear of death.
VAULT-714: A silk tapestry woven in China in the fourteenth century, under the Yuan dynasty. It maps the universe of Buddhist tradition, with Mount Meru at the centre of the world. The weaving technique, in which each colour is worked separately, is called kesi.
VAULT-715: A bronze mirror cast in China in the middle or later 700s, during the Tang dynasty. Its decorated back carries the Eight Trigrams and an inscription explaining that the circle stands for heaven and the square for earth. The other side was polished to reflect.
VAULT-716: One of seven tapestries on the hunt of the unicorn, designed in France and woven in the southern Netherlands between 1495 and 1505. The unicorn dips its horn into a stream while hunters and animals look on. The set belonged to the La Rochefoucauld family for centuries before John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought it and gave it to the Cloisters.
VAULT-717: One of seven tapestries on the hunt of the unicorn, designed in France and woven in the southern Netherlands between 1495 and 1505. The unicorn sits chained to a pomegranate tree inside a low fence, on a field of flowering plants. It is often called The Unicorn in Captivity.
VAULT-718: An engraving made about 1470 by Martin Schongauer, who worked in Colmar on the upper Rhine. Demons lift the hermit Saint Anthony into the air and beat him. Schongauer was the leading German engraver before Dürer, and his prints travelled widely across Europe.
VAULT-719: A lithograph of 1888 from the first of three portfolios Redon made after Gustave Flaubert's novel The Temptation of Saint Anthony, published in 1874. Redon worked first in charcoal and tried to carry its dense blacks into his lithographs.
VAULT-720: An oil painting of 1883 by the Swiss painter Arnold Böcklin, who spent much of his working life in Italy. He painted creatures from classical myth in natural settings. His work was taken up by the Symbolists and later by Giorgio de Chirico.
VAULT-721: A stoneware pouring vessel made in Vietnam in about the fifteenth or sixteenth century. It is shaped as a phoenix and painted in cobalt blue under the glaze. Vietnamese blue-and-white wares of this period were traded widely across Southeast Asia.
