VAULT-722: A porcelain ewer made in China in the 1000s, during the Northern Song dynasty. The phoenix's beak forms the spout. Ewers of this type have been dug up at Xicun in Guangdong province, though finer examples such as this one were probably made at Jingdezhen.
VAULT-723: An ink drawing made in Istanbul in the middle of the 1500s. A dragon lunges at a pearl in the form of a seal inscribed with a verse from the Qur'an, while a lion and a phoenix grow from the branches it holds. Shahkulu trained with Persian artists, joined the Ottoman court painting workshop in 1526 and later became its head.
VAULT-724: An oil painting of 1896 by the Swiss painter Ferdinand Hodler. Hodler was born in Bern and worked in Geneva, where he died in 1918. He was a leading figure of Symbolism in Switzerland.
VAULT-725: A page from a manuscript of the Kalpasutra, a Jain sacred text, painted in India about 1465. The fourteen dreams of Devananda foretell the birth of Mahavira, the last of the twenty-four Jain teachers. The painter is unnamed and is known from this manuscript.
VAULT-726: A panel painted about 1511 by Hans Baldung, who had worked in Dürer's workshop in Nuremberg and settled in Strasbourg. Saint John the Evangelist sits on the island of Patmos writing the Book of Revelation. The eagle beside him is his symbol.
VAULT-727: An oil painting made between 1895 and 1897 by the American landscape painter Ralph Albert Blakelock. The Ghost Dance was a religious movement that spread among Native American peoples in the late 1880s. It was suppressed after the massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890.
VAULT-728: A clock of gilt bronze on an ebony base, made in Augsburg about 1630. Augsburg was a leading centre for clocks and mechanical figures in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. In clocks of this type parts of the animal move with the mechanism.
VAULT-729: A colour woodblock print in two sheets, made in Japan about 1847 or 1848. Its subject is a large mechanical figure of Asahina Saburo, a warrior of the Kamakura period known in legend for his strength. Sadahide was a pupil of Utagawa Kunisada.
VAULT-730: A leaf from a copy of al-Jazari's Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, made in Damascus in 1315. It shows a basin in the shape of a peacock for ritual hand washing. Al-Jazari, an engineer from upper Mesopotamia, finished the book in 1206. Fifteen manuscript copies survive.
VAULT-731: A brass astrolabe inlaid with silver, dated 690 in the Islamic calendar, or 1291. Its maker was a prince of the Rasulid dynasty of Yemen, who ruled as sultan from 1295 to 1296. He also wrote on astronomy and on how to build astrolabes.
VAULT-732: A book on astronomy by Petrus Apianus, printed at Ingolstadt in 1540 and dedicated to the Emperor Charles V. Its hand-coloured woodcuts, credited to Michael Ostendorfer, include paper discs that turn to work out the positions of the planets.
VAULT-733: A small study panelled in inlaid wood, made about 1478 to 1482 for Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino, in his palace at Gubbio. The flat walls are worked in different woods to look like cupboards with open doors, holding books, instruments and armour. The design is credited to the Sienese artist and architect Francesco di Giorgio Martini.
VAULT-734: A small folding shrine of gilded silver and translucent enamel, made in Paris between about 1325 and 1350. At its centre are the Virgin and Child with angels holding relics. It is attributed to the Paris goldsmith Jean de Touyl, who died in 1349 or 1350.
VAULT-735: A head of silver and gilded silver set with rock crystal and gems, made in France about 1220 to 1240. It held the skull of Saint Yrieix, a sixth-century abbot who founded a monastery south of Limoges. The town that grew up there, Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche, bears his name.
VAULT-736: A small tiered case with its sliding bead and toggle, made in Japan in the later 1800s. An inro hung from the sash of a kimono and held seals or medicines. Shibata Zeshin was a lacquer artist and painter who worked through the end of the Edo period and into the Meiji period.
VAULT-737: A carved and painted cedar rattle with pebbles inside, made by a Tsimshian artist on the Northwest Coast of Canada in the nineteenth century. Rattles in the form of a raven were carried by chiefs in ceremonial dances along the Northwest Coast.
VAULT-738: A garment of camelid wool made on the south coast of Peru about 200 to 150 BCE. The figures are embroidered in stem stitch on a plain woven ground. Paracas textiles survived because they were wrapped around the dead and buried in a very dry desert.
VAULT-739: A pair of gilt copper plaques made in Limoges between 1200 and 1250. Each is filled with twisting hybrid creatures. Limoges workshops of this period produced metalwork and enamels for churches across Europe.
VAULT-740: A stoneware candlestand made in China under the Western Jin dynasty, between 265 and 316. The bixie is a winged hybrid creature that was believed to ward off evil spirits. The piece was molded in two parts, and incised lines on the sides of the body stand for wings. Candlestands of this shape have been found in tombs.
VAULT-741: A lithograph from one of three portfolios Odilon Redon made after Gustave Flaubert's novel The Temptation of Saint Anthony, published in 1874. The novel follows a hermit in the desert and the visions that test him. Redon worked first in charcoal and tried to carry the same dense black into his lithographs.
VAULT-742: A granite sphinx with the body of a lion and the head of Hatshepsut, who ruled Egypt as pharaoh in the fifteenth century BCE. It was one of several made for her temple at Deir el-Bahri in Thebes. Her statues there were broken up after her death, and this one was put back together from fragments found by the Metropolitan Museum's excavators in the 1920s.
VAULT-743: A sphinx carved in gneiss with a lion's body and the head of Senwosret III, a king of Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty in the Middle Kingdom. He wears the striped royal headcloth. The record dates it to his reign, about 1878 to 1840 BCE.
VAULT-744: A charcoal drawing made in 1883 by the French artist Odilon Redon. For the first half of his career Redon worked almost entirely in black, in charcoal drawings and lithographs he called his noirs. He turned to pastel and oil colour in the 1890s.
VAULT-745: An oil painting on panel from about 1650. A witch riding a goat and holding a broomstick charges in from the left at a crowd of devils. Cornelis Saftleven was born in Gorinchem and worked in Rotterdam, where he painted peasant scenes, animals and fantastic subjects like this one.
VAULT-746: An engraving made in 1497, early in Albrecht Dürer's career in Nuremberg. Four nude women stand under a hanging globe, with a skull at their feet and a devil looking in from a doorway at the left. The subject has never been tied to a single story; one reading connects it to Hecate, the Greek goddess of the underworld.
VAULT-747: A hanging scroll painted on silk in 1810. Tani Bun'ichi was the adopted son of the painter Tani Bunchō. A gold inscription on the lamp stand gives the date and says that he did not like painting ghosts but tried it after listening to a man named Ono. A very similar painting by him is kept at the temple Zenshō-an in Tokyo.
VAULT-748: A Japanese hanging scroll on silk from the 1200s. It pictures a teaching ascribed to the Chinese Buddhist monk Shandao, who lived from 613 to 681: a narrow white path runs between a river of fire and a river of water toward the land of the Buddha Amida. Amida appears at the top in his Pure Land.
VAULT-749: A gilt copper relief from Nepal that carries a date equal to the year 1004. It shows the Hindu god Vishnu on Garuda, the bird-man who serves as his mount. Repoussé means the sheet metal was hammered into shape from the back.
VAULT-750: A bronze finial in the form of Garuda, the mythical bird who is the mount of the god Vishnu. It was made in the Khmer empire, in what is now Thailand or Cambodia, in the late twelfth or early thirteenth century.
VAULT-751: A colour woodblock print from about 1793. Shōki, known in China as Zhong Kui, is a figure of Chinese legend who hunts and subdues demons. The tall, narrow sheet is a pillar print, a format made to hang on the wooden posts of a house. Shun'ei was a pupil of Katsukawa Shunshō.
VAULT-752: A two-sheet colour woodblock print published in 1853. Figures from Ōtsu-e, the folk pictures sold to travellers at the town of Ōtsu, step out of their paintings in front of the artist Ukiyo Matahei. Among them are a demon, a monkey, the wisteria maiden and Fukurokuju, the god of longevity.
VAULT-753: A set of five painted handscrolls from the late thirteenth century. They tell the story of Sugawara no Michizane, a scholar and court official who died in exile in 903. After a run of disasters in the capital were blamed on his angry spirit, he was worshipped as the god Tenjin at the Kitano shrine in Kyoto.
VAULT-754: A colour woodblock pillar print from about 1767 or 1768. Suzuki Harunobu worked in Edo and was among the first artists to design full-colour prints, which appeared there in 1765. He died in 1770.
VAULT-755: A Japanese colour woodblock print from the eighteenth century by an unidentified artist. Fūjin, the god of wind, and Raijin, the god of thunder, are usually shown as a pair of sky demons. Here they sit at a board game.
VAULT-756: A six-panel folding screen from the mid-1600s, painted on paper covered with gold dust. The museum lists it under Tawaraya Sōtatsu, and its record says the gold technique and a seal reading Inen suggest a painter linked to his workshop. Thunder god screens were usually paired with a wind god; the partner to this one has not been located.
VAULT-757: A Japanese wood sculpture from the 1300s with traces of red and black pigment. Raijin is normally shown inside a ring of small drums that he beats with a stick. A metal clasp on the back of this figure shows that it once had such a ring.
VAULT-758: A photograph of a street organ player in Paris, taken in 1898 or 1899. In those years Eugène Atget made a series on the small street trades of the city. He had started photographing in the 1890s after working as an actor, and he sold his prints to artists, libraries and museums.
VAULT-759: A photograph of a narrow street on the Left Bank of Paris, taken in 1898. Eugène Atget set out to record the old streets and buildings of the city before they were pulled down. He sold the pictures as documents for artists, not as art.
VAULT-760: A portrait from 1867 of Julia Jackson, the photographer's niece and goddaughter. Jackson later became the mother of the writer Virginia Woolf and the painter Vanessa Bell. Julia Margaret Cameron took up photography in her late forties and worked at her home on the Isle of Wight.
VAULT-761: One of the photographs Julia Margaret Cameron made in 1874 to illustrate Idylls of the King, the Arthurian poems of her neighbour Alfred Tennyson. It shows the enchantress Vivien with the wizard Merlin. Cameron's husband, Charles Hay Cameron, posed as Merlin.
VAULT-762: A sequence of photographs of a cockatoo in flight. It was published in 1887 in Animal Locomotion, a set of 781 plates that Eadweard Muybridge made under the auspices of the University of Pennsylvania. He used a row of cameras whose shutters were tripped one after another by a clockwork mechanism.
VAULT-763: One of five plates in Animal Locomotion given to movements of the hand; this one follows a hand beating time to music. Eadweard Muybridge made the photographs at the University of Pennsylvania between 1884 and 1886 and published them in 1887. He had first photographed a horse in motion in 1878.
VAULT-764: A view of Yosemite Valley in California taken in early morning light. Eadweard Muybridge made it on his second trip there, which lasted from June to November 1872. Many of the pictures from that trip were taken on glass plate negatives measuring 20 by 24 inches.
VAULT-765: A picture of a piece of seaweed made in 1839, the year William Henry Fox Talbot made his photographic process public. For images like this he laid the specimen on paper he had made sensitive to light and set it in the sun. No camera was used.
VAULT-766: A view of York Minster seen down a street of the city, taken on 28 July 1845. William Henry Fox Talbot invented the calotype, a process patented in 1841 that gave a paper negative from which many prints could be made.
VAULT-767: A photograph of bare trees mirrored in the pond at Lacock Abbey in Wiltshire, the home of Talbot's family. He took it in 1841 or 1842, a few years after he invented the photograph on paper. The print was made from a calotype negative.
VAULT-768: A cyanotype of a plant specimen, made between 1851 and 1854. Anna Atkins laid plants straight onto light-sensitive paper and exposed them to the sun, which left a white outline on a blue ground. The cyanotype process had been invented by her family's friend John Herschel in 1842.
VAULT-769: A cyanotype of a seaweed, made about 1853. In 1843 Anna Atkins began issuing Photographs of British Algae, the first book illustrated with photographs. Each plate was made without a camera by placing the specimen on sensitized paper in sunlight.
VAULT-770: A cyanotype of a hart's-tongue fern, made between 1852 and 1854. Anna Atkins was an amateur botanist who recorded plants by laying them directly on light-sensitive paper. In 1843 she produced the first book illustrated with photographs.
VAULT-771: A photograph of the works on show at the Paris Salon of 1852. Gustave Le Gray trained as a painter before turning to photography. He devised the waxed-paper negative used for this print and taught many French photographers of the 1850s.
VAULT-772: A photograph from 1856 of the Reine Hortense, the yacht of the French emperor Napoleon III, at the port of Le Havre. Gustave Le Gray made a series of seascapes on the Normandy coast that year.
VAULT-773: A view of the medieval walls of Carcassonne in southern France, taken in 1851. That year the French government sent Gustave Le Gray and four other photographers out to record the country's historic monuments, a survey known as the Mission Héliographique.
VAULT-774: A seascape with a single sailing ship, taken in 1856. Gustave Le Gray made it on the Normandy coast, and it was shown in London that year. This print comes from an album titled Vistas del Mar.
VAULT-775: A seascape from 1857, number 16 in the album Vistas del Mar. Photographic plates of the time could not record sea and sky properly in one exposure. Gustave Le Gray, who had trained as a painter in Paris, solved this by printing from two negatives, one exposed for the water and one for the sky.
VAULT-776: A studio portrait from about 1865 of the photographer Nadar and his wife Ernestine posed in a balloon basket. Nadar was the working name of Gaspard-Félix Tournachon, a Paris caricaturist, writer and portrait photographer. He was also a balloonist, and in 1858 he took the first photographs from the air. This print was made in the 1890s.
VAULT-777: A photograph of the balloon Le Géant on the Champ de Mars in Paris on 18 October 1863, at its second launch. The photographer Nadar had the balloon built; it carried a two-storey basket. The first flight, on 4 October, went well. The second ended in a crash in Hanover that left Nadar with a broken leg.
VAULT-778: A portrait from 1855 of the novelist and playwright Alexandre Dumas, author of The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, who was a friend of the photographer. Nadar was the alias of Gaspard-Félix Tournachon. In 1874 he lent his studio to the group of artists who held the first Impressionist exhibition there.
VAULT-779: A panorama of the Yosemite high country seen from Sentinel Dome, made up of more than one print and taken in 1865 or 1866. Carleton Watkins, based in San Francisco, first photographed Yosemite in 1861 with a camera that took very large glass plates.
VAULT-780: A photograph from 1861 of the Grizzly Giant, a giant sequoia in the Mariposa Grove in California. It comes from Carleton Watkins's first trip to Yosemite. In 1864 President Lincoln signed the act that set aside Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove for public use.
VAULT-781: A view into Yosemite Valley taken in 1865 or 1866. Carleton Watkins carried his equipment in by mule and used a mammoth-plate camera whose glass negatives measured up to 18 by 22 inches. Most of his negatives and prints were destroyed in the San Francisco earthquake and fire of 1906.
VAULT-782: A photograph of Bridalveil Fall in Yosemite Valley, taken in 1865 or 1866. The waterfall drops 620 feet to the valley floor. Carleton Watkins, who worked from San Francisco, was one of a small number of photographers then making very large mammoth prints of landscapes.
VAULT-783: A photograph of a locomotive in a rail yard, taken in 1902 from the back of a moving train as it left Long Island City, New York. It was published in the first issue of Camera Work, the journal Alfred Stieglitz edited, in January 1903. This print was made between 1920 and 1939.
VAULT-784: A photograph taken in 1907 aboard a liner sailing from New York to Europe. It looks down from the first-class deck onto the passengers travelling in steerage, the cheapest class. Alfred Stieglitz published it in his journal Camera Work in 1911. This photogravure was his own copy.
VAULT-785: A photograph from 1908 of a young girl at work beside the spinning machines of a cotton mill. Lewis Hine took it for the National Child Labor Committee, which used his pictures of working children in its campaign to change the law. Hine had trained as a sociologist and worked as a teacher before he became a photographer.
VAULT-786: A photograph of an immigrant family in Chicago, taken in 1910. Lewis Hine had begun photographing new arrivals at Ellis Island in New York a few years earlier. From 1908 he worked for the National Child Labor Committee, recording children at work across the United States.
VAULT-787: A portrait of a Piegan man named New Chest, photographed in 1910. The Piegan are one of the nations of the Blackfoot Confederacy. The picture is plate 200 of The North American Indian, the twenty-volume work Edward S. Curtis published between 1907 and 1930.
VAULT-788: A portrait of a man named Wolf, photographed in 1908. Apsaroke is the spelling Curtis used for the Apsáalooke, also called the Crow. The picture is plate 142 of The North American Indian, the twenty-volume work Curtis published between 1907 and 1930.
VAULT-789: A photograph from 1904 of a Navajo (Diné) weaver at an upright loom. It is plate 34 in the first portfolio of The North American Indian, the twenty-volume work Edward S. Curtis published between 1907 and 1930.
VAULT-790: A photograph from 1899 of a woman and a girl standing in a doorway. The sitters were the writer Agnes Rand Lee and her daughter Peggy. Gertrude Käsebier ran a portrait studio in New York and in 1902 was a founding member of the Photo-Secession, the group led by Alfred Stieglitz. This photogravure was published in 1901.
VAULT-791: A photograph taken in 1867 on a government survey expedition in Nevada. The wagon in the dunes is a former Civil War ambulance that Timothy O'Sullivan had turned into a travelling darkroom. Only the wagon and two sets of footprints appear in the sand.
VAULT-792: A photograph from about 1862 of the Bièvre, a small river that ran through the south of Paris to the Seine. Tanneries and dye works lined its banks, and it was later covered over inside the city. Charles Marville became the official photographer of the city of Paris in 1862.
VAULT-793: A photograph of an old street on the Left Bank of Paris, taken between 1865 and 1869. From 1862 Charles Marville was the official photographer of the city. Paris commissioned him to record its narrow medieval streets before they were demolished in the rebuilding directed by Georges-Eugène Haussmann.
VAULT-794: A view over the rooftops of Paris from 1856 or 1857, with the dome of the chapel of Les Invalides on the skyline. Plates of the 1850s could not record sky and ground correctly in one exposure. Charles Marville exposed this one for the clouds, so the city below is dark.
VAULT-795: A photograph from 1856 of the south porch of Rosslyn Chapel, a fifteenth-century church near Edinburgh. Roger Fenton trained as a painter and a lawyer and was a founder of the Photographic Society in London in 1853. He gave up photography in 1862.
VAULT-796: A photograph of the cathedral domes inside the Moscow Kremlin, taken in 1852. Roger Fenton went to Russia that year to photograph a bridge being built over the Dnieper at Kyiv and made views of Moscow and other cities on the same trip. The print was made from a paper negative.
VAULT-797: A photograph of a ravine near Sevastopol strewn with Russian cannonballs, taken in 1855 during the Crimean War. Roger Fenton was commissioned to photograph the British army and spent March to June of that year with the troops, working from a horse-drawn darkroom. Exposure times were too long to record fighting. He showed the pictures in London that autumn.
VAULT-798: A photograph from 1886 that records the successive positions of a flying bird. Étienne-Jules Marey was a French physiologist who studied how bodies move. He called his method chronophotography, and in 1882 he built a camera shaped like a rifle to follow birds through the air.
VAULT-799: A photograph of a fencer in motion, made in 1906. Georges Demenÿ was for many years the assistant of the physiologist Étienne-Jules Marey in Paris, where the two used photography to analyse movement. He later applied the same methods to physical training.
VAULT-800: A lantern slide from the 1890s showing a cyclist in a string of positions on one plate. Étienne-Jules Marey, a physiologist, put a slotted disc that turned behind the lens of his camera, so a figure moving against a dark background was recorded several times in a single exposure. He named the process chronophotography.
VAULT-801: Étienne-Jules Marey was a French physiologist who studied how animals and people move. In 1882 he devised chronophotography, a way of recording the successive phases of a movement in a single photograph. This print, made between about 1883 and 1887, shows a heron in flight.
VAULT-802: The painter David Octavius Hill and the photographer Robert Adamson worked together in Edinburgh from 1843 until Adamson's death in 1848. They photographed the fishing families of Newhaven, a village on the Firth of Forth near the city. The print was made from a paper negative by the calotype process.
VAULT-803: The sitters are the daughters of the Reverend James Grierson of Errol, Scotland. David Octavius Hill, a painter, and Robert Adamson, a photographer, made portraits together in Edinburgh from 1843 until Adamson's death in 1848. They used the calotype process, which prints from a paper negative and needed a long exposure.
VAULT-804: Félix Teynard was a civil engineer from Grenoble who travelled up the Nile in 1851 and 1852, photographing the monuments with paper negatives. This view shows part of the temple complex at Karnak. His photographs were published in Paris in the album Égypte et Nubie.
VAULT-805: The photograph shows the lower part of the colossal seated statues of Ramesses II at the Great Temple of Abu Simbel in Nubia. Félix Teynard, a French civil engineer, made it from a paper negative during his journey along the Nile in 1851 and 1852. In his day sand still covered much of the temple front.
VAULT-806: Frederick H. Evans was a London bookseller who became known for his photographs of English and French cathedrals. This is a lantern slide, a photograph on glass made to be projected, taken at Ely Cathedral in 1891. The Prior's Door is a carved Norman doorway of the twelfth century.
VAULT-807: This lantern slide, a photograph on glass made for projection, shows the doorway from the Galilee Porch into the nave of Ely Cathedral. Frederick H. Evans made it about 1891, while he was still working as a bookseller in London. He gave up the bookshop in 1898 to photograph full time.
VAULT-808: Samuel J. Miller owned a daguerreotype portrait studio in Akron, Ohio, where this likeness was made between 1847 and 1852. Frederick Douglass had escaped from slavery in 1838 and become a speaker, writer and leader of the movement to abolish it. Northeastern Ohio was a centre of abolitionism before the Civil War, and Douglass sat for many portraits.
VAULT-809: This is a page from an English album of about 1850, with a fern recorded by the cyanotype process. The plant was laid on paper coated with iron salts and left in the sun, which turned the uncovered paper blue. John Herschel had introduced the process in 1842.
VAULT-810: William Henry Fox Talbot was an English inventor of photography, and his negative and positive process let many prints be made from one image. The negative for this print was probably made without a camera, by laying a piece of lace on sensitized paper and exposing it to the sun. Talbot hoped such photographs would make intricate patterns easier to copy for manufacture.
VAULT-811: Jaromír Funke was a Czech photographer active in the 1920s and 1930s. In the late 1920s he arranged panes and spheres of glass, bottles and other objects to make abstract pictures out of reflected light and cast shadows. This print dates from between 1927 and 1929.
VAULT-812: Kandinsky painted a series of works he called improvisations between 1910 and 1914, while he was living in Germany. He had published his book Concerning the Spiritual in Art in 1912, arguing for painting that did not imitate the visible world. Two cannons can be made out at the lower right of this canvas of 1913.
VAULT-813: Kandinsky was born in Moscow and moved to Munich in 1896 to study painting. He made this landscape in 1912, the year after he and Franz Marc founded the Blue Rider group there. He returned to Russia when war broke out in 1914.
VAULT-814: Klee painted this in 1937 on a sheet of newspaper, and the printed text shows through his marks. The article that can be read discusses the Spanish Civil War. It belongs to a group of large works with thick lines and sign-like shapes from his last years, made in Switzerland after he left Germany in 1933.
VAULT-815: Klee returned often to the subject of the tightrope walker. He made this colour lithograph in 1923, when he was teaching at the Bauhaus, the German school of art and design. The small figure is drawn in fine pen lines above a landscape of stairs and paths on a pink ground.
VAULT-816: Mondrian was a founding member of De Stijl, the Dutch movement that began in 1917. For this painting of 1921 he turned a square canvas on its corner, so that the horizontal and vertical lines meet diagonal edges. He was living in Paris at the time.
VAULT-817: During the 1910s Mondrian moved from Cubism to an abstract style built on a grid. He limited himself to horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colours, and black and white. The strip of wood around this canvas of 1927, painted the same grey as the surface, is his original frame.
VAULT-818: This painting shows a field near the hamlet of Oele in the eastern Netherlands, where Mondrian spent the summer of 1907. He was then a landscape painter. In the following decade he gave up depicting nature for the geometric abstraction he is known for.
VAULT-819: Franz Marc was a German painter and printmaker who took animals as his main subject. With Wassily Kandinsky he founded the Blue Rider group in Munich in 1911. He cut this woodcut in 1913 and was killed at Verdun in 1916.
VAULT-820: Marc painted this in 1913 after a stay in the town of Merano in the Tyrol. The houses and mill stand on the left, and trees and animals fill the right. Marc was a founder of the Blue Rider group in Munich and was killed at Verdun in 1916.
VAULT-821: This woodcut dates from 1912, the year Marc and Wassily Kandinsky published the Blue Rider Almanac in Munich. Animals were the main subject of his paintings and prints. He joined the German army in 1914 and was killed at Verdun in 1916.
VAULT-822: In this woodcut of 1912 a tiger turns toward a smaller animal behind it. Marc belonged to the Blue Rider group in Munich and made animals his main subject. He enlisted in the German army and was killed at Verdun on 4 March 1916.
VAULT-823: August Macke was a German painter linked with the Blue Rider group in Munich. He made this linoleum cut in 1912. He was killed in France in September 1914, in the second month of the First World War, at the age of twenty-seven.
VAULT-824: Die Brücke, meaning The Bridge, was a group of artists founded in Dresden in 1905 by Kirchner, Erich Heckel, Karl Schmidt-Rottluff and Fritz Bleyl. The members made their own posters and prints for the group's exhibitions. This lithograph dates from 1907.
VAULT-825: Kirchner painted this in 1909, when he was working in Dresden as a member of the group Die Brücke. It shows two wrestlers locked together on a coloured mat. During the 1930s, 639 of his works were removed from German museums and destroyed or sold abroad.
VAULT-826: Kirchner was discharged from the German army after a breakdown in 1915 and went to a sanatorium near Davos in Switzerland. He stayed in the Alps for the rest of his life, and the mountains became his main subject. He drew this view in 1918 or 1919 with black ink brushed over graphite.
VAULT-827: Käthe Kollwitz was a German printmaker and sculptor who took the working poor of Berlin as her subject. Her husband was a doctor who treated them, and his patients were often her models. She made this colour lithograph in 1903.
VAULT-828: Umberto Boccioni was a painter and sculptor of the Italian Futurist movement. Here a bottle on a table is opened up into curving planes, as if seen from several sides at once. He modelled the sculpture in plaster, and this bronze was cast in 1950, long after his death in 1916.
VAULT-829: Boccioni modelled this striding figure in plaster in 1913. He was a leading artist of Italian Futurism, a movement that took speed and modern machinery as its subjects. He died in 1916 after a fall from a horse during army training, and the bronze casts were all made after his death. This one dates from 1950.
VAULT-830: This set of lithographs from 1923 shows different arrangements of three heads, each printed in a single colour. The tones were made by spattering lithographic ink onto the stone from a brush. Oskar Schlemmer taught at the Bauhaus in the 1920s and also designed for the stage.
VAULT-831: Modigliani was born in Livorno and moved to Paris in 1906. Most of his paintings are portraits and nudes with long necks and faces. This one dates from about 1918 or 1919, shortly before his death in Paris in January 1920 at the age of thirty-five.
VAULT-832: Modigliani painted this portrait in 1918. He was an Italian painter and sculptor who had lived in Paris since 1906, and he spent much of 1918 and 1919 in the south of France. He died in Paris in January 1920.
VAULT-833: The sculptor Jacques Lipchitz commissioned this double portrait in 1916 to mark his marriage to the poet Berthe Kitrosser. He also meant the commission as a way to help Modigliani, a friend who was short of money. Both artists were then working in Paris.
VAULT-834: Robert Delaunay was a French painter who took modern Paris as a subject from about 1909 onward. This lithograph of 1926 shows the bridges over the Seine and the cathedral of Notre-Dame. With his wife, the artist Sonia Delaunay, he developed a style of abstract painting built on contrasts of colour.
VAULT-835: The Eiffel Tower was the subject Robert Delaunay returned to most often. He first painted it in 1909 and went on drawing and painting it for the rest of his career. This lithograph was made in 1926.
VAULT-836: José Guadalupe Posada was a Mexican printmaker who illustrated cheap broadsides, songbooks and news sheets in Mexico City. He is best known for his calaveras, skeletons dressed as the living. This is a zincograph, a print from a zinc plate etched in relief so it could be set alongside type.
VAULT-837: Emiliano Zapata led a peasant army in the state of Morelos during the Mexican Revolution, which began in 1910. Posada made this portrait in the last years of his life, and this sheet is a later impression from his plate. Posada died in Mexico City in 1913 and Zapata was killed in 1919.
VAULT-838: Charles Demuth painted this watercolour about 1923 in his home town of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, while he was ill with diabetes. He drew the flower in graphite, then brushed on the colour and used a blotter to give it texture. The museum bought it from its first exhibition, at the Daniel Gallery in New York.
VAULT-839: Marsden Hartley was an American painter from Maine. He made this painting in Berlin in 1913, when he was close to the German Expressionists. Like Wassily Kandinsky, he wanted painting to work more like music.
VAULT-840: George Bellows came to New York from Columbus, Ohio, in 1904 and studied under the painter Robert Henri. He is linked with the Ashcan School, a group that painted everyday life in the city. This view of the Hudson River dates from 1908.
VAULT-841: In January 1914 Bellows wrote to a friend that there had been no snow to paint that winter. A blizzard reached New York City soon afterward, and this painting followed. It shows skaters and onlookers out in the cold.
VAULT-842: Bellows painted this portrait in July 1915 in Ogunquit, Maine. Rain kept him indoors for much of that summer, and he turned to portraits. The sitter's name is not known.
VAULT-843: Fernand Khnopff was a Belgian painter and draughtsman of the Symbolist movement. He was a founding member of Les XX, the exhibiting society formed in Brussels in 1883. He made this drawing about 1887 in charcoal and graphite, softening the tones by rubbing.
VAULT-844: Henri Rousseau taught himself to paint while working as a toll collector for the city of Paris. He retired in 1893 to paint full time, and this view of the edge of the city dates from about that time. He showed his work each year at the Salon des Indépendants, which had no jury.
VAULT-845: Rousseau never left France. He built his jungle scenes from travel books and visits to the botanical garden in Paris. He was working on this painting in December 1907 while in prison for fraud, and was released early to finish it for the Salon des Indépendants, where it was shown in March 1908.
VAULT-846: This lithograph of 1893 shows Bonnard's sister Andrée with her infant son Jean, born the year before. Bonnard put himself at the lower right, looking at his nephew. The print was published in L'Estampe originale, a Paris publication of original prints issued in the 1890s.
VAULT-847: Édouard Vuillard was a French painter and a member of the Nabis, a group formed in Paris around 1890. He is known for interiors and for large decorative paintings made for the homes of friends and patrons. This landscape dates from 1899.
VAULT-848: This is one of nine panels Vuillard painted in 1894 showing children at play in two Paris parks, the Tuileries Gardens and the Bois de Boulogne. A girl hides behind a tree in a game of hide-and-seek while women sit on green chairs. Vuillard also designed scenery, costumes and programmes for the theatre.
VAULT-849: Vallotton based this painting of 1899 on a photograph of his own household. He was born in Lausanne, moved to Paris as a young man and married there in 1899. Étretat is a resort town on the Normandy coast.
VAULT-850: Vallotton designed, cut and printed his own woodcuts, and in the 1890s they were the work he was best known for. Woodcut had fallen out of use among artists by the middle of the nineteenth century, and he helped revive it. This print of 1896 uses only black and white.
VAULT-851: Around 1900 Vallotton turned from printmaking to oil painting, and this landscape was made that year. He was born in Switzerland and worked in France. In 1892 he had joined the Nabis, a circle of painters in Paris.
VAULT-852: The Wiener Werkstätte, or Vienna Workshops, was founded in Vienna in 1903 by the architect Josef Hoffmann and the designer Koloman Moser. It made furniture, metalwork, textiles and other goods until it closed in 1932. This linen was block printed between 1903 and 1905, in the workshop's first years.
VAULT-853: Liubov Popova was a Russian painter who gave up easel painting in the early 1920s for design. In 1923 and 1924 she drew patterns for printed cloth for the First State Textile Printing Factory in Moscow. This design, probably for a textile, dates from those years. She died in Moscow in 1924.
VAULT-854: In 1919 Kurt Schwitters began a kind of art he called Merz, a syllable cut from an advertisement for a bank. This is one of six lithographs in a portfolio of 1923, made at a printing plant in Hanover. He made collages there from freshly printed scrap paper and transferred them to the lithographic stone while the ink was still wet.
VAULT-855: Paula Modersohn-Becker settled in 1898 in Worpswede, an artists' colony on the moors near Bremen. She drew this charcoal study of trees there about 1900 to 1902. She died in Worpswede in 1907 at the age of thirty-one.
VAULT-856: Paula Modersohn-Becker was a German painter who worked in the artists' colony of Worpswede, near Bremen, and made several long stays in Paris. She painted this still life about 1902 on board. She died in 1907 at the age of thirty-one.
VAULT-857: Matisse painted this between 1921 and 1923, when he was living in Nice. He had earlier visited exhibitions of Islamic art and travelled to Algeria and Morocco, where he collected pottery, textiles and tiles. The patterned screen behind the woman comes from those interests.
VAULT-858: Matisse was forty-five when the First World War began, and the army turned him down for service. He kept painting through the war years, trying out new ways of composing and handling paint. This still life dates from 1916.
VAULT-859: Louis Marcoussis was born Louis Casimir Ladislas Markus in Warsaw and moved to Paris in 1903. There he met Georges Braque, Pablo Picasso and the poet Guillaume Apollinaire, who urged him to take the name of a French village. This Cubist painting of about 1923 shows a table from several viewpoints at once.
VAULT-860: Ferdinand Hodler was a Swiss painter, born in Bern, who spent his working life in Geneva. From the 1890s he painted large compositions of symbolic figures. This canvas dates from between 1896 and 1898.
VAULT-946: A mask of hammered sheet gold made on the north coast of Peru between about 900 and 1100 by metalworkers of the Lambayeque culture, also called Sicán. Its face is painted red with cinnabar. Masks of this kind were attached to the wrapped bodies of high-ranking people in their tombs.
VAULT-947: A mask of cartonnage, layers of linen or papyrus stiffened with plaster, covered in gold leaf and paint. It was made in Egypt in the first century BC, probably at Hawara, to cover the head and chest of a mummy. Along the bottom the god Osiris sits enthroned between birds that stand for the goddesses Isis and Nephthys.
VAULT-948: A grey earthenware figure made in northern China in the 500s to be placed in a tomb. It stands for the ox, one of the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac, which mark years in a repeating cycle. Sets of the twelve animals were buried with the dead.
VAULT-949: Posada drew this skeleton figure of Francisco Madero, who led the uprising of 1910 against Porfirio Díaz and was president of Mexico from 1911 until he was killed in 1913. Posada died the same year in Mexico City. This impression was printed in 1944, when the Art Institute of Chicago held an exhibition of his work.
VAULT-950: Franz Marc painted these three blue horses in Bavaria in 1911. That year he and Wassily Kandinsky founded the Blue Rider group in Munich. Marc was killed at Verdun in 1916 while serving in the German army.
VAULT-951: Egon Schiele painted this self-portrait in Vienna in 1912, when he was twenty-two. He made a portrait of his companion Wally Neuzil the same year as its pair, and the two hang together in Vienna. Schiele died in the influenza epidemic of 1918.
VAULT-952: Velázquez painted this in Madrid in the later 1650s for Pedro de Arce, a huntsman to King Philip IV. Women spin and wind wool in the foreground, and in the room behind is the contest between the goddess Athena and the weaver Arachne from Ovid. Strips of canvas were added to its edges in the eighteenth century.
VAULT-953: Gauguin painted this in Tahiti in 1897 and 1898 on a length of coarse sackcloth. He wrote the title in French in the upper left corner and signed and dated it in the upper right. It was sent to Paris and shown at Ambroise Vollard's gallery in 1898.
VAULT-955: Timothy O'Sullivan took this photograph of dead soldiers on the battlefield at Gettysburg in July 1863, a few days after the fighting. Alexander Gardner printed it and published it in Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the War in 1866. O'Sullivan later photographed the American West for government surveys.
VAULT-956: Hugo Simberg finished this painting in Helsinki in 1903. The path the two boys walk follows the shore of Töölö Bay in the city. He painted a larger version as a fresco in Tampere Cathedral in 1905 and 1906. In 2006 visitors to the Ateneum voted it Finland's national painting.
VAULT-957: James Ensor painted this small panel in Ostend in 1891. Skeletons and masks appear throughout his work of these years; his family kept a souvenir shop in Ostend that sold carnival masks. The French for pickled herring, hareng saur, sounds like art Ensor.
VAULT-958: Arnold Böcklin, a Swiss painter born in Basel in 1827, made this self-portrait in Munich in 1872. A skeleton plays a violin at his shoulder, an old motif in German and Swiss art. Later painters including Lovis Corinth made self-portraits with skeletons after it.
VAULT-959: Klimt painted this in Vienna in 1901, using gold leaf with oil paint. It shows Judith, the widow in the biblical Book of Judith who beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes. The metal frame carries the title in German and was made by his brother Georg Klimt. It is also known as Judith I, since he painted a second Judith in 1909.
VAULT-960: Munch painted this in 1899 and 1900. It belongs to the group of paintings he called the Frieze of Life. The dancers are on the shore at Åsgårdstrand, the village on the Oslo Fjord where he spent his summers.
VAULT-961: Hilma af Klint painted The Ten Largest in Stockholm in 1907, ten pictures each about three metres tall on the stages of human life. They are part of a cycle she called the Paintings for the Temple. She died in 1944 and asked that her abstract work not be shown for twenty years after her death.
VAULT-962: Rossetti painted several versions of this subject; this one is dated 1874 and was bought by the shipowner Frederick Leyland. Jane Morris was the model. Proserpine is the Roman goddess held in the underworld for part of each year after eating pomegranate seeds there. Rossetti wrote a sonnet in Italian for the picture and painted it on the canvas.
VAULT-963: Giorgione painted this in Venice in the first decade of the 1500s. The Venetian writer Marcantonio Michiel saw it in 1530 in the house of Gabriele Vendramin and described it as a small landscape with a storm, a gypsy woman and a soldier. Its subject has never been settled.
VAULT-964: Leonardo painted two versions of this altarpiece. In 1483 a confraternity in Milan commissioned it for their chapel in the church of San Francesco Grande. The earlier version is in the Louvre in Paris; this is the later one, worked on from the 1490s and finished in 1508, which hung in the chapel.
VAULT-965: Hugo Simberg painted this small picture in 1896, when he was twenty-three. Skeletons in black robes water and tend plants in a garden. He painted a larger version as a fresco in Tampere Cathedral in 1905 and 1906.
VAULT-966: Bosch painted this tall, narrow panel in the Netherlands around 1485 to 1490. It was once the wing of a folding altarpiece that has since been taken apart; other pieces of it are in Paris, New Haven and Rotterdam. Death enters at the door while an angel and a demon contend for the dying man.
VAULT-967: Cézanne painted this still life of four skulls in his last years at Aix-en-Provence. Skulls appear in several of his oils and watercolours from 1898 until his death in 1906. He kept skulls in his studio at Aix.
VAULT-968: Bouguereau painted this in Paris in 1850, when he was twenty-four, and showed it at the Salon. The scene is from Canto 30 of Dante's Inferno, where Dante and Virgil watch Gianni Schicchi attack the alchemist Capocchio in the circle of the falsifiers. Bouguereau won the Prix de Rome the same year.
VAULT-969: Willem Claesz. Heda painted this still life in Haarlem in 1628, and it is among his earliest dated works. A skull, an overturned glass, a pipe and a brazier of coals stand for the shortness of life, the theme of the vanitas pictures painted in the Dutch Republic. Heda went on to specialise in tabletop still lifes in a narrow range of greys and browns.
VAULT-970: Caravaggio painted this in Malta in 1607 or 1608, during the year he spent with the Knights of Saint John. The coat of arms at the lower right is that of Ippolito Malaspina, a senior knight of the order. The painting was stolen from the cathedral in Valletta in 1984 and recovered a few years later.
VAULT-971: Vereshchagin painted this in 1871 after travelling with the Russian army in Central Asia, as part of his Turkestan series. The pyramid of skulls draws on accounts of the conqueror Timur. On the frame he wrote a dedication to all great conquerors, past, present and to come. He died in 1904 when the battleship he was aboard struck a mine in the Russo-Japanese War.
VAULT-972: Mantegna was court painter to the Gonzaga family in Mantua from 1460 until his death in 1506. He painted this in tempera on canvas, with the body of Christ seen feet first and sharply foreshortened. A painting of this description was found in his studio when he died.
VAULT-973: Max Klinger was a German printmaker, painter and sculptor from Leipzig. Eve and the Future is a series of six etchings he published in 1880, and this is the last plate. The series alternates scenes of Eve in Eden with visions of what follows the Fall.
VAULT-974: A photograph taken at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, in July 1863, in the days after the battle. It shows dead soldiers lying on the field. Major General John F. Reynolds of the Union army was killed there on the first day of fighting. Alexander Gardner published the picture in his Photographic Sketch Book of the War in 1866.
LIT-828: To the Lighthouse is Virginia Woolf's fifth novel, published by the Hogarth Press in London in 1927. This passage comes from the third part, where the painter Lily Briscoe returns to the Ramsays' summer house on the Isle of Skye and takes up a picture she had left unfinished ten years earlier.
LIT-829: Orlando: A Biography was published by the Hogarth Press in 1928. Its hero begins as a young nobleman in the reign of Elizabeth I, lives for more than three hundred years and becomes a woman partway through. Woolf dedicated the book to Vita Sackville-West.
LIT-830: Tolstoy wrote A Confession between 1879 and 1882, after finishing Anna Karenina. The Russian censor stopped its publication in 1882, and it was first printed in Geneva in 1884. The fable he retells here is an old one found in the legend of Barlaam and Josaphat.
LIT-831: The Hollow Men was first printed complete in T. S. Eliot's Poems 1909-1925, published in London by Faber and Gwyer in 1925. It has five numbered sections, and this is the last. Eliot was born in St. Louis, Missouri, and had lived in England since 1914.
LIT-832: This is the last of the fifty-two sections of Song of Myself, the poem that opened the first edition of Leaves of Grass in 1855. Whitman revised the book through several editions until 1892. The poem had no title in 1855 and was given its present name in the 1881 edition.
LIT-833: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner opened Lyrical Ballads, the collection Coleridge and Wordsworth published together in 1798. Coleridge revised the poem for later editions and added marginal notes in 1817. These stanzas come from Part IV, after the crew have died and the Mariner is left alone on the ship.
LIT-834: These are the closing lines of The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock. The poem was first printed in Poetry magazine in Chicago in June 1915, at the urging of Ezra Pound, and gave its name to Eliot's first book, Prufrock and Other Observations, in 1917.
LIT-835: Bai Juyi was a Tang dynasty official and one of the most widely read Chinese poets. In 815 he was sent away from the capital to a minor post at Xunyang on the Yangtze, where this poem is set. Arthur Waley's English version appeared in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems in 1918.
LIT-836: Bai Juyi lived from 772 to 846 and served as an official under several Tang emperors. Annam was the Chinese name for the region that is now northern Vietnam. Arthur Waley's English version appeared in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems in 1918.
LIT-837: Acquainted with the Night was collected in Robert Frost's West-Running Brook, published in New York by Henry Holt in 1928. It has fourteen lines in terza rima, the interlocking three-line rhyme scheme Dante used for the Divine Comedy.
LIT-838: The Emperor of Ice-Cream first appeared in The Dial in July 1922 and was collected the next year in Harmonium, Wallace Stevens's first book, published by Alfred A. Knopf. Stevens worked as a lawyer for an insurance company in Hartford, Connecticut, and was forty-three when the book came out.
LIT-839: These lines come from the preface to Milton, a poem Blake wrote, etched and printed himself; its title page is dated 1804. Hubert Parry set them to music in 1916, and under the name Jerusalem they became one of the best-known hymns in England.
LIT-840: Emily Brontë dated this poem 13 December 1836, when she was eighteen and living at the parsonage in Haworth, on the edge of the Yorkshire moors. It was not printed in her lifetime and was first published from her manuscripts in the early twentieth century.
LIT-841: Bashō wrote this verse in Edo around 1680. The bird of the original, karasu, is usually translated as crow; Basil Hall Chamberlain, whose 1902 version this is, wrote rooks. According to Chamberlain the verse was inscribed on a sketch of crows on a leafless branch.
LIT-842: Bashō wrote this verse in 1690, while he was staying in a hut in the hills above Lake Biwa. According to Chamberlain, whose 1902 translation this is, it was his parting word to a visitor there. Bashō died four years later in Osaka.
LIT-843: Matsuo Bashō lived from 1644 to 1694 and spent much of his later life travelling Japan on foot. This verse is one of the specimens Basil Hall Chamberlain translated in his 1902 paper on Bashō for the Asiatic Society of Japan, one of the first long studies of the haiku in English.
LIT-844: These are the opening lines of a ghazal from the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi, the large collection of lyric poems Rumi composed in Persian at Konya and named for his teacher Shams of Tabriz. R. A. Nicholson of Cambridge printed it as number 35 in his 1898 selection, with the Persian text facing the English.
LIT-845: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, an Italian poet living in Milan, published the founding manifesto of Futurism in French on the front page of the Paris newspaper Le Figaro on 20 February 1909. This English version was printed in the catalogue of the Futurist painters' exhibition at the Sackville Gallery in London in March 1912. The manifesto has eleven numbered points; the first eight are shown.
LIT-846: Sullivan Ballou was a lawyer from Rhode Island and a major in the Second Rhode Island Infantry. He wrote this letter to his wife Sarah from Camp Clark in Washington on 14 July 1861, and was mortally wounded a week later at the First Battle of Bull Run. The original letter has not survived, and the printed versions differ slightly in wording.
LIT-847: Kafka wrote A Hunger Artist in 1922 and it was first printed that October in the Berlin magazine Die neue Rundschau. It became the title story of the last book he prepared for the press, which he was correcting in proof when he died in June 1924. The story follows a professional faster who performs in a cage for paying crowds.
LIT-848: A Room of One's Own grew out of two lectures on women and fiction that Virginia Woolf gave at Newnham and Girton, the women's colleges at Cambridge, in October 1928. The Hogarth Press published the expanded text as a book in October 1929. This passage comes from its opening pages.
